Issue Reading note
The November 2022 Indicor divestiture recast the whole history Indicor is reported as discontinued operations for all periods presented. The current continuing-operations basis exists only from FY2020; FY2016–FY2018 are fully pre-divestiture and FY2019 is on a third basis of its own. The -8.9% FY2019 and -14.9% FY2020 "revenue declines" in a naive ten-year series are divestiture accounting, and segment data on the three-segment basis does not exist before FY2020.
FY2025 margins overstate two of three segments' current run-rate Network Software segment operating margin was 41.0% in Q2 2026 against 43.5% for FY2025 and a 45.2% FY2024 peak; Technology Enabled Products was 33.3% against 34.5%. Only Application Software improved. Anchoring on FY2025 overstates the present by 250bp and 120bp respectively.
The share count broke a twelve-year pattern in three quarters Diluted weighted-average shares rose every year from 100.9m (2014) to 108.2m (FY2025), then declined to 100.6m in Q2 2026 after $3,224m of repurchases. Any per-share series spanning Q4 2025 needs the share count stated beside it.
GAAP earnings in FY2026 are dominated by a private-stake mark Q2 2026 GAAP diluted EPS of $11.62 against adjusted $5.38 is almost entirely an $828.6m Level 3 fair-value gain on Roper's retained 43.4% of Indicor. Management has said all future Indicor impacts will be excluded from non-GAAP results in every future period.

Two disclosure conventions in Roper's filings are easy to misread:

  • "Reoccurring" is a distinct disclosed revenue stream, not a misspelling of recurring. It is transactional and volume-based fees, largely integrated payments, and it grew from $401m (FY2023) to $833m (FY2025). Its gross margin is much lower, so mix explains segment gross-margin moves that otherwise look like operating deterioration.
  • Two different segment margins circulate under one name. The 10-K and 10-Q segment operating margin is after acquired-intangible amortization (FY2025: Application Software 26.8%, Network Software 43.5%, Technology Enabled Products 34.5%). The segment EBITDA margin management quotes on calls is before it (42.5%, 54.1%, 35.7%). Both exclude unallocated corporate general and administrative expense plus enterprise-wide stock-based compensation, $290m in FY2025 or 3.7% of revenue. Every margin below uses the filed basis unless labelled otherwise.

1. Business description, model and unit economics

Roper owns 29 businesses, 21 of them software, and runs them from a corporate centre of about 130 people out of roughly 19,400 employees (CEO Neil Hunn, Citi Global TMT conference, 2026-09-10; 10-K FY2025, Human Capital Management). Each business sells the system of record, the data network or the engineered device for one narrow profession: practice and financial management for large law firms, contract accounting for government contractors, agency management for property and casualty insurance brokers, load matching for freight brokers and truckers, water meters for municipal utilities.▪ Buyers are operating executives at organisations with no meaningful IT function. No customer was 10% or more of any segment or of total revenue in 2025 (10-K FY2025, Customers), and distribution runs through direct sales offices, manufacturers' representatives, resellers and distributors.

FY2025 revenue was $7,903m across three reportable segments, classified by business model and delivery of performance obligations:

The reoccurring line's growth rates are acquired revenue arriving, not organic volume. Procare closed February 2024 and Transact August 2024; with both fully in the prior-year base, Application Software reoccurring revenue grew 4.1% in Q1 2026 and 0.7% in Q2 2026, 2.5% for the half▪ (10-Q Q2 2026, Note 13). Across the two software segments, management's own organic cut of the streams in Q2 2026 was +7% recurring, -2% reoccurring and -4% non-recurring (Q2 2026 call, CFO Jason Conley).

The sign flipped inside twelve months. Organic reoccurring revenue grew 5% for Roper and 5% for Network Software in FY2025. In Q2 2026 it declined 2% for Roper and 4% for Network Software, while reported reoccurring revenue still grew 8% and 20%. Every dollar of growth in the fastest-growing disclosed revenue category is now acquired.▪ [deck: Q4 2025, 2026-01-27, slide 21; deck: Q2 2026, 2026-07-23, slide 18]

1.1 Application Software — twelve systems of record, $4,483m

Twelve businesses sell the transactional record for one profession each: Aderant (law firms), Deltek (government contractors and project-based businesses), Vertafore (property and casualty insurance distribution), Clinisys and Data Innovations (clinical and diagnostic laboratories), Strata (hospital financial planning), Frontline (K-12 administration), Procare (early-childhood education), Transact/CBORD, rebranded Illumia in March 2026 (campus commerce and tuition payments), CentralReach (applied-behaviour-analysis therapy), PowerPlan (regulated utilities) and IntelliTrans (bulk commodity logistics).

The alternative at the point of purchase is one or two other vertical systems that already encode the same compliance rules: DCAA-compliant job-cost accounting for Deltek Costpoint, state producer-licensing rules for Vertafore Sircon, CLIA and CAP laboratory workflow for Clinisys, payer-specific ABA billing codes for CentralReach. Penetration inside those niches is high. Deltek serves 98% of the top 100 federal contractors and 95% of the top 100 architecture and engineering firms; Vertafore serves 100 of the top 100 brokers, 66 of the top 100 on an agency management system, and 96 of the top 100 property and casualty carriers; Strata plus Syntellis reach about 70% of US health systems▪ (Investor Day 2023 deck, slides 53, 83; Q3 2023 call).

What sets price. The CFO stated the recurring equation on the Q3 2024 call: "we have 95-or-so percent gross retention. So we're going to attrit 5-or-so percent. We're going to offset the vast majority of that at each business unit level with price. It's just in the algorithm... Then obviously a cross-sell and upsell from there to get you net retention in the 105-ish range across the blended enterprise, and we have net new on top of that." Price replaces churn; it does not expand take.▪ Asked in April 2026 how much more price was available, Hunn put the whole software portfolio's opportunity at "50 or 100 basis points... over the next couple of 3 years" (Q1 2026 call).

Two disclosures pin the attrition term. Management repeats mid-90s enterprise gross retention on every recent call, and purchase accounting assigns customer-relationship useful lives of 18 years (Transact), 19 (CentralReach) and 20 (Procare), which on a straight-line basis implies 5.0-5.6% annual attrition (10-K FY2025, Note 2). The per-business disclosures from the March 2023 Investor Day are higher and lower than the blend: Deltek 97% gross retention excluding data subscriptions, up from 93% at the 2016 acquisition; Vertafore 92% gross and 108% net, up from 91% and 105%; Aderant 113% net, up from 102%. CentralReach is the one case with a second cut, and it matters: mid-to-high 90s on logos, low 90s when clinician seats are counted, with net retention of 115-120% (Q1 2025 call). The seat is the billing unit.

The build gives $1,417m of cost of sales against $1,413m reported, 0.3% high. The payments margin was bounded two ways. The FY2024 10-K states that Procare and Transact together reduced segment gross margin by 180 basis points and segment SG&A by 70 basis points; solving for their combined revenue and margins gives a blended 45–52% gross margin for the pair. Isolating the payments portion, using Procare's disclosed "75% or so... payments" mix (Q1 2024 call) and assuming half for Transact, gives a payments gross margin of 32–42%. Card-acquiring arithmetic from outside the filings lands in the same place: a 2.9% merchant discount against 1.9% of interchange and network cost produces about 34%.

Stripping the payments stream at a 37% gross margin, the rest of Application Software expanded from 70.3% (FY2023) to 72.6% (FY2025), 230 basis points, and to 73.4% in Q2 2026, while reported segment gross margin moved 90 basis points. The direction survives the assumption: at a 32% payments margin the FY2023-25 expansion is 270bp, at 42% it is 190bp.

The drivers reconcile to the reported rate. Recurring plus reoccurring is about 85% of the segment and grew in the mid-single-digit-plus range organically in Q2 2026, while non-recurring at about 15% declined low single digits: 0.85 × 6.0 + 0.15 × (−2.0) = 4.8%, matching the reported H1 2026 organic figure. And it explains the deceleration from 7.5% (FY2022) to 5.4% (FY2025) and 4.5% in Q2 2026. Price escalation holds. Seat counts are flat to shrinking in the two largest verticals. Payments stopped growing organically. Licences are in structural decline. Only CentralReach's clinician count compounds at a double-digit rate, and it is about 3% of the segment.▪

What drives the cost curve. A marginal subscription dollar costs about 29 cents in hosting, support and delivery; a marginal payments dollar costs about 63 cents in interchange, network and sponsor-bank fees; a marginal licence dollar consumes implementation services and little else. Below the gross line, segment depreciation and other amortization of $702m equals 15.7% of segment revenue, against capital spending of $79m. Realized incremental EBITDA margin over FY2023-25 was 40.2%, below the segment's own 42.5% average and below the "45%+ operating leverage" management published at the 2023 Investor Day▪ (slide 117). That 40.2% is Application Software alone, struck on segment EBITDA, which excludes the corporate expense and the other two segments; the consolidated measure on management's own adjusted definition is lower in every year since the algorithm was published, and §10.3 gives the series. Acquired revenue arrives at roughly half the segment's operating margin, so a higher acquisition rate pushes reported leverage further below the stated algorithm.

1.2 Network Software — nine data networks, $1,601m

Nine businesses sell access to a network or a proprietary data set: DAT (freight load matching, with Loadlink, Trucker Tools, Outgo and Convoy), ConstructConnect (pre-construction project data and takeoff), iPipeline (life insurance and annuity distribution), MHA (alternate-site group purchasing), SoftWriters (long-term-care pharmacy operating system), SHP (post-acute benchmarking), iTradeNetwork (perishable-food supply chain), Foundry (visual-effects compositing) and Subsplash (faith-based engagement and giving).

The segment is described externally as transactionally priced two-sided networks. The disclosed split is narrower: transaction-priced revenue was 19.4% of the segment in FY2025 and 19.6% in Q2 2026, while subscription-type recurring revenue was 72.1% and 72.9%.▪ Management describes DAT itself in subscription terms: "the way DAT's business works, as you know, it's mainly on the carrier front. It's monthly subscriptions" (Q2 2026 call).

Business-line weights. Roper does not disclose revenue for any of the nine. Two decompositions of disclosed organic growth give a range for the freight businesses. On the Q4 2024 call management said that excluding freight matching and Foundry the segment "grew in the mid-singles area" in FY2024, when segment revenue grew $36m entirely organically; solving that identity puts freight match plus Foundry at 17–31% of FY2023 revenue. Running the same equation on the FY2022 boom, when segment revenue grew 12.7% organically and "growth was led by our freight matching businesses," puts freight match alone at 15–35% of FY2021 revenue. Taking Foundry at $85–105m, the DAT complex works out at roughly $290–420m of FY2025 revenue, 18–26% of the segment▪ [estimate: algebraic decomposition of disclosed organic growth against management's own ex-freight statements; ±25% on any single line].

The 2025 acquisitions are tighter. Two disclosed acquisition-contribution percentages — 4.4 points on the FY2025 base and 8.1 points on the H1 2026 base — solve day-weighted to put Subsplash plus Convoy at roughly $110–115m of annual revenue, with Subsplash at roughly $80–100m against its disclosed $800m purchase price.

What sets price. Tier migration is the largest of three mechanisms: "like 70% of the ARPU increase has been because customers have elected to a higher package because there's been more value to sort of get from the network" (Q3 2022 call). Conversion uplift is the second: perpetual and maintenance customers moving to subscription pay 2–2.5x the prior maintenance fee (Investor Day 2023), and every new commercial Nuke licence has been subscription-only since the end of 2023. Take rates and volume fees are the third: MHA's administrative fee, Subsplash's payment spread, Outgo's factoring fee, Convoy's per-delivered-load fee.

DAT's published tiers are the only realized price points available anywhere in the segment, and they are published list prices: DAT One carrier plans run about $45 a month (Express) to $345 a month (Pro Premium), broker plans about $159 to $449 a month, with 30 days' notice on monthly plans [web, accessed 2026-09-11]. Set against a dry-van spot linehaul rate of $2.21 per mile in early September 2026 (dat.com, accessed 2026-09-11) [web], a top-tier carrier subscription costs roughly one to two 800-mile loads of gross revenue a year. The subscription is not the constraint on a carrier's decision.

Building cost of sales up from those rows gives $220–295m against $255m reported (10-K FY2025, Note 14). It reconciles because almost nothing in this segment's cost of sales scales with a physical unit. The one variable input is interchange on the payments stream, which is why gross margin moves when a payments business is acquired and barely moves otherwise. Solving the disclosed FY2025 gross-margin decline from 85.0% to 84.1% against the disclosed 4.4-point acquisition contribution implies the acquired revenue entered at a 59–64% gross margin, consistent with roughly half of Subsplash being payments at 25–40% and half SaaS at about 80%.

Donations to congregations (Subsplash) Dollars donated to US congregations × the digital share × the card-versus-ACH mix 2–3% Zero organic contribution until Q4 2026 New

Two drivers management leads with do not show up in the realized numbers. The first is the network effect. Over FY2023-25 the network grew in absolute scale while segment organic growth decelerated from 12.7% to 2.5% and partly recovered to 4.1%, and Roper's own explanation names the cause: "our freight matching businesses are navigating a drawdown of carriers following exceptional marketplace growth over 2021 and 2022, which is mixing down the growth rate for the segment" (Q4 2023 call). Revenue moved with the count of paying carriers, so the count of paying carriers is the volume driver. The second is transaction monetisation. Convoy, Outgo and Trucker Tools were bought to move DAT from subscription to per-transaction economics — "With Convoy, DAT is evolving into a full end-to-end agentic and ML-powered marketplace, participating in the workflow and the economics of the transaction itself" (Q1 2026 call). The segment's reoccurring stream grew $47m over FY2023-25 and most of that increment is Subsplash payments. As of Q2 2026 the transactional pivot has product evidence and no revenue evidence, and management says why adoption is slow: "you're having to do a change management in the workflow about how loads are brokered. There's a human element of that" (Q2 2026 call).

Operating leverage, and where it came from. Realized incremental operating margin was 61% (FY2021), 60% (FY2022), 101% (FY2023), 94% (FY2024), 23% (FY2025) and 16% in Q2 2026. The readings above 90% are not leverage on growth. Segment SG&A dollars declined from $593m to $588m in FY2024 while revenue grew $36m, and the 10-K attributes the improvement to "expense reductions resulting from cost structure rationalization at our businesses serving the freight match market and operating leverage on higher organic revenues." On the measure that strips acquisitions, core segment margin moved −10bp (FY2025), −20bp (Q1 2026) and +30bp (Q2 2026). Flat core margin on 4-5% organic growth means the marginal organic dollar converts at roughly the average segment EBITDA margin of 51-54%, not at the 84% gross margin: about 30 points of each incremental gross-margin dollar go to sales, engineering and hosting added alongside the revenue.

1.3 Technology Enabled Products — eight device franchises, $1,819m

Eight businesses sell engineered devices with a consumables tail: Verathon (GlideScope video laryngoscopes, BFlex single-use bronchoscopes, BladderScan), Northern Digital (optical and electromagnetic tracking sensors sold into OEM navigation platforms), CIVCO (ultrasound needle guides and probe covers), Neptune (water meters, AMR and AMI endpoints, Muni-Link cloud billing), rf IDEAS (RFID credential readers), Inovonics (wireless life-safety sensor networks), FMI (metering pumps) and IPA (surgical scrub dispensing). Product revenue was $1,773m of the segment's $1,819m in FY2025; the four-way revenue disaggregation does not separate consumables from capital equipment, so the mix shift management discusses every quarter is invisible in the filed tables.

Business-line weights. On the Q4 2024 call the CEO said "Neptune is, I think, something like 40% of the segment," a verbal figure that has never appeared in a filing. Solving the mix identity from disclosed segment organic growth against management's per-business growth descriptions across three quarters gives Neptune at $450–650m, midpoint about $550m [estimate: mix identity, Q4 2025 / Q1 2026 / Q2 2026 calls]. A second check from Badger Meter's 9.0% software attach rate applied to Roper's $46m of TEP recurring software revenue gives $460–660m. Verathon, disclosed at about $350m of 2022 revenue on a "low double digit" growth profile at the 2023 Investor Day, compounds to $465–505m [estimate: disclosed 2022 base at the stated growth profile]. The residual $615–665m covers Northern Digital, CIVCO, IPA, FMI, Inovonics and rf IDEAS, of which Northern Digital is the largest on the evidence of the calls and the only one whose revenue is nowhere disclosed.

Unit economics. Only the Neptune row can be reconciled, and the reconciliation is a consistency check because two unknowns are fitted against one disclosed constraint.

Unit Units/yr Realized price Input cost per unit Gross profit Implied GM

Prices are from the Erie County Water Authority's sole-source contract with Neptune, effective 21 January 2021 through 31 December 2023 at a total value of $6,274,105 (ecwa.org, accessed 2026-09-11) [web]. Neptune at about $700m and a 45% gross margin plus the other seven businesses at a fitted 66% reproduces the reported 58.1% segment gross margin.

What sets price, and what it cannot do. Four features of that contract explain most of Neptune's 2026 margin behaviour. Article 3.03 fixes price for the term: "the unit price for materials and supplies under this Agreement shall remain firm until all materials and goods are delivered. The Manufacturer understands no cost increase shall be charged for any reason whatsoever during the term." Article 1.02.D makes quantities non-binding, so Neptune takes volume risk as well as input risk. The 2021-23 contract was 4% above the contract effective 15 August 2015, roughly 0.7% a year before mix. And the content ladder is priced: 26-42% more per connection for ultrasonic at the same unit volume.

Copper moved from about $4.35 a pound in July 2024 to about $6.59 in August 2026, and the United States imposed a 50% Section 232 tariff on semi-finished copper products from 1 August 2025 (whitecase.com, accessed 2026-09-11) [web]. Neptune attempted a surcharge in July 2025 and withdrew it: "we pushed the... tariff or a raw material sort of surcharge into the market that really had a negative demand impact in the short run. The signal from the customer was... we'd rather do it through regular way pricing versus surcharging," with recovery through list price taking "a couple quarters to sort of work your backlog and get into the market" (Q1 2026 call). Sole-source position protected volume and renewal; it did not shorten the repricing lag.▪ At $4.48 of extra copper on a $155 meter, the raw-metal delta alone is 2.9 points of gross margin on the mechanical residential line, or $8–10m a year across 1.8–2.2m bronze-bodied meters [estimate: units at a 70–85% mechanical mix].

Cost structure. SG&A held between 23.1% and 24.4% of segment revenue across ten consecutive quarters spanning a 20% revenue increase, so this segment's operating margin is set by gross margin less a near-fixed ratio. That caps how much leverage volume alone can deliver and is consistent with a realized five-year incremental operating margin of 33.0% against the 45% EBITDA incremental management cites. Capital spending is 0.6% of segment revenue, depreciation and amortization 1.3%, and inventory of about $142m is effectively the company's whole inventory balance.

2. Key technologies and technical differentiators

Roper does not win on technology. It wins on owning the system of record in markets too small for a large competitor to bother with, and on the switching cost created when a customer configures its own rules, permissions and data inside that system.▪ The purchase-price allocations show it.

When Roper buys a vertical software business, an independent appraiser splits the purchase price across the assets acquired. Across three deals spanning the pre-AI and AI eras, the appraiser assigned the software itself 4-6% of the price and gave it less than half the useful life of the customer relationships▪:

Acquisition Closed Purchase price Customer relationships Technology Technology as % of price
Vertafore 3 Sep 2020 $5,399m $2,230m, 17-year life $310m, 8-year life 5.7%
CentralReach 23 Apr 2025 $1,850m $776m, 19-year life $66m, 6-year life 3.6%
Subsplash 25 Jul 2025 $800m $328m, 17-year life $37m, 6-year life 4.6%

Sources: 10-K FY2020 Note 2 (Vertafore); 10-K FY2025 Note 2 (CentralReach, Subsplash).

CentralReach is the business Roper points to most often as its AI proof point. Its code was valued at $66m against $776m of customer relationships and was assigned a shorter life, six years, than the eight years assigned to Vertafore's pre-AI code five years earlier. Across the whole company at 31 December 2025, identified intangibles at cost were $14,087m, of which customer relationships were $12,302m (87.3%), unpatented technology $880m (6.2%), trade names $896m (6.4%) and patents and other protective rights $9m (0.06%). The 10-K states: "We believe none of our operating units are substantially dependent on any single item of intellectual property, including a trade secret, patent, trademark, trade dress, or copyright."

Roper publishes no research and development expense line. The company-wide research, development and engineering figure of $853m in FY2025 is reported inside SG&A and is not split by segment. Capitalized technology spending is 1.3% of revenue — $47m of capital expenditure plus $57m of capitalized software — against $858m of acquired-intangible amortization, 8.3x as much. Roper buys technology; it does not build much of it on the balance sheet.

Vertical systems of record. Each business owns the transactional record for one workflow: Deltek Costpoint and Vantagepoint for government-contract and project accounting, Vertafore AMS360 and Sagitta for agency management, Aderant Expert Sierra for law-firm time, billing and collection, Clinisys for laboratory information management, PowerPlan for regulated-utility tax and asset accounting. The barrier is the customer's own configuration, not the vendor's code. Hunn's description of Vertafore states the mechanism: "Thousands of customer environments are configured around specific data, products, rules, permissions and processes" (Q2 2026 call). A competitor can write equivalent software; it cannot write the customer's twenty years of rules and historical data into it. Aderant added more than 220 law firms to Expert in the five years to March 2023, 39 of them in the AmLaw 200, and lost none.▪

The substitution threat is a horizontal platform plus a general model that absorbs the vertical rules cheaply enough to make a small market worth entering. The CFO's answer on this is the only competitive-encroachment evidence Roper has offered: "we have had a couple of instances where point solutions have come in, not part of the full workflow, but something that our business didn't do. And we were able to replicate that in a matter of weeks and kind of shut out that competitor" (Oppenheimer conference, 2026-08-11). He named one exposed business without identifying it: "one business that repackages public company information, and it's a data business... We have seen some AI native start-ups there, but they're really nipping at the low end of the customers."

The agentic AI layer. Roper builds task-replacement agents on top of the existing system of record: read an unstructured input, write a structured record into the workflow the customer already uses, hand the exception back to a human. It does not train models. Vertafore's Velocity is the reference implementation, launched 14 April 2026 with six agents embedded in AMS360, Sagitta, BenefitPoint and Surefyre, providing "orchestration, human-in-the-loop controls, and large language model routing" (iireporter.com, accessed 2026-09-11) [web].

The quantified value delivered is management's own time-and-motion work, and none of it is independently audited:

Business Task Before After Price
SoftWriters Long-term-care prescription verification $1–$2 of human labour per script Agent, at "a quality level that's higher than a human" about $0.30 per script
SoftWriters Order entry at a 150-facility customer up to 90 seconds about 18 seconds transactional
DAT / Convoy Broker a spot load about ten phone calls, $100–$200 of broker labour match, close, factoring and reconciliation $40–$60
Vertafore Carrier statement reconciliation 17 minutes 30 seconds credit draw-down
Vertafore Submission processing about an hour about 2 minutes credit draw-down
CentralReach AI-generated session notes 5–10 minutes about 30 seconds per learner

Sources: Q1 2026 and Q2 2026 calls; Goldman Sachs Communacopia and Citi Global TMT, September 2026.

Where the differentiation claim is weakest. Applied Systems, Vertafore's direct private competitor in agency management, announced seven AI products on 8 October 2025, six months before Velocity launched (reinsurancene.ws, accessed 2026-09-11) [web]. The overlap with Vertafore's six agents is close to one for one: Applied Recon against the reconciliation agent, Epic AutoFill and Submissions Manager against submission processing, Epic Bridge against email agent automation, Epic Max against research. Both vendors are incumbents with configured installed bases and proprietary data. The agentic layer separates incumbents from non-incumbents, and does not separate Roper from the competitor that matters most in its second-largest software franchise.▪

Roper's own filings say the same thing. The FY2025 10-K added language absent from FY2024: "The rapid pace of AI advancement may make it difficult to maintain competitive advantages, and AI capabilities could quickly become commoditized, reducing our ability to differentiate our offerings." The Q2 2026 10-Q added a further clause: "New AI offerings may disrupt our offerings or transform workforce needs and may negatively impact demand for our offerings." The phrase "AI-enabled" appears sixteen times in the FY2025 10-K and zero times in the FY2024, FY2023, FY2022 and FY2021 filings.

The AI accelerator team. A central group of about 30 people, grown from two in October 2025, that partners with each operating company on "a continuum from providing consultative support all the way to like working shoulder to shoulder with our technical teams," then moves on (CFO, Citi, 2026-09-10). It is roughly a quarter of Roper's corporate headcount and 0.15% of the company. Twelve to fifteen of the 21 software companies had agentic products in market by September 2026. The claimed development-productivity effect is large: ConstructConnect "moved its entire product and engineering organization into agentic coding processes and tools, shipping 4 times the features versus a year ago" (Q1 2026 call), and enterprise-wide Hunn describes "not 30% to 50% improvement, but multiple fold, like 3x to 5x sort of product velocity."

The cost is disclosed only as a multiple: AI spend is "up about — on an annualized basis, about 3x since January. We've been really pushing. We think it's going to go up by the end of the year" (Q2 2026 call), against an undisclosed base. The team is "maybe the halfway point of where we think that investment is going to be in terms of head count, but probably much higher on spend because we've started at the more senior level." Software-segment core EBITDA margin declined 10 basis points in Q2 2026 "which includes investment in our AI team."

The same push produced a risk disclosure in the Q2 2026 10-Q: "We have experienced, and expect to continue to experience, instances of unauthorized or inadvertent use of AI technologies by personnel, however, such instances have not been material to the Company to date," with the specific exposure named as "the submission of proprietary source code, confidential information, customer information, trade secrets, or other sensitive data to AI systems that are outside our controlled environments." Roper is moving all 21 software businesses onto agentic coding by the end of 2026 while disclosing that source-code exposure incidents have already occurred.

Proprietary vertical data. Hunn's stated theory of what makes an AI winner: "first, you have to be able to take this probabilistic outcome to deterministic. That's largely done with the context and data knowledge graphs that we have across all of our businesses. Then you have to apply that in a workflow with essentially no latency and you have to have the customer trust" (Goldman Sachs, 2026-09-09). The named assets are DAT's freight rate and capacity history, SHP's post-acute benchmarks, ConstructConnect's pre-construction project data and Strata's healthcare cost data. The data accumulates only from operating the workflow, and a new entrant cannot buy it. Roper publishes no record counts, coverage percentages or query volumes, so the evidence is the 84.1% Network Software gross margin and the scale of the DAT network.

Third-party foundation models are a purchased input. The FY2025 10-K names OpenAI, Anthropic, Google and Microsoft as model providers running on Amazon Web Services, Google Cloud Platform, Microsoft Azure and Oracle Cloud, and states: "As AI becomes more central to our offerings, our exposure to pricing changes from these providers increases, and we may not be able to pass such cost increases on to our customers." The four cloud platforms have been named since FY2021; the model providers are new to FY2025. Roper's mitigation is model downgrading and prompt engineering: "we're using local smaller language models, maybe even older versions... at Vertafore, we've taken that cost of goods down meaningfully in a matter of weeks" (Q1 2026 call). The CFO expects agentic gross margins to "start off worse than SaaS, but you can work that down over time" (Oppenheimer, 2026-08-11).

Where the engineering is. Northern Digital sells the sensor and field-generator layer that medical-device OEMs embed in navigation platforms; the OEM builds the catheter or console, and NDI supplies the measurement of where the tip is. The barrier is design-in — once qualified, the sensor is in the OEM's regulatory submission, and changing it means re-validating the platform — plus a physics problem that does not yield to software, since sub-millimetre tracking inside a body in the presence of metal distortion is an accuracy problem.▪ NDI states that nearly 90% of surgical navigation systems on the market incorporate its technology and that it has supplied some OEMs for more than twenty years (surgicalroboticstechnology.com, accessed 2026-09-11) [web, company-sourced]. The independent alternatives named in market summaries are Polhemus, AmfiTrack and Radwave (openpr.com, accessed 2026-09-11) [web]. The substitution threat is image- or impedance-based localization that removes the need for a discrete sensor; electrophysiology mapping systems already combine impedance and magnetic localization, and a shift in weighting would reduce sensor content per catheter.

Verathon's differentiation is benchmarked against an unnamed competitor on its own bench data. The BFlex 2 page claims "Up to 125% better suction than a leading competitor to help manage challenging plugs and viscous secretions" and "Up to 68% lower insertion force than a leading competitor, enabling easier, more controlled tool use," each footnoted "Data on file — Verathon benchtop study" (verathon.com, accessed 2026-09-11) [web]. Roper states Verathon is the US market share leader in single-use bronchoscopes without disclosing a figure (Q4 2025 call).

Neptune's switching cost is the installed endpoint base and its upgrade path. A utility that has installed R900 endpoints can move from automatic meter reading to full advanced metering infrastructure without replacing them, which makes changing vendors expensive in a way the meter itself does not.

Foundry is the one business with a named existential technology risk, and the CEO named it. "If you believe that all high-dollar content is going to be completely generative, then there's not a post-production step to do. So that's like the existential threat for that business" (Goldman Sachs, 2026-09-09). His counter is that generative tools increase computer-generated content volume and therefore compositing volume. Foundry is less than 1% of revenue, under $79m, and returned to year-over-year ARR growth in FY2025 with net retention back above 100% for the first time since the 2023 strikes.

Roadmap exposure. The ground-to-cloud conversion is the largest unshipped-technology dependency in the software segments. Deltek has announced end of support for the on-premise Costpoint government-contracting product in the first quarter of 2028, moving customers to a cloud subscription at "over 2x from maintenance to subscription," across "the next 5 years or so" (Q2 2026 call; Oppenheimer, 2026-08-11). Deltek is Roper's largest maintenance base, and its size is no longer public: the last disclosed split was FY2022, when $900m of $2.9bn of recurring revenue was on-premise maintenance. The FY2025 disaggregation note folds SaaS, post-contract support and annual term licences into one recurring line.

3. Competitive advantages and moat assessment

Roper's own closing claims at its 2023 Investor Day were "Demonstrated ability to improve our businesses," "Disciplined & analytical approach to capital deployment" and "Our culture is a competitive advantage" (slide 118), all three of which are claims about the holding structure and not about any segment. Section 3.4 assesses that structure on its own evidence and reconciles the company-level return on invested capital. One gap bears on what it can conclude: Roper has never published a realized cash-on-cash return, an internal rate of return or a year-five EV/EBITDA for a completed acquisition, so what the corporate centre earns on the price it pays is argued from entry multiples, deployment intensity and four disclosed post-acquisition series.

3.1 Application Software

The advantage is real today and defensible for now, with identified paths to erosion, and the excess return comes from the capital structure of the operating businesses, not from pricing power: management's own description is that price replaces churn.▪

FY2025 segment operating profit was $1,203m on capital expenditure plus capitalized software of $79m, 1.8% of segment revenue. Strip the purchase-accounting goodwill of $15,917m and the acquired intangibles out of the $25,373m of segment assets and the tangible capital employed is roughly $2,000m of receivables, contract assets, capitalized software and property — against which the customer base prepays. Consolidated current deferred revenue was $1,907m and net working capital was negative $1,390m at 12/31/2025. Customers finance the working capital, and growth needs almost no new capital.

Management claims: defensible niche markets where Roper leads or is "a competitive alternative to the market leader"; small markets ("our biggest TAM is about $4 billion a year... Most of our TAMs are $1 billion or less. So the size of the prize is just quite small. It's already very, very well vended, particularly by us and a very small number of competitors"); regulatory specification (18 of 21 software businesses in regulated end markets); a customer with no IT function ("we are the IT budget. Like they don't have Salesforce administrators"); mid-90s gross retention; and a financing-cost edge over the sponsors it buys from ("We borrow at whatever, 5.5% plus or minus, and our competitors borrow at 10% plus or minus in private equity"). Sources: 10-K FY2025 Item 1; Goldman Sachs Communacopia and Citi Global TMT, September 2026.

External sources: RBC cut its target to $398 from $539 and moved to Sector Perform on 2026-01-29, flagging "weaker organic growth expected in the second half of the year," naming Deltek and Procare among three underperformers, and citing "the growing risk from AI across Roper's businesses" (finance.yahoo.com, accessed 2026-09-11) [web]. Unanet positions itself as the mid-market alternative to Deltek Costpoint, winning on usability and speed to value while Costpoint wins on depth and complex contract structures [web, vendor-sourced]. Constellation Software, the structural analogue, grew 4% organically in FY2025 and 3% in Q2 2026 (1% constant currency), so slower organic growth is not company-specific to Roper. The external view and management's view agree on the facts and disagree on the interpretation: both identify Deltek and Procare as the weak points and AI as the live question; management treats AI as market-expanding for incumbents, RBC as a risk. Roper's own risk factors are closer to RBC than to its transcripts.

Ground-up view: minimum efficient scale is low and the prize is small, so entry is not blocked by capital. It is blocked by switching costs that come from the customer's own configuration, and by a regulatory specification that gives a horizontal ERP no reason to build the vertical. Buyer power is low because the customer cannot self-build, cannot run a competitive integration and cannot credibly threaten to switch cheaply. Supplier power is rising in one place: a new usage-priced cost of goods sold from four model providers, in a segment whose gross margin is already flat.

Claimed source Test it must pass What the evidence shows Counter-evidence

Pricing power Realized price outruns input-cost inflation Gross margin held between 68.4% and 69.4% for five years through a cloud transition and a payments mix shift Price is described as offsetting churn, not expanding take; total remaining opportunity put at 50–100 basis points over two to three years; segment operating margin unchanged at 26.8% between FY2021 and FY2025

Roper screens for network effects at acquisition, which implies scarcity inside the portfolio

Return on invested capital. Segment return uses the Note 14 segment operating profit, after acquired-intangible amortization and before the $290m of unallocated corporate expense, taxed at the 20.6% FY2025 effective rate, over segment total assets. Roper does not disclose segment liabilities, so the base is gross and the return is understated against one net of deferred revenue and payables. The reference cost of capital is approximately 8% after tax, from a 5.5% pre-tax marginal borrowing cost taxed at 20.6%, equity at roughly 8.5%, and a 16% debt weight.

Peer return on invested capital is after-tax operating income over total assets less current liabilities, computed identically for every listed company. Excluding goodwill and acquired intangibles, invested capital is negative for Roper consolidated and for Bentley, so the ex-goodwill measure does not discriminate across this cohort.

Over five years the margin gap has stopped widening. Application Software gross margin moved from 69.4% (FY2021) to 68.5% (FY2025) and segment operating margin from 26.8% to 26.8%, across an 89% revenue increase; on the amortization-free basis segment EBITDA margin declined from 43.4% (FY2023) to 42.4% (H1 2026).▪ Over the same span Bentley expanded operating margin 540 basis points, Autodesk 530, Veeva 290, SS&C 180 and Intuit 140. Organic growth decelerated in a straight line: 5.9%, 5.6%, 5.4%, 5.2%, 4.5%. The one measure improving is the return on incremental segment assets, as the 2023-24 acquisitions mature. Most peers also accelerated in the most recent quarter: Veeva, Autodesk, SS&C and Intuit each expanded operating margin more than 200 basis points year over year, and Veeva and Autodesk grew revenue at more than twice Application Software's rate. Tyler and Bentley moved the other way.

Three paths to erosion are named by Roper itself. The CEO said three businesses have a pricing meter that may have to be redesigned because agentic AI reduces the seat count it is billed against, and the two specified for near-term work are property and casualty insurance and legal — Vertafore and Aderant, the segment's two strongest franchises — with Deltek a possible third over a multi-year horizon▪ (Goldman Sachs, 2026-09-09). The first wave of the Vertafore change ships in the first part of 2027, and management describes it as revenue-neutral by design, which removes the upside case from the two businesses most exposed.

Analogues. Constellation Software is the closest public comparison: the same portfolio of first- or second-place vertical systems of record in small regulated markets, funded by group cash flow and serial acquisition. It breaks on price paid — Constellation ended FY2025 with $16,171m of assets on $11,623m of revenue, 1.39x, against Application Software's $25,373m on $4,483m, 5.66x, so Roper capitalizes roughly four times as much balance sheet per revenue dollar for a similar economic asset.▪ Part of that gap reflects Constellation's older, largely amortized asset base and shorter IFRS intangible lives, so four times is a maximum estimate of the price gap. SS&C Technologies is the second analogue, a leveraged serial acquirer of vertical financial-services systems of record with comparable switching costs, breaking on delivery model: services and operations hold its gross margin at 48.2% against 68.5%. Tyler Technologies is the third, a vertical system of record in a regulated end market with a payments attach that mirrors Illumia and Procare, breaking because Tyler grows almost entirely without acquisition.

3.2 Network Software

Network Software earns excess returns today and the position is defensible, but it is open to erosion and the strength is uneven across the nine businesses.▪

The operating economics are close to the best in software: 84.1% gross margin, 43.5% segment operating margin, capital expenditure of $9m on $1,601m of revenue, and negative tangible working capital. Between FY2020 and FY2025 the segment operating margin widened from 35.8% to 43.5%.▪

The strongest evidence is at DAT. Convoy raised roughly $260m in its final round and reached a $3.8bn valuation attempting to replace the brokered spot-freight market with an automated digital brokerage; it ceased operating on 2023-10-19, Flexport bought its technology for about $16m, and DAT bought that technology from Flexport for a reported $250m in July 2025 [web, FreightWaves, GeekWire, TechCrunch, accessed 2026-09-11]. Uber Freight, the other well-capitalised attacker, was still running operating income of about negative 1.5% of gross bookings as of its most recent disclosed quarter. The neutral matching and data layer held its economics while the capital that tried to take the transaction itself was destroyed.▪ DAT's own pricing held through the downturn: carrier counts on the network declined for roughly three years and turned positive only in Q1 2026, and DAT still grew recurring revenue at a mid-single-digit rate on average revenue per user expansion.

Growth, multi-homing and dispersion run the other way. Growth: organic revenue grew 4.6% (FY2023), 2.5% (FY2024), 4.1% (FY2025) and 4.4% in H1 2026. Verisk compounded revenue at 6.2% and MSCI at 13.1% over the five years to FY2025 with far less acquisition contribution. An advantage built on network effects should compound as share and engagement; here it shows up as margin and retention instead. Multi-homing: brokers post loads on DAT and on Truckstop and carriers subscribe to both, and every comparison guide found says so [web, trade press, accessed 2026-09-11]. That is consistent with a scale advantage where the larger board is worth more and the smaller board is still worth paying for, and inconsistent with exclusivity.▪ Dispersion: segment reoccurring revenue grew 20% in total in Q2 2026 and declined 4% organically, which the 10-Q attributes to the alternate-site group purchasing business; iPipeline's non-recurring professional services declined while Vista-backed Zinnia consolidates the life and annuity software stack around it; Foundry declined through FY2024 and into H1 2025. Against those, SoftWriters, ConstructConnect and DAT are performing.

Management's own 2019 framing is narrower than the segment-wide language it later used, and it matches the growth record better. On the Q1 2019 call the CEO distinguished DAT — "it's truly a two-sided network where both sides incrementally gain more value as the size of network improves" — from ConstructConnect and iTradeNetwork, "what we'll call one-sided networks where we need sort of the anchor tenants," whose performance "is driven because of the execution of the software and the sales and the distribution capabilities of the business." The Q1 2020 and Q2 2020 calls described the segment's businesses collectively as having "very strong network effects."

Return on invested capital. Roper discloses no segment liabilities, so invested capital subtracts an estimated share of deferred revenue and accrued liabilities, hair-cut for DAT's monthly billing.

Adding back acquired-intangible amortization of about $162m and deducting capital expenditure gives a cash return of 11.2–11.7%. Roper's realized pre-tax cost of debt in FY2025 was 3.8% ($325m of interest on average total debt of $8,513m), about 3.0% after tax, with debt at 32.0% of total capital; at an 8–9% cost of equity the weighted figure is 6.6–7.5%, and a 7–8% range is used here. Both return measures exceed it. The spread is roughly 150–350 basis points on the reported basis and 350–450 on the cash basis, and the band is that wide because the deferred-revenue allocation is undisclosed.

From FY2023 to FY2025 segment operating profit rose $63m (NOPAT +$50m) while segment assets rose $1,095m, a 4.6% return on the incremental capital. The comparison is unkind to the 2025 deals, which closed mid-year and one of which is loss-making by design — management said Convoy "is an unusual transaction for us as it currently is not profitable." It is still what the capital has earned so far, and it is below the cost of capital.

Allocating Roper's corporate expense at 3.7% of revenue puts Network Software at about 39.8% fully loaded, just below Verisk, Moody's and S&P Global and far above the vertical-software cohort. Capital intensity of 0.6% against Verisk's 7.9% and CoStar's 9.5% is the structural difference: Verisk and CoStar own data-collection infrastructure, while Roper's networks are assembled from what participants post. Growth is where the segment is weakest against the comparables that match its economics.

Through FY2025 the margin evidence favoured Roper without qualification: the segment expanded operating margin 770 basis points from FY2020 and closed most of the gap to the embedded data franchises. The direction reversed in the last three quarters. Segment operating margin went 45.2% (FY2024) to 43.5% (FY2025) to 41.0% (Q2 2026); adjusted EBITDA margin 56.1%, 54.1%, 50.9%.▪ Management puts two causes on it, both of them choices — Subsplash sells integrated giving at a payments-like gross margin and Convoy is being funded to profitability inside DAT — and core margin moved −20bp then +30bp in the two quarters of 2026, so the underlying businesses are holding price. Gross margin says the same more cleanly: 84.3% in Q2 2026 against 83.2% a year earlier.

Analogues. Verisk is the closest comparison: it sells an industry its own pooled data back to it at a 69.9% gross margin and a 43.7% operating margin, the same mechanism as DAT iQ, SHP's benchmarks and ConstructConnect's project database. It breaks because Verisk's standing as a statistical agent with state insurance regulators gives it a legal position none of Roper's networks hold. MSCI at a 54.7% operating margin and 13.1% five-year growth is what the same mechanism looks like when the reference data becomes a contractual benchmark instead of a purchased input; Network Software does not reach it on either measure. CoStar is the cautionary version of the same form: an equally dominant two-sided data marketplace whose FY2025 operating margin was negative 2.2% because it spent the franchise's cash entering an adjacent market.

3.3 Technology Enabled Products

The advantage is real and its arithmetic is exceptional, but its source is not the one management describes.▪

TEP earns a 34.5% segment operating margin — 30.5–30.8% after allocating corporate cost by revenue or by operating-profit share [estimate: pro-rata allocation, 23.0% × $290m = $67m, or 24.8% × $290m = $72m] — and roughly a 30% return on segment assets, against a peer-group median operating margin of 18.8% and median return on invested capital of 9.2%. It produced $2,997m of cumulative operating profit over the six years 2020-2025 while spending $57m of capital expenditure, 1.9 cents of capital per dollar of operating profit, and Roper added $72m of goodwill to the segment across those six years while deploying $8,960m into acquisitions company-wide over 2023-2025 alone. Returns at that level, sustained without reinvestment to defend them, match the strongest franchises.

Pricing power is not the reason. TEP gross margin was 61.5% in 2020 and 56.9% in the first half of 2026, and it has not recovered to the 2020 level in any intervening year.▪ When Neptune tried to pass through the August 2025 copper tariff as a surcharge, customers refused the mechanism, order flow stalled for two quarters, and Roper withdrew it. Ambu, which competes directly with Verathon in single-use bronchoscopy and entered video laryngoscopy with the CE-marked SureSight portfolio in the March 2026 quarter, earned a 60.3% gross margin in that quarter against TEP's 56.9%, and grew its Respiratory business 12.2% organically against TEP's 7.1% (ambu.com, accessed 2026-09-11) [web].

What holds the returns up is switching cost at two of the eight businesses plus an extraordinarily small capital base. At Northern Digital the tracking sensor is designed into another manufacturer's cleared medical device, so replacing it means the OEM re-validates its own product and, depending on the change, re-files.▪ At Verathon the GlideScope system is in more than 6,000 of roughly 6,300 US acute-care facilities and consumes a disposable blade per intubation, about five million blades in 2022, so the installed base produces recurring per-procedure revenue. Neptune is weaker on both counts: it was named fifth among the top five North American water AMI endpoint vendors by installed base (globenewswire.com, accessed 2026-09-11) [web], its revenue declined year over year in each of the first two quarters of 2026, and it is the business where the pricing attempt failed.

Claimed source Test What the evidence shows
Pricing power Realized price outruns input-cost inflation, visible in gross margin Fails. Gross margin 61.5% (2020) → 59.2% → 56.9% → 57.1% → 57.6% → 58.1% (2025) → 56.9% (H1 2026). The July 2025 surcharge was withdrawn
Switching costs, Northern Digital Customer bears a re-qualification cost; relationships persist across decades Passes, on company and vendor evidence. Sensor designed into OEM cleared devices; partnerships "for more than 20 straight years"
Switching costs, Verathon Installed base converts to repeat consumable volume Passes on volume. Present in more than 6,000 of about 6,300 US acute facilities; about 5m single-use devices shipped in 2022; consumables 53% of Verathon revenue in 2022. No price evidence, and the consumable is the lower-gross-margin item
Scale Unit-cost or margin gap widens with volume Passes on operating cost, not on cost of goods. SG&A declined from 26.2% of revenue (2020) to 23.6% (2025) on 56% higher revenue while gross margin declined 3.4 points
Intellectual property Protection concentrated in defensible filings Fails as a stated basis; Roper states no operating unit depends substantially on any single item of intellectual property
Regulation FDA clearance or utility approval excludes entrants Clearance is a cost of entry: Ambu, Medtronic, Karl Storz and Olympus all hold it in airway, and five vendors hold AMI positions in water. It delays; it does not exclude
Distribution Channel access rivals cannot replicate Fails. Direct sales offices, manufacturers' representatives, resellers and distributors, the same channels competitors use

On what TEP charges and what it costs to run, the advantage narrowed by about four points over five years, and every point of it came from peers improving while TEP held: Badger Meter's operating margin rose from 15.3% to 20.0%, Itron's from −0.5% to 13.2% and Xylem's from 7.5% to 13.5%, against TEP's 35.3% to 34.5%. On capital the advantage widened from 12.8 points to 20.5, for a reason unrelated to competition: peers spent five years buying growth and adding purchase price to their balance sheets while TEP's asset base was flat. The return premium is a capital-allocation outcome first and an operating outcome second. An acquirer paying a market price for these eight businesses today would not earn 30%: at 15x FY2025 segment operating profit a buyer would pay about $9.4bn and earn roughly 5% after tax on it.▪

The evidence supports the middle placement: excess returns today, defensible for now, with the attack visible where it is happening. Ambu's CE-marked SureSight portfolio is a funded, credible attempt on GlideScope that has not been turned back, and Ambu grew Endoscopy Solutions 16.0% organically in the June 2026 quarter against TEP's whole-segment 7.1%.

Analogues. AMETEK is the closest whole-segment match: a decentralized portfolio of niche engineered-product franchises bought years ago and run for margin, at 1.8% capital intensity and a 25.8% operating margin. It matches on structure and differs on when the assets were bought, because AMETEK keeps buying, so its balance sheet holds recent purchase prices that pull its return to 11.3% against TEP's 30%. Badger Meter is the direct comparison for the Neptune half — same product, same municipal buyers — and breaks because Badger Meter is a pure play while Neptune is a fifth of a segment that can absorb its down-cycle. Stryker is the closest comparison for Verathon: capital placement followed by a per-procedure disposable sold into a trained surgical workflow, at a 64.0% gross margin. It breaks on scale and capital intensity, since Stryker spends 3.0% of revenue on capital expenditure and 6.5% on research and development against TEP's 0.6% and an undisclosed figure.

3.4 The holding company

The corporate centre adds value through three mechanisms that can be identified and priced, and at the entry multiples of the last five years most of what it adds is paid across to sellers. Roper earned a 30.8% free-cash-flow margin in FY2025 and 6.4% on the capital it deployed to assemble that cash flow.▪ The advantage inside the operating businesses is stronger than the advantage inside the centre. Nothing well funded has been aimed at the holding structure itself; the one direct challenge, the 2026 proposal to spin the two software segments, drew 0.6% support and argued about the portfolio's composition (§10.2).

Roper runs 29 businesses from about 130 people in 42,000 square feet in Sarasota (Citi Global TMT, 2026-09-10; 10-K FY2025, Items 1 and 2). The centre sets no budgets, runs no shared services of consequence, and underwrote no synergies on Deltek, Vertafore or Frontline. It allocates capital, allocates leadership and spreads operating practice. Management does not claim portfolio synergy, and the customer sets do not support one: the businesses sell to law firms, school districts, freight brokers, water utilities, behaviour-analysis clinics and churches. Every disclosed cross-entity gain in the decade is a bolt-on folded into an existing business: EPSi and Syntellis into Strata, Transact into CBORD as Illumia, Sunquest into Clinisys, Loadlink, Trucker Tools, Outgo and Convoy into DAT, Surefyre into Vertafore.

What the centre costs. The segment note defines corporate expense as "unallocated corporate general and administrative expenses and enterprise-wide stock-based compensation," and Note 1 adds that stock-based compensation is not allocated to the segments (10-K FY2025). Splitting the two changes the number.

$m FY2020 FY2021 FY2022 FY2023 FY2024 FY2025
Corporate expense 180 190 209 227 267 290
Enterprise-wide stock-based compensation 108 123 119 124 146 166
Cash corporate G&A 72 67 91 103 122 124
Corporate expense, % of revenue 4.5% 3.9% 3.9% 3.7% 3.8% 3.7%
Cash corporate G&A, % of revenue 1.8% 1.4% 1.7% 1.7% 1.7% 1.6%

The $290m excluded from every segment margin above is 3.7% of revenue and 11.5% of the three segments' combined operating profit of $2,525m. Less than half of it is the centre. Enterprise-wide stock-based compensation of $166m is equity pay for roughly 19,400 employees across 29 businesses, booked centrally because Roper does not allocate it, and the residual $124m is the centre's cash operating cost, 1.6% of revenue and 4.9% of combined segment operating profit.▪ About $17m of half-year cash cost moves with the deal calendar: cash corporate G&A was $52m in H1 2026 against $70m a year earlier, down 24.9%, which the 10-Q attributes to "a reduction in fees for professional services and lower acquisition-related expenses" in the half when acquisition spend was $27.5m against $2,005m.

Against the other serial acquirers the cash cost is ordinary. Teledyne's corporate expense was $87.5m in FY2025, 1.4% of revenue; Dover's corporate expense and other $164.5m, 2.0%; IDEX's corporate and other $92.2m, 2.7%. The three peers each define the line differently from Roper and from each other on where equity compensation sits, so the comparison places Roper inside the normal range for a multi-business holding company without settling it more finely. Against the alternative of 29 separate public companies, board fees, external audit, SEC reporting, investor relations, D&O cover and a corporate finance function run $5m to $15m a year for companies of $100m to $4,500m of revenue, $145m to $435m in aggregate [estimate: 29 companies at $5m to $15m each].

What the centre earns on that cost. Funding cost is the largest of the three and the most durable, because it comes from the balance sheet and no operating decision at a business unit produces it. Roper's $8,500m of senior unsecured notes were scheduled to require $318.3m of interest in 2026, an average 3.7%, and the blended pre-tax rate across all debt in Q2 2026 was about 4.1% (10-K FY2025, contractual obligations; 10-Q Q2 2026). Hunn puts the gap against the competing bidder at five to six points: "We borrow at whatever, 5.5% plus or minus, and our competitors borrow at 10% plus or minus in private equity. And so it's a cost of capital advantage for us" (Citi, 2026-09-10). Five to six points of spread on $9,356m of debt is $470m to $560m a year before tax, three to four times the centre's entire cash operating cost.▪ Diversification across 29 unrelated end markets with close to zero cyclical revenue also lets Roper hold an investment-grade rating at 3.0-3.5x net leverage, which a single-vertical software company could not sustain at the same rating [estimate: 100 to 250 basis points on $9,356m, $95m to $235m a year pre-tax].

Tax capacity is second. Roper quotes a purchase price net of a net-present-value tax benefit on nine disclosed deals, about $1,140m against $18,392m of gross price, 6.2%, amortized over 13 to 15 years (§11.3). A step-up is worth its present value only to a buyer with taxable income to deduct it against, and a sponsor-owned target shielding its income with interest expense has less of it. Roper's own capacity is finite: it disclosed $49.3m of Section 163(j) interest-limitation carryforwards at 12/31/2025.

The permanent-owner offer is third. Management fit decides deals that have already cleared the financial screen: "the #1 reason we walk away if it meets our financial criteria is just the management team" (Q1 2019 call). Roper looked at Vertafore in 2016, walked away on the team, stayed close to the business for four years, re-engaged with a new team in 2019 and bought it in 2020 for $5,335m.

Cost: enterprise-wide stock-based compensation 166 any owner of these businesses incurs an equivalent
Overhead saved against 29 standalone public companies 145 to 435 [estimate: 29 companies at $5m to $15m each]
Funding spread against the sponsor bid 470 to 560 five to six points on $9,356m, management's own spread
Funding spread against a standalone investment-grade software company 95 to 235 [estimate: 100 to 250 basis points on $9,356m]

On every line the centre covers its cash cost several times over. The surplus does not reach shareholders, because each mechanism improves what Roper can pay for an asset and it is spent in competitive processes where price clears. The entry yield on acquired forward EBITDA halved from 7.1% on Deltek in 2016 to 4.5% on CentralReach and Subsplash in 2025, and the multiple management quotes is the net multiple after the tax benefit, which puts the tax capacity explicitly into the bid.▪ Hunn states the resulting arithmetic himself: "we paid 22x next 12 months for those deals. We underwrote those to be about 9 or 10x year 5 EBITDA... we could have bought ourselves back in year 5 at about 15x. So about a 50% risk premium to do — to deploy the balance sheet towards acquisitions" (Citi, 2026-09-10). A 9-10x year-five multiple on cost is a 10-11% pre-tax yield on the purchase price in year five, roughly 8-9% after tax, with any excess return arriving from compounding after that.

The acquisition funnel. Investor Day slide 108 is the only quantified description Roper has published of the constraint on its deployment. Conley described the 1,200 as the population of software and technology businesses that went to market in 2022, and called 2022 "a pretty light year because the leverage loan market was locked up for some period of time."

Stage Count Conversion from the prior stage Cumulative
Annual software targets identified about 1,200 — 100%
Reviewed 235 19.6% 19.6%
NDAs signed 93 39.6% 7.8%
Management meetings 71 76.3% 5.9%
Indications of interest 25 35.2% 2.1%
Full diligence 16 64.0% 1.3%
Transactions closed 6 37.5% 0.5%

Source: [deck: Investor Day 2023, 2023-03-21, slide 108]. Those six closings deployed $4.2bn to $4.3bn.

The funnel measures a screen and not exclusivity. Roper's access is universal inclusion in the processes that fit its criteria, against a seller base the head of M&A put at about 20 large private equity firms holding 80% of the assets of interest, all of them running competitive auctions. The steepest cut below the initial criteria screen is a people screen: Roper drops 46 of the 71 businesses whose management it meets, and the last stage loses 10 of the 16 processes it has already committed diligence resource to.▪ Management names the reason for the first of those two cuts, and it is not price: "the #1 reason we walk away if it meets our financial criteria is just the management team" (Q1 2019 call). Hunn's words for the top of the funnel: "we know that we get a look at everything that would fit our criteria. There's never been a transaction that's happened that we say, wow, we didn't get a look at that." Widening it into middle-market sponsors would take "1 or 2 people," so the part of the position Roper does not already hold costs one or two hires.

The width is table stakes and the invitation at the large end is not. Constellation Software tracks a database of about 40,000 opportunities against Roper's 1,200 annual targets, and reports that 40 to 70 large vertical-market-software businesses sell each year, that it is aware of about 80% of them, that it is invited into 16% of those processes, and that it has closed three large deals in 26 years. It lowered its own hurdle rate in 2019 for acquisitions requiring at least US$100m of equity in order to compete for them.▪ [web, Constellation Software President's Letters, quarterly MD&As and the 2019-05-01 press release, csisoftware.com, accessed 2026-09-11] Universal invitation at the size Roper needs to deploy at is the substance behind the "buyer of choice" claim, and it earns a right to bid.

Post-acquisition improvement. Investor Day slides 104 to 107 give pre-tax cash-flow compound growth rates since acquisition, and no other post-acquisition performance series exists anywhere in Roper's disclosure.

Business Acquired Price at entry Cash-flow CAGR since acquisition Years to March 2023
DAT 2004, inside TransCore within $600m for all of TransCore +16% about 19
Northern Digital 2011 $204m +16% about 12
Strata, plus the 2020 EPSi bolt-on 2015 $140m plus $365m +28% total, +23% organic about 8
Foundry 2019 $543m +21% about 4

The outcomes are strong and the sample is management's own. The four businesses cost under $1.9bn in total, about 7% of the $27,009m deployed between FY2016 and FY2025, and none is among Roper's ten largest acquisitions. Three of the four were bought before Roper became a software acquirer at scale, and Foundry, the one showcased business whose record after the slide was printed is disclosed, declined by double digits through 2024.▪ The ten largest are Vertafore $5,399m, Frontline $3,738m, Deltek $2,800m, Procare $1,860m, CentralReach $1,850m, iPipeline $1,625m, Transact $1,607m, Sunquest about $1,415m, Syntellis $1,381m and PowerPlan $1,111m. None of them appears on slides 104 to 107, and together they account for most of the capital deployed.

On the large deals the record splits, and §11.4 gives it deal by deal. Growth after acquisition matches growth before it on the two largest with disclosed entry trajectories: Vertafore entered with "consistent mid-single-digit organic growth... really for the past decade" and delivered "steady mid-single-digit revenue growth" in Q1 2026; Deltek entered as a mid-to-high-single-digit grower, delivered mid-single-digit-plus over a decade and is at the lower end of mid-singles now. Frontline entered on five years of high-single-digit organic growth, needed a new management team in 2024, and has had no growth rate disclosed since 2023. Against those, CentralReach is ahead of its deal model with recurring software revenue growing well north of 20%, Transact is ahead on revenue, and Aderant's share of the AmLaw 200 moved from 31% at the 2015 acquisition to 48% by March 2023 and about 65% by mid-2026 on Hunn's account, with its growth rate tripled. The same-store measure Roper does publish, core EBITDA margin excluding businesses owned less than a year, improved 10 to 80 basis points a quarter through 2025 and declined 70 basis points at the enterprise level in Q2 2026.

What Roper buys has also changed, and the change is deliberate. Weighted by entry revenue, the 2016-2022 cohort of Deltek, iPipeline, Vertafore and Frontline entered at a 44.0% EBITDA margin; the 2023-2025 cohort of Syntellis, Replicon, Procare, Transact, CentralReach and Subsplash entered at 37.6%, against Roper's own 39.7% consolidated adjusted EBITDA margin in FY2025. That 6.4-point step down is the mechanical source of the margin dilution management attributes to payments mix at Transact and Subsplash.

Business-level retention was disclosed once, at the 2023 Investor Day, and never updated: Deltek gross retention from 93% at acquisition to 97%, Aderant net retention from 102% to 113% with SaaS moving from nil to 80% of bookings, and Vertafore from 91% gross and 105% net to 92% and 108% with EBITDA margin from 49% to 50%, over roughly two and a half years of ownership of the largest acquisition in company history [deck: Investor Day 2023, 2023-03-21, slides 58, 68, 90].

Against the other serial acquirers. Acquisition spend is cash paid for businesses net of cash acquired from each year's own cash flow statement as originally filed, free cash flow is operating cash flow less capital expenditure on the same basis, and return on invested capital is operating income taxed at that year's effective rate over average invested capital including goodwill and net intangibles. Roper's $253m of capitalized software over the decade is excluded from the capital-expenditure line for comparability with peers who capitalize little or none, which is why its ten-year deployment ratio is 170% here against the 173% in §10.3.

Computed from each company's own SEC filings on 2026-09-11. Fortive's FY2025 return pairs a post-Ralliant numerator with a denominator that still averages in Ralliant, so 5.7% understates the standalone business; Teledyne publishes no organic or core growth measure in any year of the window, and its FY2025 disclosure of $270.1m of incremental acquisition revenue against 7.9% total growth implies roughly 3%.

Roper is the most acquisition-intensive of the nine named serial acquirers on whatever measure each publishes. It deployed 170% of ten-year free cash flow against a 66% to 112% range for the six SEC-filing industrials, 145% over the matched FY2021-FY2025 window against Constellation Software's 116%, Topicus's 86% and Halma's 68% to 85%, and 161% cumulatively since FY2007, the highest of thirteen SEC-filing serial acquirers. It also holds the most acquisition-derived balance sheet, 90.0% of total assets in goodwill and intangibles against a 53.6% to 80.8% range.▪ The three non-SEC analogues are measured on their own published cash-flow definitions, which differ from each other and from Roper's, so the ranking is firmer than the gaps [web, csisoftware.com, topicus.com and halma.com, accessed 2026-09-11].

Roper earns the highest operating margin in the cohort, 28.3% against a 17.0% to 25.8% range, and grew organically faster in FY2025 than every one of the six by more than three points, so the 6.4% is not an operating shortfall. AMETEK isolates the cause. It held goodwill-inclusive return on invested capital at 13.1% to 13.2% across the same five years while acquiring continuously, on a decentralized portfolio of niche leaders run from a small centre, which is the structure Roper runs. It deploys 77% of free cash flow against Roper's 170% and pays 2x to 3x sales against Roper's 7x to 9x.▪ Part of the 6.4% is the asset class: four of the six peers saw goodwill-inclusive returns decline over five years, and Danaher, the largest of them, is at 6.1%, below Roper. The rest is the price paid.

Three return series, reconciled. Three return-on-invested-capital figures for Roper are in public circulation and appear to disagree. They measure the same ratio on three bases, and the differences are arithmetic.

Series What it measures FY2025 on its own basis
The Proposal 6 proponent's 8.3% average under Jellison declining to a 6.7% six-year average NOPAT after amortization over average invested capital including goodwill, computed from each year's statements as originally filed not stated by the proponent; the FY2019-FY2024 average on this construction is 6.6%
The continuing-operations series, 5.0% (FY2021) rising to 6.4% (FY2025) the same ratio with a continuing-operations numerator over an as-reported denominator 6.4%
The pre-amortization alternative quoted at about 9% adds $858m of acquired-intangible amortization to the numerator and leaves the intangibles in the denominator at net book value 7.6% once the denominator is grossed up for the same item

Computing both sides from each fiscal year's own 10-K as originally filed removes the mismatch.

FY2017 FY2018 FY2019 FY2020 FY2021 FY2022 FY2023 FY2024 FY2025
As filed, single basis 10.1% 9.3% 9.0% 6.7% 5.9% 5.7% 6.0% 6.3% 6.4%
Continuing-operations numerator over as-reported denominator 10.1% 9.3% 8.0% 5.0% 5.0% 5.7% 6.0% 6.3% 6.4%

The divergence is confined to FY2019, FY2020 and FY2021, where the recast numerator excludes TransCore, Zetec and Indicor while the year-end balance sheets still consolidate them, and it understates those three readings by 1.0 to 1.7 points. The proponent's 6.7% is the as-filed measure and it is right: the FY2019-FY2024 average on that basis is 6.6%. The Board's objection, that the proponent failed to adjust for discontinued operations, changes a growth CAGR materially and changes a return ratio very little, because a divestiture removes earnings and capital together. FY2017's 10.1% is flattered by a 6.1% effective tax rate under the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act remeasurement and is about 7.7% at a pre-Act rate, so the era comparison is roughly 8-9% then against 6.4% now. The 9% figure adds back a charge without restoring the capital the charge consumed: adding the $4,118m average balance of accumulated acquired-intangible amortization to invested capital alongside the $815m of acquired-intangible amortization in the numerator gives 7.6%, and the $43m of capitalized-software amortization inside the $858m cash-flow line is a genuine replacement cost against $57m of annual capitalized-software spending.

Sections 10 and 13 use the as-filed single basis, 6.4% for FY2025, with the continuing-operations readings for FY2019-FY2021 footnoted in §13.1 and the pre-amortization alternative shown at 7.6% wherever it appears. What no disclosure settles is the record before FY2016, so the proponent's sixteen-year 8.3% average and the Board's refusal to restate it both stand on two overlapping years.

Where this leaves the holding company. The three mechanisms are structural, repeatable and quantified, and together they cover the centre's cash cost several times over. At 22.0x and 22.2x forward EBITDA on the 2025 platform deals they are spent on the bid, which is the mechanism behind a 6.4% return on a 30.8% free-cash-flow margin. The improvement claim is supported on four businesses that cost about 7% of the decade's deployed capital and excludes all ten of the largest acquisitions, so what the centre does to the businesses that absorbed most of the capital cannot be measured from outside.

The analogues for the holding company, chosen by the shape of the advantage:

Analogue Why it holds Where it breaks
Constellation Software Group cash flow funding the next acquisition, a permanent-owner promise, a small centre, decentralized operating autonomy Deal size and price. Constellation buys many small businesses from founders in non-intermediated processes; Roper buys six to nine large ones a year from about 20 sponsors at 14x to 22x forward EBITDA
Danaher in its Danaher Business System era A named operating system taught into acquired businesses by a central group Measurability. The Danaher system produced factory and working-capital outputs visible in a margin series; Roper's growth system produces product velocity, leader selection and practice transfer, none of it separately reported
AMETEK A decentralized portfolio of niche leaders with serial bolt-on acquisition and a light centre Price and the return that follows: 2x to 3x sales and 13.2% on invested capital against 7x to 9x and 6.4%

This placement would be overturned by any of the following, in the order each would arrive. A realized year-five EV/EBITDA on the 2024-2025 vintage near the 9x to 10x Roper underwrote. Deployment of the stated $5bn or more at the 13x to 18x management now expects, which would leave the funding and tax advantage with Roper at the price it pays. Consolidated organic growth reaccelerating to 6% or 7% in FY2027, the first year in which reported organic growth approximates a pure same-store number because acquisition spend was $27.5m in the first half of 2026. And a core-margin series expanding faster than 40 to 80 basis points a year once the cost of the central AI team Roper began building in October 2025 annualizes.

4. Competitive landscape and market sizing

Roper competes in roughly 29 separate markets and names a competitor in none of them. The whole competition disclosure says: "Generally, our products and solutions face significant competition, although in certain niche markets there are a limited number of competitors. We believe that we are a leader in most of our markets, and no single company competes with us over a significant number of product lines" (10-K FY2025, Item 1). Every competitor pairing below therefore comes from outside the filings.

Management's claim is that scale runs in Roper's favour everywhere: "we're the leader in a small market which means, by definition, all of our competitors are smaller" (Citi Global TMT, 2026-09-10). It holds in several lines and fails in others, and the failures are concentrated in Application Software.▪ Durability is assessed in §3.

4.1 Application Software
