That limits the runway: Deltek's two highest-share markets leave little room for share gain, and the markets with headroom are the ones where Autodesk, Procore, Trimble and Sage are each larger than Deltek in total.▪ The near-term catalysts management names are One Big Beautiful Bill appropriations flowing into defence contractor spend, and the announced end of support for on-premise Costpoint in Q1 2028, which the CFO said "should move it over 2x from maintenance to subscription."

Law-firm practice and financial management — Aderant. Aderant states 2,500-plus unique clients in 21 countries, that 97% of the AmLaw Top 200 and 86% of the Global 100 use an Aderant product, and that 220-plus firms replaced a legacy system with Aderant Expert in the five years to 2022. It says US share rose from 31% (2015) to 48% (2022) and that it moved from second to first. Thomson Reuters Elite is the incumbent it took share from: Aderant states 39 AmLaw Top 200 firms moved from the largest competitor to Expert in the decade to 2022 and none moved the other way, while Thomson Reuters states 89% of AmLaw firms use at least one Elite product [web]. Intapp, Litera, Clio, LEAP, Centerbase and Smokeball are in adjacent or smaller-firm tiers. No independently audited share figure exists for this market, and web-tracking installation counters measure a different population — all firm sizes, where SMB tools dominate by count — so they neither confirm nor rebut the company figures.

Clinical and laboratory information systems — Clinisys and Data Innovations. This is the line where "all of our competitors are smaller" does not hold.▪ Epic held 43.7% of the US acute-care electronic health record market in 2025, up from 42.3%, gained 77 multispecialty hospitals, and won both of the only two enterprise-wide decisions by systems with more than ten hospitals (beckershospitalreview.com, accessed 2026-09-11) [web]. Beaker is the default laboratory system for an Epic hospital, and the lab decision is increasingly made as part of the EHR decision. Clinisys at about $420m [estimate] has grown by buying laboratory information system vendors: Sunquest (2012), CliniSys (2021), Promium (2023), Orchard Software (July 2025). Oracle Health holds 21.9% of acute-care EHR and is losing; LabWare, LabVantage, Thermo Fisher, CompuGroup, Meditech and TruBridge make up a fragmented tail. Third-party sizing of the global laboratory information system market is inconsistent — one aggregator says the top ten vendors held 18% of 2024 revenue while another gives Clinisys alone 9.2% of pathology modules — so no share figure from that family is used.

Campus commerce and tuition payments — Illumia. Illumia serves 10,000-plus higher-education, healthcare and senior-living institutions and 1,500-plus higher-education institutions specifically. TouchNet is owned by Global Payments; Nelnet Campus Commerce serves 1,100-plus higher-education institutions; all three were named in PayPal and Venmo's August 2026 tuition-payment integration (newsroom.paypal-corp.com, accessed 2026-09-11) [web]. Flywire won Penn State's full domestic tuition billing in April 2026 after a decade as its international-payments vendor (ir.flywire.com, accessed 2026-09-11) [web]. This is the Application Software line whose competitor set includes a payments company with a much larger balance sheet and a listed payments specialist actively taking accounts, and it is also the line that drags segment gross margin.

Early-childhood education — Procare. Procare serves 37,000 owners and operators, with payments at about 75% of its revenue, and management states it has "about 1.5x relative market share." Brightwheel reports 50,000-plus early-education centres worldwide and about $37.5m of 2024 revenue on a third-party estimate [web, low confidence]. Revenue per centre is roughly $7,600 at Procare against roughly $750 at Brightwheel [estimate: each company's revenue divided by its centre count; the Brightwheel revenue input is a third-party estimate]. Procare's revenue lead comes from monetising payment flow, not from a larger footprint.

K-12 administration — Frontline. Frontline serves 10,000-plus educational organisations, with human capital management about 50% of its ARR at acquisition, student management 30% and business operations 20%. PowerSchool, taken private by Bain at a $5.6bn enterprise value on 2024-10-01, serves 18,000-plus customers and 60m-plus students and held 23% of identified US and Canadian student-information-system implementations; its last public disclosure was ARR of $720.3m at 3/31/2024, growing 18% (marketbrief.edweek.org, accessed 2026-09-11) [web]. On the shared adjacency, student management, PowerSchool is roughly four times Frontline's scale by ARR and was growing faster at the last comparable print.

Healthcare financial planning — Strata. Strata contributes the hospital data behind Kaufman Hall's National Hospital Flash Report, drawn from more than 1,300 hospitals. Kaufman Hall (Vizient) overlaps as much as it competes; Health Catalyst is the adjacent analytics layer; Epic, Oracle Health, Workday and Sage Intacct encroach from the general ledger upward.

ABA therapy software — CentralReach. 200,000-plus professionals on the platform against Rethink Behavioral Health, Catalyst (Therapy Brands), Motivity and Hi Rasmus, each much smaller. This is the clearest case in the segment where management's claim holds, and 75% of new business in Q1 2026 was AI or AI-influenced, up from zero two years earlier.

Where that claim fails, sized. Roughly $1.5–1.8bn of FY2025 segment revenue, on the order of a third of the segment, competes against a player larger than the Roper business facing it▪: Illumia against TouchNet inside Global Payments and a payments-native Flywire; Clinisys against Epic; Frontline's student-management line against PowerSchool; Deltek's construction, consulting and creative lines against Autodesk, Procore, Trimble and Sage [estimate: the four business-line weights above, each a low-to-medium-confidence figure, summed; the band is wide because every input is estimated].

DAT publishes the larger number on every measure it discloses, but the two firms' figures are not on a common basis: DAT's 700,000 is daily posts, which can include a load posted more than once in its life, while Truckstop's 80m is annual loads. Annualising DAT's posts gives about 255m against Truckstop's 80m, so the ratio is indicative of a roughly three-to-one gap and not a measured share. DAT's own volume is also stated three ways across its own materials — 291m loads and trucks posted annually, 266m transactions, and nearly 700,000 daily posts — and none is reconciled. Management's scale figure changed within a year as well: "over 1.2 million loads posted and 15 million rate views every single day" (Q3 2025 call) became "roughly 750,000 unique loads are advertised on our network every day" at both September 2026 conferences. The 2026 figure is qualified as unique loads and the 2025 figure as posts, which would reconcile them if duplicate postings are about 38% of the total; no bridge is published.

DAT sets price. Management has described 2025 and 2026 growth as coming from price actions rolling into recurring revenue and from average revenue per user expansion. Published entry pricing is close between the two firms, about $45-49 a month at both, so the premium DAT captures is in volume and rate data. The rate data is harder to replicate than the board: Triumph paid $160m for Greenscreens, a rate-data business with roughly $8m of revenue, which prices what a challenger thinks the data layer is worth [web, FreightWaves, accessed 2026-09-11].

Neutrality is the live question. Highway, a carrier-identity vendor, bought Newtrul to launch a private load board and is selling jointly with Triumph, a factoring company. DAT's own moves into factoring (Outgo) and brokerage automation (Convoy) narrow the same neutrality it claims: "What sets DAT apart is this end-to-end product capability and its role as a neutral trusted partner, a Switzerland-like player that equally serves the entire freight brokerage market" (Q3 2025 call).

Pre-construction project data — ConstructConnect. A two-firm market against Dodge Construction Network, with adjacent pressure from Autodesk BuildingConnected, Procore and Trimble in bid management. ConstructConnect adds 15,000 new US and Canadian projects a month, holds 2m-plus plans and specifications and employs 400-plus researchers; Dodge tracks 700,000-plus unique projects annually with 400-plus field specialists. The two claim the largest North American database on units that do not compare. Neither firm has pricing power over a small-business base that renews annually. What has changed is Dodge's balance sheet: S&P recorded ten consecutive quarters of revenue decline through Q2 2024 on "rising small to midsize business (SMB) customer churn" and "account management missteps," a selective default, an upgrade to CCC+ on 2024-12-06 after a distressed debt restructuring, leverage around 10x and $100m of new capital in November 2024▪ (S&P Global Ratings, Dodge Construction Network LLC, 2022-12-15 and 2024-12-06). Over the same window Roper reported construction-led organic growth in FY2023, FY2025, H1 2026 and Q2 2026.

Alternate-site healthcare — MHA, SoftWriters, SHP. MHA is a group purchasing and reimbursement intermediary, not a software seller, and the economics differ: it negotiates contracts with manufacturers and payers on behalf of long-term care, infusion and specialty pharmacies and earns administrative fees on volume it does not control. MHA calls itself "the country's largest alternate site GPO"; Innovatix (Premier Inc.) calls itself "the nation's leading non-acute care group purchasing organization" with more than 16,000 members and 3,300-plus contracts from 1,400-plus suppliers, and won Omnicare's exclusive GPO mandate in May 2025 [web, accessed 2026-09-11]. Neither publishes purchasing volume for the segment, so the competing claims cannot be settled from public data. Roper's Q2 2026 10-Q names "declines in our alternate site group purchasing business" as one of two organic detractors in the quarter. SoftWriters serves 800 pharmacies across 49 states with 2m patients; RedSail Technologies serves nearly 12,000 pharmacies across community, long-term-care and outpatient settings.

Life insurance and annuity distribution — iPipeline. An oligopoly of order-entry and illustration platforms between carriers and distributors. iPipeline connects 100-plus carriers, 2,500-plus broker-dealers, brokerage general agencies, independent marketing organisations and managing general agencies, and 500,000-plus agents, with $33bn of life and $55bn of annuity premium collected in 2022 — figures iPipeline has not refreshed, so they are four years stale. Zinnia bought Ebix's life and annuity software assets including AnnuityNet in early 2024 with a $300m Vista Credit facility; Hexure and Equisoft are the other named platforms. The carriers set price in practice, and Q2 2026 organic weakness was in non-recurring professional services, the part of revenue that depends on carrier project budgets.

Perishable food — iTradeNetwork. $50bn of invoices processed annually across 2,500-plus trading partners and 3m-plus users, with 8 of the top 10 North American foodservice distributors, 13 of the top 20 North American grocers and 8 of the top 10 global food and beverage manufacturers. SPS Commerce and Descartes are larger in adjacent retail and logistics data exchange; Trustwell and Famous compete in traceability and produce ERP. This business is named in no MD&A growth-driver list across FY2023-25.

Faith-based giving — Subsplash. Subsplash serves 20,000-plus faith-based organisations and 24m donors. Pushpay serves 15,000-plus customers and holds about 25% of Protestant large churches, about 10% of Protestant midsize and about 4% of Catholic, with roughly half its revenue from subscription and half from processing fees, on S&P-adjusted EBITDA margins of 22% rising toward 24% (S&P Global Ratings, Pushpay Holdings Ltd., 2024-07-30). S&P's own assessment of Pushpay names the threat from the other direction: competitors "like Subsplash and Tithely, which primarily cater to small and midsize churches, could expand into the large church market." Subsplash serves more organisations than Pushpay on roughly half the revenue, which is the arithmetic of serving smaller congregations, and grows in the high teens organically against S&P's 2-5% forecast for Pushpay. S&P also describes this customer base as "highly fragmented and price-sensitive" with minimal switching costs, consuming only 1-2% of a church's operating budget.

Visual effects — Foundry. Nuke has been the compositing standard at the top of the market since its 2001 Academy Technical Achievement Award, with site licences at Industrial Light & Magic, Weta, Double Negative and Framestore. Below that tier the substitutes are free or nearly free: Nuke lists at $3,839 a year, NukeX $5,219 and Nuke Studio $6,379, against Blackmagic's Fusion Studio free inside DaVinci Resolve or $295 perpetual, and Adobe After Effects at about $276 a year (foundry.com and shade.inc, both accessed 2026-09-11) [web]. Foundry sets price inside the feature-film tier; everywhere else Blackmagic sets it at zero. Foundry declined through the 2023 writers' and actors' strikes, resumed sequential ARR growth in Q2 2025 and returned to year-on-year ARR growth in FY2025; that recovery cannot yet be separated from the market's own recovery.

4.3 Technology Enabled Products

Municipal water metering — Neptune. Badger Meter's 10-K names the supplier set directly: "Sensus (Xylem Inc.), Neptune (Roper Technologies, Inc.), Hach (Veralto Corp.), Itron Inc., Aclara (Hubbell Inc.), Mueller Water Products Inc., Kamstrup and others," serving more than 50,000 US water utilities.

Xylem / Sensus FlexNet licensed-spectrum AMI network Measurement and Control Solutions segment $2,086m, of which "smart metering and other" $1,726m including electricity, gas and non-North-American water Segment revenue −5.9%, organic −1.4%; US water down on lower shippable backlog Segment operating margin 11.7%
Badger Meter ORION endpoints; BEACON SaaS revenue $73.6m, a 9.0% attach on utility water sales Utility water $816.1m; total $916.7m Utility water $195.0m, −8.1%; H1 −8.8% Total operating margin 17.7% (20.0% FY2025)

Neptune is smaller on revenue than both Badger Meter's utility water business and Xylem's smart metering line, though the Xylem line is not a like-for-like comparison because it spans electricity, gas and markets outside North America.▪ US installations were about 25.09m meters in 2025 and are forecast at 26.16m in 2026, with mechanical and basic meters 63.8% of 2025 units (mordorintelligence.com, accessed 2026-09-11) [web]; Badger Meter independently estimates about 40% of US utility connections have converted to an AMI radio solution. Both sources agree most connections are still unconverted, which is the runway the whole industry sells into.

The incremental margin is in the software layer, and Neptune is under-indexed to it. Badger Meter earns higher prices and margins "on meters coupled with radio technology, software, water quality monitoring... and on ultrasonic compared to mechanical meters," and its SaaS revenue grew from $42.2m to $73.6m in two years and is described as margin accretive. Roper's equivalent disclosure is $46.1m of Technology Enabled Products recurring software revenue in FY2025 — which covers Neptune and Muni-Link together, not Neptune alone — against $26.1m and $17.3m in the two prior years, 2.5% of segment revenue, growing 23% organically in Q2 2026 from a small base.

Airway and endoscopy visualization — Verathon. Roper's 2023 positioning put Verathon as global leader in video laryngoscopy, global number two and "rapidly gaining share" in single-use bronchoscopy, and global leader in bladder volume measurement, across a served market of "$1B+, growing double digits." By the Q4 2025 call Roper stated that "Verathon is the U.S. market share leader in single-use bronchoscopes."

Player Scale metric Position and direction Latest quarter
Roper / Verathon 95% of US hospitals use a Verathon product; 4.8m single-use video-laryngoscope consumables shipped annually; 6m annual GlideScope intubations; 175m annual BladderScan exams (2023 disclosure) Global leader in video laryngoscopy and bladder volume; stated US leader in single-use bronchoscopes "Solid growth" on BFlex and GlideScope; launched the CFlex single-use cystoscope and BFlex specimen collection
Ambu A/S Pioneer and global leader in single-use flexible bronchoscopes since 2009; more than 3,000 US hospitals use Ambu disposable bronchoscopes Global leader in single-use endoscopy, broadening into urology, ENT and GI; obtained full European CE mark for the SureSight video laryngoscope portfolio in the March 2026 quarter Group organic +10.3% in the June 2026 quarter, Endoscopy Solutions organic +16.0%; group EBIT margin before special items 13.0% (FY2024/25)

Ambu is roughly twice Verathon's size at group level and growing faster in the overlapping category. Both companies claim share gains in the same conversion, and since Roper discloses no Verathon growth rate the claims cannot be netted; if both hold, the single-use market is growing faster than either incumbent and the share shift is coming out of reusable scopes.▪

Precision tracking — Northern Digital. This is the most concentrated line in the segment. NDI's own materials claim nearly 90% of surgical navigation systems incorporate its technology, a claim about installed systems, not about revenue share, that no independent source confirms. The surgical navigation system market was about $1.23bn in 2025 growing at a 6.2% compound rate (futuremarketinsights.com, accessed 2026-09-11) [web], and NDI sells a component into that, so its served market is a fraction of the system market. Polhemus is the principal independent electromagnetic alternative, with AmfiTrack and Radwave as newer entrants. The structural weakness is customer power: NDI's customers are medical-device OEMs building cardiac, neurological and orthopaedic platforms, and Stryker and Medtronic run their own navigation programmes. Roper discloses no customer concentration for NDI, and the 10% threshold that produces the "no customer" disclosure is set against $7,903m of company revenue, not against NDI's much smaller base.

Accessories, credentials and the remainder. CIVCO holds more than 50% of the US needle-guide and probe-cover market, ahead of BD, in a category of about $335m globally in 2025 growing 5.1% a year (idataresearch.com and mordorintelligence.com, both accessed 2026-09-11) [web]; the structural threat is ultrasound OEMs embedding guidance into the imaging platform, which converts a consumable into a feature. rf IDEAS competes with HID Global (Assa Abloy), ELATEC and Identiv; ELATEC was acquired by Allegion on 1 July 2025 for $382m against about $70-75m of expected 2026 net sales (allegion.com, accessed 2026-09-11) [web], which moved rf IDEAS's closest independent peer inside a large security platform. FMI competes into the same applications as IDEX's Fluid and Metering Technologies segment, plus ProMinent, Grundfos and Watson-Marlow. Inovonics competes with Honeywell, Johnson Controls, Resideo and Napco. IPA has no named public comparator.

4.4 Share counter-evidence, ranked by how much each would change the structure

  1. Epic's EHR share gains pull the laboratory system with them. Epic at 43.7% and rising, Beaker as the default for an Epic hospital, and Clinisys buying competitors (Orchard, July 2025) instead of winning new hospitals.
  2. AI-driven seat compression in the two largest software lines. Management named Vertafore and Aderant as the businesses whose seat-based pricing meter must change, with the first Vertafore wave shipping in early 2027, and possibly Deltek later. The exposure is roughly $1,020m of revenue [estimate: Vertafore about $750m plus Aderant about $270m], about 23% of the segment.
  3. Autodesk moving up from design into project financials. AECO revenue of $3,583m growing 22%, against a whole-Deltek estimate of about $850m, at the same firms where Autodesk already owns the design layer.
  4. OEM in-sourcing at Northern Digital. NDI is the fastest-growing business in Technology Enabled Products and sells into the bill of materials of OEMs who can build the same layer. Smith+Nephew's June 2019 purchase of the optical tracking specialist Atracsys is the nearest transaction, and the acquirer said it planned for the business "to continue serving these markets" as a stand-alone unit, so it is not a precedent for removal from the merchant market (startupticker.ch, accessed 2026-09-11) [web]. The exposure cannot be sized because no NDI customer concentration is published.
  5. Payments encroachment at Illumia. Flywire took Penn State's full domestic tuition billing in April 2026; TouchNet is owned by Global Payments.
  6. Lower entry barriers as water metering converts from mechanical to static. Badger Meter's own risk disclosure states the case: "Static water metering has lower barriers to entry than mechanical metering that could affect the competitive landscape in North America." Neptune's foundry and backward-compatible register architecture matter less when the meter is a solid-state device, and Roper says the static shift is currently helping Neptune.
  7. Every large endoscopy incumbent is now in single-use scopes. Verathon's US bronchoscope leadership was won in a category two players deep in 2019 and six deep now.
  8. Brokers building their own matching. The largest brokerages already run proprietary digital matching, and Flexport's neutral Convoy Platform was a direct attempt at the layer DAT occupies. Roper removed that one by buying it.
  9. PowerSchool under Bain with 18% ARR growth against Frontline's student-management line.
  10. Unanet at the bottom of the government-contracting ERP market, where Deltek's own end-of-support decision on on-premise Costpoint in Q1 2028 forces a migration decision on its largest maintenance base, which is also a re-competition event.

5. Value chain and profit pools

Roper sells into three structurally different chains, and the profit pool, the binding input and the price setter differ in each.

5.1 The vertical software dollar

For every $1,000 of an end customer's annual operating cost:

Layer Named participants Capture per $1,000 of customer cost Gross margin at that layer Who sets the price at this interface
The customer's own labour Law-firm timekeepers, agency producers, district staff, registered behaviour technicians, government-contract accountants $250–$600 depending on vertical — The local labour market
Roper's vertical system of record Deltek, Vertafore, Aderant, CentralReach, Frontline, Clinisys, Strata About $10 [management's own generalisation; the two independent checks below bracket it at $5–$40] 68.5% Application Software, 84.1% Network Software, 72.6% blended Roper at renewal, bounded by the customer's software budget
Integrated payments inside that software Illumia, Procare, Subsplash $833m company-wide, 10.5% of FY2025 revenue 50–65% [estimate: solving the two-component segment gross-margin mix across FY2023-25; a gross merchant-discount book would show 20-30%, so the result is consistent with a revenue-share structure] The processor and the card networks; the software vendor takes a share
Cloud hosting and foundation models AWS, Google Cloud, Microsoft Azure, Oracle Cloud; OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Microsoft Part of the $2.74 of cost of sales Roper incurs per $10 of software revenue AWS operating margin 39.4% in Q2 2026; Microsoft Cloud gross margin 66% in FY2026 The provider. The FY2025 10-K states Roper "may not be able to pass such cost increases on to our customers"

Roper's own $10 splits into $2.74 of cost of sales, $7.26 of gross profit, $3.12 of segment operating profit and $0.37 of unallocated corporate expense at the FY2025 rate.

Two independent checks bracket management's "about 1% of the cost bar." At CentralReach, about $175m of revenue across more than 200,000 platform professionals is at most $875 per professional per year, against a technician billing 1,200-1,400 hours a year at a median $14.18 per 15-minute unit, or $68,000-$79,000 of clinic revenue [web, ABA reimbursement schedules, accessed 2026-09-11] — 1.1% to 1.3%, and lower per actual biller because the platform count includes non-billing staff. In property and casualty distribution, an independent agency earns 10-15% commission on new premium and spends about 3-5% of its revenue on software, with agency management systems at $85-$200 per user per month [web, accessed 2026-09-11]; Roper's capture is roughly 0.1-0.4% of the premium dollar and 1-4% of the agency's own revenue. The binding ceiling in insurance is not the agency's cost bar but its total software budget, which Vertafore already shares with comparative raters, carrier portals, CRM and marketing tools.

Tyler Technologies is the closest listed benchmark for the same layer. It names its primary cost components as "hosting costs, merchant fees, and personnel expenses" and earned a 46.5% gross margin in FY2025 against Roper's 68.5% and 84.1%. Tyler's transaction-based fees of $808m are almost the same dollar amount as Roper's reoccurring revenue of $833m, on a revenue base under a third of Roper's. Tyler also states the pricing mechanism at the payments interface: FY2025 transaction-fee growth came partly from "price increases by certain third-party processing partners from whom we receive a share of revenues." The processor raises price and the software vendor takes a share of the result.

5.2 The freight dollar

A dry-van truckload of about 800 miles at the DAT-published spot linehaul rate of $2.21 per mile in early September 2026 generates about $1,770 of linehaul revenue before fuel surcharge.

Layer Capture on that load Who sets the price
Motor carrier linehaul about $1,770 The spot market, indexed by DAT's own RateView
Freight broker gross margin roughly 12-18% of the shipper's all-in rate [web, industry convention] Broker-shipper negotiation
Broker's labour to move one load $100-$200 The labour market
DAT subscription $45-$345 a month per carrier seat, $159-$449 per broker seat, list [web] DAT, with Truckstop the only scale alternative
Invoice financing Advances against the carrier's invoice The bank buying the receivable

The pricing anchor Roper is now using is the broker's labour line, not the software line: "we can automate the manual, the dozen or so phone calls to broker a load into no phone calls and do it for a fraction of the labor cost," at $40-$60 against $100-$200 (Q2 2026 call; Citi, 2026-09-10). That is a move from the customer's software budget into the customer's labour budget, and the pricing form is a fixed credit block: "it's going to be like an old-school cell phone or mobile plan, which is you buy a chunk of credits or usage capability against the tool, but it's going to be a fixed amount... it's going to be use it or lose it, so we can take it as recurring as opposed to reoccurring revenue" (Citi, 2026-09-10). That structure puts the inference cost risk on Roper and books the revenue in the higher-margin line, the opposite of the payments arrangement where the processor sets price and Roper takes a share.▪

Two-sided dynamics moved in Roper's favour in 2026. Dry-van spot linehaul averaged $2.41 per mile in July 2026 excluding fuel, up 47% year over year, with equipment posts at historic lows and capacity limited by driver availability and regulation (fleetequipmentmag.com, accessed 2026-09-11) [web]. The Supreme Court's unanimous decision in Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II on 2026-05-14 held that state-law negligent-selection claims against freight brokers are not preempted by federal law (dlapiper.com, accessed 2026-09-11) [web], raising broker insurance and diligence costs. Roper's CEO described that as favourable because it "put[s] more emphasis on the brokers to vet the carriers, which is precisely what Convoy and DAT does extremely well." That is management's position; no financial effect has been disclosed either way.

5.3 The water meter dollar

This is the chain where the binding input is physical and the price setter has moved to the supplier.

Layer Economics Who sets the price
Copper and bronze ingot Copper at $6.478 a pound on 2026-09-11, up 41.4% over twelve months (tradingeconomics.com, accessed 2026-09-11) [web] The global copper market, bid by data-centre demand
Meter and endpoint manufacture Neptune, Badger Meter, Itron, Sensus, Master Meter, Mueller — together more than 85-90% of the North American market [web]. Installed cost of an AMI meter roughly $200 Historically the manufacturer; in 2025 the customer refused a surcharge
Municipal water utility Recovers through rates The rate regulator or city council
Household ratepayer — The utility's tariff

Neptune is more exposed than its listed competitors because it melts its own metal. Badger Meter buys finished castings and "relies on single suppliers for most brass castings"; Roper's then-CEO said in 2017 that "we're absolutely vertically integrated. We have our own foundry." In 2016 and 2017 that integration was presented as the reason Neptune outgrew competitors through a copper cycle; in 2025 and 2026 it puts Neptune's cost of goods one step closer to the ingot price. The direction of the Q2 2026 move runs against both listed pure plays: TEP gross margin declined 162 basis points year over year while Badger Meter's declined 30 and Itron's FY2025 gross margin rose 330 on mix and manufacturing efficiency. The structural hedge is a mix shift toward static meters, which use less bronze.

Management's baseline is that the input cost stays high, and attributes the cause to the same buildout its software segments depend on: "we expect, by the way, ingot cost — the baseline assumption we have is ingot cost is going to stay high. I mean this is with all the data centers and just the demand for copper, this is a derivative impact of that" (Q1 2026 call).

The customer's own project economics are the weakest in Roper's portfolio here. A peer-reviewed randomized field experiment at a California utility found the installed cost of an AMI meter is "roughly $200" and that AMI-enhanced messaging reduced consumption by 5.24 gallons per household per day, giving net savings of $9.34 per household per year and a payback period of 41 years under universal installation; targeted at homes with detected leaks, consumption declined 30.0 gallons per day, net savings rose to $60.68 a year and "the payback period is approximately four years" (iopscience.iop.org, accessed 2026-09-11) [web]. The utility-side case is better and still a municipal capital project: avoided manual-read labour of $10-$20 per meter per year, with three- to seven-year paybacks for utilities running 5,000 or more meters on manual routes once billing accuracy is included [web, accessed 2026-09-11]. A customer whose own project pays back in three to seven years, funded through a rate case, has no room for a mid-contract price step, and told Neptune so.

5.4 The interface that actually binds

The binding constraint is the supply of vertical software businesses priced to clear Roper's return hurdle.▪ Hunn at Morgan Stanley on 2026-03-04: "every business we bought has come from private equity and they own a business for 3 to 5 years." The upstream supplier of Roper's growth is the private-equity industry.

Management states the hurdle: "we need to underwrite somewhere in the 10x year 5 EV to EBITDA as a baseline. So tax effect that inverse that formula is sort of get year 5 ROIC" (Goldman Sachs, 2026-09-09). A 10x year-five EBITDA underwrite implies a pre-tax year-five return on deployed capital of about 10%.▪

Deal Announced Price used Forward revenue Forward EBITDA Entry EV/EBITDA Entry EV/revenue Year-5 EBITDA CAGR needed to reach 10x
Vertafore 2020-08-13 $5,350m about $590m (2021E) about $290m (2021E) 18.4x 9.1x 13.0%
Frontline Education 2022-08-30 $3,375m net of about $350m of tax benefit about $370m (2023E) about $175m (2023E) 19.3x 9.1x 14.0%
CentralReach 2025-03-24 $1,650m net of $200m of tax benefit about $175m about $75m 22.0x 9.4x 17.1%

Sources: the three M&A decks. The Vertafore slide discloses no tax benefit, so its multiple may be modestly overstated against the other two.

The price Roper paid to sponsors rose across five years while listed software de-rated. Frontline was announced with a high-single-digit organic revenue outlook, which on its own does not deliver the 14.0% EBITDA compounding its entry multiple requires; bolt-ons and margin expansion have to supply the rest. CentralReach was announced with a 20%-plus organic revenue and EBITDA growth profile, which does clear 17.1% if it holds for five years.

The price Roper now wants to pay: "the returns that we can potentially drive to the enterprise and the cash flow compounding that could accelerate to the extent we can buy the businesses we bought 18 months ago for 30%, 40%, 25% lower prices are quite compelling" (Goldman Sachs, 2026-09-09). Applied to the 22.0x CentralReach entry, a 25-40% lower price is 13.2x to 16.5x, which would cut the required year-five EBITDA compounding from 17.1% to between 5.7% and 10.5%. Hunn quotes the sponsors' own reset: "the new 15 is yesterday's 25."

5.5 Bargaining power, and who is locking up whom

Interface Direction Evidence
Private-equity sellers to Roper Against Roper through 2025, now turning Entry multiple rose from 18.4x (Vertafore, 2020) to 19.3x (Frontline, 2022) to 22.0x and 22.2x (CentralReach and Subsplash, 2025). Acquisitions collapsed from $8,960m over 2023-25 to about $50m in H1 2026
Cloud and model providers to Roper Against Roper The FY2025 10-K is the first to name OpenAI, Anthropic, Google and Microsoft as model suppliers and the first to state the cost may not be passable to customers. Minimum fixed-price purchase commitments falling due beyond twelve months tripled from $256m (FY2023) to $771m (FY2025), against product revenue growth of 15.5% and software revenue growth of 32.0% over the same two years. Acquired vendor contracts cannot be excluded as the cause, so the inference is directional
Bronze ingot to Neptune Against Roper Copper up 41.4% over twelve months; TEP gross margin down 162 basis points year over year in Q2 2026 against Badger Meter's 30
Payment processors and card networks to Roper Against Roper on mix Reoccurring revenue rose from 6.5% to 10.5% of total revenue in two years at an implied 50-65% gross margin, against 68.5% for Application Software
Roper to software customers In Roper's favour Mid-90s enterprise gross retention; customers prepay $2,078m of deferred revenue; Deltek's Costpoint end-of-support in Q1 2028 moves customers to cloud at "over 2x"
Roper to municipal utilities Against Roper The July 2025 surcharge was withdrawn after customers rejected it
Roper to large alternate-site healthcare buyers Against Roper Network Software recurring revenue declined at MHA on "more large customers with lower unit economics, and that actually hits the revenue line" (Q2 2026 call)
Freight market to DAT In Roper's favour for the first time in years Carrier additions rising, spot strengthening against contract, rejection rates rising

The chain funds Roper. Customers prepay $2,078m of deferred revenue ($1,907m current, $171m non-current) against $1,391m of minimum fixed-price purchase commitments, so net the chain hands Roper about $686m of interest-free funding.▪ Revenue recognised in FY2025 out of the opening deferred balance was $1,717m, so the balance turns roughly once a year. Roper's own framing in the FY2025 MD&A: "Consistent negative net working capital demonstrates Roper's continued focus on asset-light business models."

Circular flows. Three run between Roper and its own markets, and two of them are new. Outgo, acquired May 2025 and folded into DAT, factors carriers' freight invoices, selling them to a third-party financial institution on a non-recourse basis while retaining a beneficial interest fair-valued at $10.1m at 30 June 2026, with $4.5m of cash inflows in the half reported within investing activities. Against H1 2026 free cash flow of about $1,005m the add-back is 0.4%; the size is trivial and the change in position is not, because DAT has moved from a neutral matching venue to a credit provider on one side of its own market. Second, since the 2022 Indicor transaction Roper has been required to pay Clayton, Dubilier & Rice quarterly, either about $29m a year in cash or in kind through transfer of about 1.7% of its Indicor ownership a year, an obligation that ends when Indicor reaches $425.0m of EBITDA in any three twelve-month periods or on an Indicor IPO; it was suspended indefinitely when Indicor agreed the AMETEK sale. Third, Roper's 43.4% Indicor stake is marked at $1,792m at 30 June 2026 after the AMETEK agreement, and AMETEK appears in Roper's own peer set and is now the buyer of assets Roper sold in 2022.

Where the profit pool is. The highest-margin layer across the three chains is Roper's own network software, at 84.1% gross and 43.5% segment operating margin. Layers upstream and downstream in the vertical software chain earn less on a comparable base: Tyler at 46.5% gross, Badger Meter at 41.7%, Itron at 37.7%. The one exception upstream is the hyperscaler. Roper's constraint is access to more of that pool, and the assets that compound the way Roper underwrites are the ones sponsors are least willing to sell cheaply.

FY2024 5.6% 2.5% 9.3% 5.8%
FY2025 5.4% 4.1% 6.5% 5.4%
Q1 2026 5.2% 5.2% 7.1% 5.6%
Q2 2026 4.5% 3.6% 7.1% 4.9%

Sources: 10-K FY2022 through FY2025 MD&A; 10-Q Q1 and Q2 2026 MD&A.

Consolidated organic growth declined 4.5 points from FY2022 to Q2 2026, and every year steps down. Foreign exchange is not part of the story: it contributed 0.2 points in FY2025 and 0.2 points in Q2 2026, and only 9% of revenue is in non-USD functional currencies.

The growth is concentrated in one revenue stream. In Q2 2026, organic growth by stream inside the two software segments was +7% recurring, −2% reoccurring and −4% non-recurring (Q2 2026 call). Weighting those by the FY2025 software-segment stream mix — recurring 72.9%, reoccurring 13.7%, non-recurring 13.4% — gives 0.729 × 7 + 0.137 × (−2) + 0.134 × (−4) = 4.3%, which reconciles to the disclosed software-segment organic rates. Blending with Technology Enabled Products at 7.1% on its 23.6% revenue weight gives 4.9%, matching the consolidated figure. So the 73% of software revenue that recurs grew 7%, and the remaining 27% subtracted about 0.8 points. Every growth driver Roper describes outside subscriptions shrank in the latest quarter.▪

Driver against realized, three tests.

Deltek and government contracting. Calendar H1 2026 federal contract obligations were $379.3bn, up $48.1bn or 14.5% against H1 2025, with defence at 55% of the total (fed-spend.com, accessed 2026-09-11) [web]. Deltek grew at "the lower end of mid-single digits for the year as compared to the solid mid-single digit plus grower it's been over the decade that we've owned the business" (Q4 2025 call). The end-market money grew 14.5% and the software supplier to that market grew in the low-to-mid single digits.▪ Three explanations are on the record and only one is a demand explanation: a transmission lag, because "the benefit reaches us only after our customers win awards and invest in systems"; an accounting mix effect, because most government-contracting enterprise expansions are still sold as perpetual licences and conversion to cloud suppresses reported revenue during the transition; and procurement disruption from DOGE, agency reorganisations and the shutdown. The second reverses mechanically and the third dated from 2025. The open question is whether Deltek's normalised rate is the prior decade's mid-single-digit-plus or something lower now that the licence base is converting, and underneath it, that the billable firm count declined 6.9% in one year.

DAT and freight. DAT publishes the volume series itself. Its Truckload Volume Index for July 2026, released 2026-08-11, declined year over year in all three equipment types: dry van 252 (−3%), reefer 181 (−13%), flatbed 291 (−7%) [web, DAT release, accessed 2026-09-11]. Prices moved the other way, with July 2026 dry van spot at $2.41 per mile excluding fuel, up 47%. Management's Q2 2026 headline was "at DAT, we're seeing improving freight market conditions for the first time in many years," and the qualification is in the same paragraph: "We still need to see load volumes improve before becoming fully bullish on the recovery." The recovery under way is a capacity contraction that lifts price. For DAT that is revenue-positive, because higher spot rates pull carriers back onto the spot market and onto load boards, but a price-led recovery caused by carriers leaving the industry is a different underwriting from a volume-led one, since the subscriber pool is the population of carriers.▪ Roper publishes no DAT subscriber count or ARPU, so the split cannot be measured. Guidance now assumes "a modest benefit in '26" (Q2 2026 call), a change from the earlier "no meaningful freight market recovery."

AI and agentic products. Management's magnitude estimate: "We're sort of a 5% to 7%, 6% to 8% sort of organic growth business. I think this is hundreds of basis points, but it's not a doubling of the growth rate of the enterprise" (Goldman Sachs, 2026-09-09). Realized through Q2 2026 is not material: "will it be material revenue in the second half? It will not be for us this year," and "we haven't really baked in anything meaningful for AI above what the businesses are delivering today. And so that's more of a plan for '27." The cost has already landed. Applying management's own range to FY2025 revenue, 200 to 400 basis points of added organic growth implies $158m to $316m of incremental annual revenue▪ [estimate: management's spoken "hundreds of basis points" applied to the disclosed revenue base; the high end is capped by the "not a doubling" constraint]. For scale, the entire reoccurring stream took two years to build from $401m to $833m, an increase of $432m.

6.2 Market growth against company growth

Management sizes its own markets small and deliberately: the largest single market is about $4bn a year and most are $1bn or less, "already very, very well vended, particularly by us and a very small number of competitors." Across 29 business units and $7,903m of revenue, the aggregate market is $20.8bn to $37.6bn [estimate: the largest market at the disclosed $4bn, the remaining 28 at an assumed $0.6bn to $1.2bn average given "most are $1 billion or less"], implying a blended share of 21% to 38%. The cross-check from the other direction agrees: $7,903m across 29 units is $272m of average revenue per unit, 27% of a $1bn average market.

At roughly a quarter to a third of its own defined addressable markets, and in markets management describes as already well vended, the share-gain contribution available to organic growth is limited by arithmetic.▪ The flagship share-gain case is also largely complete: Aderant's share "has gone from, like, 35% to 65%" since Roper acquired it (Q2 2026 call; the Q1 2026 version is 35-40% to 60-65%). Doubling share again is not available.▪ Forward growth has to come from market growth, price and market redefinition — cloud conversion, payments attach, agentic SKUs — instead of from taking the remaining share inside the existing definitions.

Industry software dollars are booming and Roper's software organic growth is not. Gartner's July 2026 forecast puts worldwide software spending at $1.44 trillion in 2026, growing 15.1% (gartner.com, accessed 2026-09-11) [web]. Roper's two software segments grew 4.5% and 3.6% organically in Q2 2026. The aggregate is inflated by AI infrastructure software and hyperscaler spend that has no counterpart in mid-market vertical systems of record, so this is not a share-loss calculation. It does establish the shape: industry dollars are being repriced upward by AI while Roper's vertical software organic growth decelerates. Management agrees on the mechanism — asked whether AI budget reallocation was hurting customer IT spend, the CEO answered "the punchline on that, the TLDR is no."

Peer growth cohort, split by exposure. Calendar Q2 2026, on each company's own disclosed basis:

Company Cohort CQ2 2026 growth Basis
Constellation Software Vertical-software serial acquirer 3% (1% after FX) organic
Topicus.com Vertical-software serial acquirer 4% organic
Roper Vertical-software serial acquirer 4.9% organic
Tyler Technologies Vertical-software operator about 6.2% organic, derived from 8.2% total less about 2 points of acquisition
SS&C Vertical-software operator 7.6% adjusted organic, constant currency
Bentley Systems Vertical-software operator 12.2% constant-currency total, not adjusted for acquisitions

AMETEK Diversified industrial acquirer 10% organic

Sources: each company's Q2 2026 release or call, all accessed 2026-09-11 [web]. The bases differ and the two total-revenue rows overstate against an organic figure.

Roper grew faster than the two vertical-software roll-ups and slower than every vertical-software operator and every diversified industrial acquirer in the set.▪ The industrial cohort's acceleration has a cause Roper does not share: Teledyne and AMETEK cited record orders on AI-infrastructure demand, and IDEX cited "AI-driven demand for data center power and semiconductor markets, as well as strength in space and defense." Roper has no revenue exposure to AI infrastructure. It is a buyer of frontier-model capacity and pays hyperscaler prices for it. Grouped by exposure instead of by label, Roper grew like the capital-deployment cohort it belongs to, not like the vertical-software operators it compares itself to on calls.

6.3 Cyclical against secular

The 2023 Investor Day made the strongest version of the non-cyclicality claim: cyclical revenue went from 44% of the company to "approaching 0," and "there's virtually no cyclicality. That's the operating risk, right? As compounders, everything needs to move forward and nothing can go backwards."

The 2024-2026 record does not support that. FY2025 organic growth came in at 5.4% against an initial January 2025 guide of 6% to 7%, and management reconciled the whole shortfall to three businesses: "it's Deltek because of GovCon, it's Neptune because of the dynamics we talked about and it's Procare. That almost fully reconciles the difference." That is 0.6 to 1.6 points of consolidated organic growth, 11% to 23% of the guided rate, lost in one year to three named businesses. Two of the three drags are cycles.

Business The cycle it tracks
Deltek Federal appropriations and procurement policy: DOGE, the shutdown, One Big Beautiful Bill timing
DAT The truckload capacity cycle, carrier entry and exit
Neptune Municipal water capital budgets and channel-backlog normalisation

The portfolio reshaping removed exposure to upstream oil and gas and to short-cycle industrial demand and replaced it with exposure to federal procurement policy, the trucking capacity cycle and municipal capital budgets.▪ Those three cycles run through the largest business of the largest segment, the largest business of the smallest software segment, and the segment with the highest organic growth rate. The amplitude is lower than industrial pumps and the cycles are less correlated with each other, which is a real improvement in quality. The claim of virtual acyclicality is not supported by the realized 2025 shortfall.

The segment recut also removed a disclosure. Roper deleted the risk factor "Some of the industries in which we operate are cyclical, and, accordingly, our business is subject to changes in the economy" from the FY2022 10-K, the first annual report after the industrial sale. Since then the largest organic-growth disappointments have come from cyclical demand at DAT, Foundry, ConstructConnect and the federal budget cycle at Deltek.

6.4 Shifts that change the slope

Upward. The ground-to-cloud conversion is the largest. At the 2023 Investor Day management put the on-premise annual maintenance base at about $900m converting at 2 to 2.5x the maintenance price, with the caveat that "my guess is that takes every bit of a decade," and the CEO added: "I really don't think it has any long-term impact... it's a tailwind, but it's not like a predominant part of the growth algorithm." A $900m base converting at 2 to 2.5x over a decade is roughly $90m to $135m of incremental annual revenue if spread evenly, about 1.1 to 1.7 points of growth on the FY2025 base, and it is not evenly spread: Deltek's Costpoint end-of-support date is Q1 2028.▪ Agentic monetisation is the second, priced as a subscription to an orchestration layer with stair-step consumption tiers plus straight transactional pricing at DAT and SoftWriters, and sized by management at hundreds of basis points. Payments attach is the third, and it is the one whose organic rate has already turned negative.

Downward. Foundation-model pricing pass-through is the structural one: Roper's AI spend is up about 3x annualised since January 2026 and rising, and the FY2025 10-K says exposure to provider pricing increases as AI becomes central and may not be passable to customers. If agentic SKUs are priced in stair-step consumption tiers while token costs are variable, the gross margin of the new revenue is a function of a supplier's price list. AI-native entrants at the low end are the second, and management's own acknowledgement names one exposed business and describes the defence as market size: "the size of the prize is quite small... already very, very well vended." The legal billing model is the third: firm-level AI adoption rose from 26% in 2024 to 42% in 2026 and more than half of legal professionals expect AI efficiency to reduce the prevalence of the billable hour (tallenxis.com, accessed 2026-09-11) [web], against Aderant's time-capture and billing products. Roper's answer is that Aderant serves "the business of law" instead of "the practice of law."

6.5 The FY2026 acceleration is arithmetic

Guidance moved from 5-6% organic in January 2026 to "the 6% area" in July. Realized H1 2026, revenue-weighted, was 5.25%. Reaching 6.0% for the full year requires about 6.75% in H2; at the softer reading of "6% area" as 5.8%, about 6.35%. Required acceleration against H1: 1.1 to 1.5 points [estimate: roughly equal half-year revenue weights].

Management's own attribution is mechanical: "a lot of the increase is sort of in the bank. It's first half doing better than we thought. And then there's the mechanics in the second half of Subsplash, CentralReach turning organic and then sort of easier comps, especially in the third quarter at TEP." CentralReach was acquired 23 April 2025 and enters the organic base in Q3 2026; Subsplash was acquired in July 2025 and enters in Q4 2026. Both grow faster than the company.

A material part of Roper's reported organic growth acceleration in H2 2026 and into 2027 comes from fast-growing acquired businesses crossing the twelve-month ownership line, not from demand improving at the businesses already in the base. Reported organic growth at this company is partly a function of the M&A cadence one year earlier.▪ With roughly $50m of bolt-ons closed in H1 2026 against $8,960m across 2023-2025, the 2027-2028 vintage of that effect is currently close to empty.

The bookings line has moved a long way. On the Q4 2024 call management said enterprise bookings "accelerated, ending in the high teens growth area in Q4"; by Q2 2026 the description is "core bookings up mid-single digit plus on a TTM basis." The two figures are on different bases — a quarterly growth rate for total bookings against a trailing-twelve-month rate for core bookings — so the gap is not a clean ten-point deceleration, and Roper publishes no numeric series that would make it clean. On the disclosure that exists, the leading indicator went from high teens to mid-single digits plus over six quarters, and the organic growth rate followed it down from 7.0% in Q4 2024 to 4.9% in Q2 2026.

7. Critical points

1. Three quarters of the last five years' revenue growth was purchased, and the purchase has stopped. Application Software revenue grew from $1,786m (FY2020) to $4,483m (FY2025). Compounding the reported organic rates off the FY2020 base gives $2,469m, so organic supplied $683m of the $2,697m increase and acquisitions $2,014m, 75% [estimate: reported organic rates compounded off the reported FY2020 base]. Company-wide, acquisitions contributed 6.7 to 8.1 points of total growth in each of FY2023, FY2024 and FY2025, and $8,956m of cash went out the door across those three years. In the first half of 2026 acquisition spend was $27.5m of cash, about $50m gross, and $2,727m went into repurchasing shares. Without a restart, FY2027 total growth loses 3 to 7 points of the pattern of the prior three years.

2. Organic growth has decelerated in each of the last three years and the deceleration is broad. Consolidated organic growth went 9.4% (FY2022), 7.8%, 5.8%, 5.4%, then 5.6% in Q1 2026 and 4.9% in Q2 2026. Application Software, 56.7% of revenue, stepped down from 6.5% in Q2 2025 to 4.5% in Q2 2026. Management's through-cycle target has been 7.0-7.5% since roughly 2023 and was restated upward in February 2026 as an "entitled" rate "north of 8%," in the same call that guided FY2026 to 5-6% and said "we're not baking in an organic inflection in 2026."

3. The FY2026 per-share growth is mostly a smaller denominator. Guided adjusted diluted EPS of $22.15-$22.30 is 11% above FY2025's $20.00. On about 101.0m weighted diluted shares [estimate: H1 actual 102.6m plus an H2 figure from the 98.9m outstanding at 7/28/2026, on the guidance's own no-further-repurchase convention], the implied adjusted net earnings are about $2,245m, up under 4%. In Q2 2026 adjusted diluted EPS rose 10% on adjusted net earnings up 2.7% and a share count 7.2% lower. Asked directly whether the guide was "essentially a share count-driven guide," the CFO answered "That's correct."

4. Returns on the capital Roper deploys are near, not above, its cost of capital, and management's own underwriting says so. Return on invested capital including goodwill was 6.4% in FY2025 and has not exceeded 10.1% in ten years, against roughly a 3.2% after-tax cost of debt and an approximate 8% blended cost of capital. Adding back the $815m of acquired-intangible amortization and grossing the denominator up for the accumulated amortization that add-back consumed takes FY2025 to 7.6% (§3.4). Management's own underwriting standard, set out in §3.1, implies a high-single-digit after-tax yield on cost in year five. Roper's preferred internal measure, cash return on investment, excludes goodwill and acquired intangibles from its denominator, which is where $31,105m of the $34,577m balance sheet and almost all of the $27,009m of deployed capital are recorded.

5. The integrated-payments stream, the fastest-growing reported line, has stopped growing organically. Application Software reoccurring revenue went $138m (FY2023) to $354m (FY2024) to $523m (FY2025), then $116.8m to $117.6m year over year in Q2 2026, up 0.7%, and 2.5% for the half, with both acquired books fully in the prior-year base. Roper paid about $3,460m for Transact and Procare. If that stream had grown at the mid-teens rate Procare's deal model assumed, H1 2026 segment revenue would have been about $32m higher, 1.3 points of segment growth.

6. Two of three segments' margins have inflected down, and the causes are mix changes management calls permanent. Network Software operating margin went 45.2% (FY2024) to 43.5% (FY2025) to 41.0% (Q2 2026) on the Subsplash payments mix and Convoy investment; Technology Enabled Products went 34.5% to 33.3% on bronze ingot cost at Neptune and a consumables mix shift at NDI and Verathon. Applying H1 2025's 35.2% operating margin to H1 2026 revenue in Technology Enabled Products leaves a $22.5m shortfall: gross margin explains $16.5m and SG&A deleverage $5.8m, and within the gross-margin piece copper accounts for roughly $4-5m (25-30%) and the consumables mix roughly $11-12m (70%). Pricing recovers the copper; nothing reverses the mix.

7. Leverage rose half a turn in six months to fund buybacks, with no acquired EBITDA in the denominator. Net debt went from $9,004m at 12/31/2025 to $10,955m at 6/30/2026 and net debt to EBITDA from 2.9x to 3.4x, funded by $2,000m of net revolver borrowing. Every prior leverage increase in the decade brought acquired earnings in; this one did not, so the half turn has to be repaid out of free cash flow and the Indicor proceeds. Undrawn revolver capacity declined from about $2,644m to about $644m, against a $700m note maturing 15 December 2026. Moody's affirmed Baa2 with a positive outlook in November 2025 at 3.0x and published a downgrade trigger above 4.0x, leaving about $1,945m of additional net-debt headroom.

8. The compensation plan pays on absolute dollars that capital deployment produces. Every annual bonus metric through 2025 was an absolute quantity — adjusted net earnings growth, then adjusted EBITDA growth — with no per-share denominator and no organic limitation, and both definitions add back acquisition-related expenses. FY2025 adjusted EBITDA grew 11.0% against a 3% threshold and a 10% target, and acquisitions plausibly supplied $120-190m of the $311m increase, 39-61% of it [estimate: acquired revenue contribution at a 25-40% first-year EBITDA margin]. From 2026 the annual bonus splits 50/50 between organic revenue growth and adjusted EBITDA core margin, and the 2026 long-term grant moves to adjusted diluted EPS with a relative free-cash-flow-margin modifier.

9. A seat-priced software base is exposed to the product Roper is building. About 57% of FY2025 revenue is software recurring revenue sold per user. Management has named three businesses whose pricing meter may have to change because agentic AI reduces the unit being billed, and two of them — Vertafore and Aderant — are the segment's strongest franchises, with the first Vertafore change shipping in early 2027 and described as revenue-neutral by design. The Q2 2026 10-Q states the same risk in the company's own words: "New AI offerings may disrupt our offerings or transform workforce needs and may negatively impact demand for our offerings."

10. The Indicor stake has become the largest swing factor in reported earnings, and about $1.1-1.2bn of cash from it is the near-term offset to leverage. The Level 3 mark moved from $535m at inception (November 2022) to $796m at 12/31/2025 to $1,792m at 6/30/2026 after Indicor agreed to sell its instrumentation businesses to AMETEK at an enterprise value of about $5.0bn. Roper's own two disclosures of the proceeds disagree by $100m on each basis: the 10-Q says "approximately $1.3 billion (estimated $1.1 billion net of income taxes)" and the call eight days earlier said "approximately $1.4 billion or an estimated $1.2 billion after tax." The last Indicor operating figures anywhere are FY2022, when it had $916m of revenue and $234m of operating income.

Items 2, 3, 5 and 9 are also pressure tests of management's own framing and are argued in §8.

8. Management claim pressure tests

Claim: organic growth of 7.0-7.5% through the cycle, with an "entitled" rate north of 8%. Delivered organic growth was 8% (FY2023), 6% (FY2024), 5% (FY2025) and is guided to about 6% for FY2026. The three completed years average 6.3% and the trend is down.▪ The February 2026 restatement of the target came in the same call that guided 5-6% and declined to assume an inflection. Management concedes the record without conceding the potential: "I'm simultaneously encouraged and frustrated on the organic growth... we have the potential, very clear potential pre-AI to be a high single-digit consistent organic growth business. It has been frustratingly difficult to get our chin on that" (Goldman Sachs, 2026-09-09). Consensus resolves this at 6.0% for CY2027, the bottom of management's own framing.

Claim: the growth shortfalls are idiosyncratic. Citi's analyst put the counter-case in its strongest form on 2026-09-10: "there have been this objective of returning the business back to kind of high single-digit organic growth. There's been a few kind of stumbling blocks along the way that derailed that. Each sort of feels idiosyncratic, but when you sort of stack them all together, Deltek, Neptune, arguably DAT." That is three separate idiosyncratic explanations in sequence over three years, from a 29-business portfolio whose stated purpose is to diversify single-asset risk. Management's answer is the same pattern from the other side: "Last year was frustrating because 17 of 25 of the businesses did what they need to do and then 3 or 4 of the larger ones had market sort of challenges."

Claim: integrated payments is the fastest-growing piece of the software segments. That is true of the reported line and not the organic one. Reported reoccurring revenue nearly doubled over two years on acquired books; organic reoccurring revenue declined 2% in Q2 2026 across the software segments and grew 2.5% in H1 2026 in Application Software.▪ Management's stated cause is implementation throughput at Procare, which it calls "completely fixable" and "eminently fixable." That repair has been promised across four consecutive quarters: "not as much as we had thought" (Q3 2025), "did not perform to our expectations in 2025" (Q4 2025), "remains a work in progress" (Q2 2026).

Claim: "we're the leader in a small market which means, by definition, all of our competitors are smaller." It holds for Aderant, CentralReach, Data Innovations, PowerPlan and Deltek's architecture and engineering line. It does not hold for Illumia against Global Payments' TouchNet and a payments-native Flywire, Clinisys against an Epic taking EHR share at 43.7% and rising, Frontline's student-management line against a PowerSchool with $720m of ARR growing 18%, or Deltek's construction and consulting lines against Autodesk's $3,583m AECO business growing 22%. Those four lines are on the order of a third of Application Software revenue [estimate: §4.1].

Claim: 84.1% gross margin and mid-50s EBITDA margins describe Network Software. They describe FY2025. Adjusted EBITDA margin went 56.1% (FY2024) to 54.1% (FY2025) to 50.9% (Q2 2026), and operating margin 45.2% to 43.5% to 41.0%. The causes are disclosed and are choices: Subsplash's payments mix and the Convoy investment inside DAT. Core margin excluding acquisitions moved −20bp then +30bp across the two 2026 quarters, so the existing businesses are holding price and the segment's margin structure has reset. Anything built off the FY2025 margin overstates the present by 250bp at the operating line and 320bp at EBITDA.

Claim: Roper's razor-and-blade franchises put the high-quality revenue in the consumable. The disclosed economics invert it. Technology Enabled Products gross margin declined 170 basis points year over year in the June 2026 quarter and 180 in the March quarter, and management attributes both to "a mix shift at both NDI and Verathon towards faster-growing consumables which carry lower gross margins." Over six years segment gross margin moved from 61.5% to 56.9% while the consumables share rose. Operating margin was defended entirely by SG&A leverage of 260 basis points, from 26.2% to 23.6% of revenue, not by price.

Claim: Neptune is a "slow and steady share gainer" that leads its market. Neptune is smaller on revenue than Badger Meter's utility water business and much smaller than Xylem's smart metering line, and it was named fifth among the top five North American AMI endpoint vendors by installed base [web]. The one recorded attempt to exercise pricing power in a cost shock was withdrawn after customers rejected it, and the disruption contributed to a mid-year cut in FY2025 organic guidance from 6-7% to "the 6% area." Against that, Neptune declined only modestly in the June 2026 quarter while Badger Meter's utility water sales declined 8.1% and Itron's revenue declined 7.2%, so the whole North American market contracted and Neptune contracted less.▪ Roper cites a third-party industry report showing its share "actually improved a little bit" in Q3 2025 without naming the report.

Claim: AI is a growth driver. Three years in, AI is a cost line. FY2026 guidance includes no AI revenue and management declined to size 2027, with the CFO on timing: "this is a $100 billion question, and we're just not there yet." Meanwhile AI spend is up about 3x annualised since January 2026 and expected higher by year end, the central team is at "maybe the halfway point... in terms of head count, but probably much higher on spend," and the CFO expects agentic gross margins to "start off worse than SaaS." The one unit-level revenue statistic is CentralReach's 75% AI or AI-influenced share of new bookings in Q1 2026, in a business that is roughly 3% of Roper revenue.

Claim: the agentic layer gives incumbents "a high, high, high right to win." That framing compares Roper to AI-native startups. Against the other incumbent in the same vertical the record runs differently. Applied Systems announced seven AI products on 8 October 2025; Vertafore launched six agents covering the same four categories on 14 April 2026. Applied shipped the directly overlapping categories six months earlier, in Roper's second-largest software franchise by acquisition price. Roper's own FY2025 10-K concedes the mechanism: "AI capabilities could quickly become commoditized."

Claim: "we've never been the buyer and fixer of an asset ever, at least intentionally" (Q2 2026 call). Two disclosed positions contradict it. Convoy, acquired 30 July 2025, was described on the Q3 2025 call as "an unusual transaction for us as it currently is not profitable, but we expect the financial returns over the next several years to be extremely attractive," at a reported price near $250m for an asset Flexport had reportedly bought for about $16m roughly twenty months earlier. And twenty-two months after a $1,750m net purchase price, Procare had management "shoring up the core product, go-to-market execution and implementation capability," with the chief executive, chief financial, chief revenue and chief technology officers all replaced.

Claim: the buyback was opportunistic. Execution was tranche-sized in round dollar amounts and paused on authorization limits. Purchases stopped at exactly $2,500.0m of remaining authorization in December 2025 and exactly $1,000.0m in March 2026, and restarted in April at $352.87 — 1.3% above the February average price — within days of the Board adding $3,000m on 2026-04-23. Pace did not rise as the price declined: February was the heaviest month at 3.431m shares and $348.32, and June, the cheapest month at $328.65, saw 0.571m shares, 83% fewer. Execution inside each month tracked the monthly mean closely. Marked at the 2026-09-11 close of $388.52, the program is 8.3% ahead in aggregate, with the first tranche at $445.87 12.9% behind.

Claim: "the capital allocation mathematically always favored M&A" until the last eight months. The revealed record matches the direction — nine years with no buyback, then $3.2bn once the share price had declined about 40% from its 2025 high. Management also frames the comparison with a hurdle in Roper's own favour: "we always look at the buyback of our own stock versus an acquisition with a risk premium. We always obviously know ourselves better than anything we could know externally, so we have to sort of be compensated the returns on that." Under that rule a buyback must clear a higher bar than an acquisition, which is the reverse of the usual treatment of a known asset against an unknown one.

Claim: "mid-teens free cash flow compounding." The claim is quoted with a rolling base year and a Section 174 adjustment: "compounded 14% if adjusted for Section 174" (Q4 2024), "an 18% CAGR since 2022... 14%" ex-174 (Q4 2025), "compounded at 18% over the past 3 years or 15% adjusted for Section 174" (Q2 2026). The single-year path underneath decelerated: adjusted free cash flow grew 16% in FY2024 and 8% in FY2025. The FY2023-FY2025 compound rate on the computed series is 12.4%.▪ FY2025 free cash flow also included roughly $150m of one-time cash tax benefit from the OBBBA repeal of Section 174 capitalization, worth about 1.9 points of the 30.8% FY2025 free-cash-flow margin.

Claim: the goodwill record is clean because no goodwill has ever been impaired. The clean record is produced by a qualitative test. In FY2025 Roper tested all 25 reporting units qualitatively and performed no quantitative assessment on any of them, against goodwill of $21,341m, 62% of total assets and more than total stockholders' equity of $19,882m, with individual reporting-unit balances from $17.5m to $3,372m. Roper has impaired intangibles once in a decade: $99.5m at Sunquest in Q4 2021, a $94.4m trade-name charge taken when the modelled royalty rate was cut from 3.5% to 0.5% as the business merged into CliniSys, plus $5.1m on a software intangible. Roper had paid about $1,415m for Sunquest in August 2012 and described it on the Q1 2021 call as having had "competitive headwinds for 4 or 5 years." So the single clearly disappointing large deal did produce a write-down, in the intangible lines and not in goodwill.

The five inflections

  • Deltek, December 2016. Roper paid $2.8bn all cash for a business expected to produce $535m of 2017 revenue and $200m of EBITDA, and told the rating agencies leverage would reach about 3.9x before declining. Combined with Aderant (October 2015) and ConstructConnect (October 2016), Roper deployed $5,485m across 2015 and 2016, 1.4x its FY2016 revenue base. Organic growth went from −0.3% (FY2016) to 5.3% (FY2017) to 9.4% (FY2018) and gross margin from 61.5% to 63.2%. That establishes the behaviour: Roper will take leverage to roughly 4x for a single asset it judges a category leader, fund it entirely with investment-grade debt, and spend the following year deleveraging.
  • The succession and the divestitures, September 2018 to November 2022. Hunn took over with no transition period and within four months had announced the sale of the camera businesses; by March 2019 he had rebuilt the reporting segments around business model. Six divestitures over four years removed the industrial portfolio. Between FY2018 and FY2023 gross margin went 63.2% to 69.7% and operating cash flow $1,430m to $2,035m, on a revenue base that grew from $5,191m to $6,178m across two changes of basis. The episode also shows how Roper handles a blocked process: the Gatan sale to Thermo Fisher was terminated on 2019-06-10 over UK regulatory approval, Roper disclosed the termination in full in the FY2019 10-K, and had signed AMETEK at the same approximately $925.0m within the following quarter, booking an $801.1m pretax gain.
  • Vertafore, September 2020. The largest deal in company history at $5,399m, funded with $3,300m of new senior notes plus $1,620m of revolver at an overall financing cost management put at approximately 1%. Acquisition spend was $6,018m in 2020 and $217m in 2021, and net debt declined $1.7bn in the following year. The 2021 pattern repeats 2017 exactly.
  • The payments-led mix shift, 2024 to 2026. Application Software reoccurring revenue went from $138m (FY2023) to $523m (FY2025) on Procare and Transact, and Network Software added Subsplash in July 2025. Consolidated gross margin declined in each of the last four years, 70.5% to 69.2%. The segment effect is sharper: Network Software operating margin peaked at 45.2% in FY2024 and was 40.8% in H1 2026, 440 basis points in eighteen months, while core margins improved 30 basis points in Q2 2026.
  • The capital-allocation break, October 2025 to July 2026. Diluted weighted-average shares rose in every year from 100.9m (2014) to 108.2m (FY2025), with no repurchase program in the FY2016 through FY2024 filings. Roper then bought 8.986m shares for $3,224m in eight months, taking the quarterly diluted count to 100.6m. Net debt went $9,004m to $10,955m, leverage 2.9x to 3.4x, equity $19,882m to $18,700m. Management's stated trigger was price: "Until the last 8 months, the capital allocation mathematically always favored M&A... with the current share price level of Roper in the broader software sector, all of a sudden, buybacks became significantly more attractive." The direction has already turned again toward deleveraging and M&A.

Behavioural patterns for the forward view

Deployment is concentrated in single years and followed by a near-stop: $3,722m (2016) then $154m (2017); $6,018m (2020) then $217m (2021); $4,280m (2022) then $2,053m (2023). H1 2026 is the fourth digestion phase. Leverage is used to roughly 4x and then retired with cash flow, and Roper has not issued equity to fund a deal in this window. A downturn is a buying condition: organic revenue declined 1.8% in 2020 and Roper spent $6,018m on acquisitions that year; the stock lost 11.6% in 2022 and Roper closed Frontline at $3,738m in October. Windfalls went back into acquisitions and debt paydown until 2025 — the $921m of pretax 2019 disposal gains and the roughly $2.6bn of 2022 Indicor cash both went into acquisitions and debt paydown — and management has earmarked the pending Indicor proceeds the same way. And segments are recut about every three years, with each recut breaking the prior series.

Two episodes the current narrative reframes

On the 2022-06-01 CD&R call the CFO told analysts the retained 49% of Indicor was "not mark to market, by the way, because it's a private thing. So it will just be a slug of assets sitting there until it gets monetized. So there won't be a ton of visibility." Roper elected the fair value option in the FY2022 10-K and changed the valuation methodology in 2023, and the mark has since been the largest swing factor in reported earnings: +$235m (FY2024), +$26m (FY2025), +$829m in Q2 2026 alone against $858m of acquired-intangible amortization for the whole of FY2025.

FY2019's record GAAP diluted EPS of $16.82 and 37.4% net margin came from $921m of pretax disposal gains on Gatan and the imaging businesses, with about $200m of the associated cash tax paid in 2020. Long-run charts built on adjusted diluted EPS exclude both the gain and the cash tax.

10. Management, incentives and capital allocation

10.1 Who runs Roper

Roper names three executive officers in the FY2025 10-K. Neil Hunn, 53, has been President and CEO since August 2018 and joined in 2011 from MedAssets, where he was EVP and CFO for ten years; the 10-K states he "led the execution of the majority of the Company's capital deployment since joining Roper," so the succession moved the existing capital allocator into the top job. Jason Conley, 50, became EVP and CFO in February 2023 after seventeen years at Roper in investor relations, financial planning, a subsidiary CFO role, Controller and Chief Accounting Officer. John Stipancich, 57, is EVP, General Counsel and Corporate Secretary, from Newell Brands.

Nine directors, eight independent, with Amy Woods Brinkley as Independent Chair since June 2021 and the Chair and CEO roles separated. Tenure runs from 2005 (Robert Johnson) and 2007 (Richard Wallman, Audit Chair) to 2024 (John Murphy, former CFO of Adobe); Thomas Joyce, retired CEO of Danaher, joined in 2021. The Compensation Committee is chaired by Laura Thatcher, who ran Alston & Bird's executive-compensation practice. Operating-company leadership turns over more often and is promoted internally: "I think 4 of the last 6 or 7 CEO promotions or hires have been internal" (Citi, 2026-09-10).

One reporting disclosure is unusual and matches the company's description of capital deployment as a Board-level activity. The FY2025 10-K states: "The Company's chief operating decision maker ('CODM') is a group that consists of the Chief Executive Officer and the Board of Directors... as such decisions are made by our Chief Executive Officer and Board of Directors collectively" (Note 15). Under ASC 280 the chief operating decision maker is usually a single executive.

The annual bonus metric, year by year.

Year Metric Threshold Target Actual Payout CEO payment
2020 Adjusted net earnings growth flat +10% below 29.2% $584,000
2021 Adjusted net earnings growth flat (20% payout) +10%, +15% for full overdrive +20.7% 150% $3,000,000
2022 Adjusted net earnings, continuing operations +2.5% +10% +15.7% 100% $2,000,000
