2025 Adjusted EBITDA growth +3% +10% +11.0% 104.8% $2,096,000

Every metric through 2025 was an absolute dollar quantity, none expressed per share and none limited to organic performance. Adjusted net earnings and adjusted EBITDA both rise when Roper buys a business, and both definitions add back "acquisition-related expenses on completed acquisitions"; the adjusted net earnings definition also adds back acquired-intangible amortization. The purchase price never appears in the metric. Thresholds were low: 2.5-3% growth paid the minimum. For 2021 only, the Committee granted an incremental opportunity worth up to 50% of target "to further incentivize the management team to deliver outstanding incremental growth to make up for the lower than anticipated earnings growth in 2020," and Hunn earned all of it; across 2020 and 2021 together he received $3.584m against a two-year target of $4.0m. The Committee did not reduce the 2020 targets when the year was bad, and disclosed both decisions.

From 2026 the annual bonus splits 50/50 between organic revenue growth and adjusted EBITDA core margin, where core margin measures businesses owned at least one year. Half pays 50% at 5.5% organic growth and 200% at 8% or better; half pays 25% at a 35% core margin and 150% at 40% or better, with an overall cap of 175%. The two halves are not calibrated the same way. Consolidated organic growth was 5.4% in FY2025 and is guided to 5-6% for FY2026, so the growth half begins paying at about the current run-rate and its maximum is well above it. Consolidated adjusted EBITDA margin was 39.8% in FY2025 and 38.6% in Q2 2026, and the core measure excludes newly acquired margin-dilutive businesses so it runs above the consolidated figure, which puts the margin half's threshold about five points below where the company already operates [estimate: the core-margin level is not disclosed, only its year-over-year change in basis points].

Long-term equity. Grants are 25% stock options and 75% performance restricted stock units by value, all cliff-vesting at three years, with no portion of the RSU grant vesting on time alone.

Grant year Metric Maximum vesting Modifier
2023 and earlier Cumulative adjusted EBITDA (50%) and relative adjusted operating cash flow (50%), 36 months 100% of target none
2024 Three-year adjusted net earnings CAGR 200% of target relative TSR, ±25%
2025 Three-year adjusted net earnings CAGR; 35% vests at 1%, 100% at 4-10% 200% of target relative TSR against the S&P 500, ±25%
2026 Three-year adjusted diluted EPS CAGR; overdrive above 9% 200% of target relative adjusted free-cash-flow margin against the S&P 500 ex-utilities, real estate and financials, ±10%

The design moved in opposite directions on leverage and on alignment. In 2024 the Committee removed the 100%-of-target cap its own 2023 proxy had listed among "risk mitigation features," replacing it with overdrive shares worth up to another 100% of target, so maximum long-term opportunity doubled. In 2025 it raised the hurdle: unmodified 100% vesting now requires a 4-10% adjusted net earnings CAGR where it previously required 3-10%, which the proxy quantifies as "an approximate incremental $58 million of adjusted net earnings for the performance period." In 2026 it moved to a per-share metric with a cash-quality modifier, stating the purpose as to "sharpen enterprise focus on organic growth, reinforce disciplined margin management, align long-term incentives with per-share value creation."

The March 2023 grant, covering January 2023 to December 2025 and certified in March 2026, vested above target on both measures: cumulative adjusted EBITDA of $8.486bn against a $6.917bn target level, 22.7% above, and adjusted operating cash flow at the 94th percentile against a 75th-percentile target. That grant had no TSR modifier, because relative TSR was not added until the 2024 grant. Over the identical window Roper's indexed TSR moved from 101 to 106 while the peer-group index moved from 97 to 258.

The 2019 five-year CEO Special Long-Term Cash Incentive, measured on cumulative adjusted EBITDA over January 2019 to December 2023, paid $17,841,683 of a $18,605,000 maximum, about 96%. The target was reset once: the 2020 proxy stated a $9.880bn threshold against the 2019 proxy's $10.325bn, footnoted as revised "to address the impact of the Company's divestitures of its Gatan and imaging businesses." Neutralizing a divestiture is ordinary design; the adjustment was downward by 4.3%, and the final result landed $89m short of the $11.29bn full-payout line, so the reset was material to the outcome.

The peer group used to set pay. Sixteen companies with a median market capitalization of $101,748m at 12/31/2025 against Roper's $47,913m, and a median revenue of $7,601m against Roper's $7,903m. Roper's market value is 47% of the peer median while its revenue is 4% above it. Four of the sixteen are alternative-asset managers — Blackstone, KKR, Ares, Carlyle — and the proxy gives the reasoning: "Given the capital deployment responsibilities of our named executive officers and the private equity-like nature of our business, we consider the compensation levels and practices used by private equity firms... While Roper's operating model is closely akin to that of private equity firms, we do not allow our named executive officers to co-invest in Company investments, nor do they benefit from carried-interest tax treatment." It concludes: "Among private equity firms, compensation for Roper's CEO is below levels that would be expected for commensurate levels of performance." Constellation Software, Topicus, Tyler, SS&C and Bentley — the listed serial acquirers and vertical-software operators nearest Roper's own model — are not in the group.

Ownership and trading. Vanguard holds 11.6% and BlackRock 9.0% at 28 February 2026. Hunn's beneficial ownership of 531,591 shares includes 341,472 exercisable options and 32,665 unvested performance RSUs, leaving about 157,454 owned shares, roughly $70m at the 12/31/2025 close, against a 7x-salary guideline. Group ownership by directors and named executive officers has not grown: 899,283 shares for thirteen people in the 2020 proxy, 819,657 for eleven in 2026, though the 2025 and 2026 tables count only named executive officers so the series is not strictly continuous. Anti-hedging and anti-pledging policies apply with no carve-outs in the 2026 proxy; the 2023 and 2024 proxies had included an exception for shares pledged by one independent director as of January 2015.

Hunn bought 10,000 shares on the open market on 12 November 2025 for $4,522,310, at $451.575 and a weighted average $452.395, three weeks after Roper announced its first repurchase authorization [web, Form 4 coverage, accessed 2026-09-11]. Conley sold 3,000 shares on 25 February 2025 at an average $588.19. In 2025 Hunn exercised 30,000 options realizing $7,704,675, Conley 12,000 realizing $4,152,621 and Stipancich 2,500 realizing $852,197. Six of Hunn's nine outstanding option tranches are struck above the roughly $341 average at which Roper repurchased 3.6 million shares in Q2 2026.

Shareholder votes. Say-on-pay support was over 93% (2023), over 89% (2024), over 91% (2025) and 94.1% of votes cast for-or-against in 2026 (83,849,113 for, 5,263,112 against, 473,255 abstaining). Support in 2026 was above the two prior years and roughly level with 2023, in the year five-year indexed TSR finished at 106 against a peer index at 258. The Committee states it contacts "six of our largest shareholders who we believed voted against the compensation program" each year.

Proposal 6 at the 2026 meeting requested a strategic review of a tax-free spin-off of the Application and Network Software segments with retention of Technology Enabled Products. The proponent's four claims were that generative and agentic AI could disrupt the software businesses; that Roper is "too large to be nimble, but too small to generate the enormous amounts of investment capital needed to compete"; that Roper has paid 15x to 23x forward EBITDA into mature end markets; and that over 2018-2024 organic revenue compounded at 5.6%, operating earnings at 6.4% and free cash flow at 8.9%, against 18% and 17% under Jellison over sixteen years, with average return on invested capital declining from 8.3% to 6.7%. The Board's response turns on the measurement window, arguing that 2019-2025 on a continuing-operations basis is the correct period and gives 6.6%, 14.7% and 16.7%, and that Roper divested businesses representing about 34% of its 2019 revenue for roughly $6bn. Neither side published a restated return-on-invested-capital series. The proposal received 536,956 for against 88,537,496, about 0.6% of shares voted on it.

Separately, WindAcre Partnership disclosed 8,630,200 shares, 8.55% of the 100,917,359 outstanding at 30 April 2026, on a Schedule 13G/A — the passive form — having added 4,401,900 shares in Q1 2026. The 2026 proxy's own footnote estimated approximately 7.1 million shares, about 6.9%, at 19 March 2026 and stated the company "has not received a Schedule 13D or Schedule 13G from this holder." No letter or director slate has been published.

Shareholders also approved a 14,150,000-share increase to the 2021 Incentive Plan, which the proxy states is "approximately 13.8% of our shares of common stock outstanding as of March 23, 2026," in the same year the company retired more than 8% of its shares. The share-count consequence is in §12.4.

FY2022 operating cash flow of $735m is not an operating decline: it reflects $954m of cash taxes paid on the Indicor disposal gain, and investing activities that year included $5,562m of proceeds from the disposition.

Over the decade acquisitions absorbed $27,009m, 173% of cumulative free cash flow; dividends took $2,306m, 14.8%; buybacks $500m, 3.2%, all of it in the last seven weeks. The funding gap was closed by $5,562m of Indicor disposal proceeds, $246m from a 2024 equity-investment sale, and about $6,085m of net new gross debt. Capital expenditure plus capitalized software totalled $727m across ten years against $27,009m of acquisitions, a ratio of 37 to 1.

The break. Between November 2025 and June 2026 Roper repurchased 8.986m shares for $3,223.8m at a blended $358.77, more than 8% of shares outstanding, funded partly by $2,000m of net revolver borrowing. Against diluted weighted-average shares of 108.2m in FY2025, that retired roughly thirteen years of the 0.66m-a-year net issuance observed from 2014 to 2025.

Roper's own published leverage history has no precedent for it. The Investor Day chart plots every quarter from Q4 2016 to Q4 2022, and every peak there follows an acquisition and is repaid inside two years: 4.2x after Deltek, 4.7x after Vertafore, back to 2.7x by Q4 2022. The 3.4x reached in Q2 2026 followed $3.2bn of buybacks against roughly $50m of bolt-ons, with no acquired earnings to grow into.▪ [deck: Investor Day 2023, 2023-03-21, slide 109; deck: Q2 2026, 2026-07-23, slide 7]

The accretion is smaller than the share count suggests. Q2 2026 adjusted diluted EPS of $5.38 rose 10% on a share count 7.2% lower. Adding back after-tax interest on the average repurchase-related debt outstanding during the quarter gives a counterfactual of $5.20 to $5.25 on 108.5m shares, so the cumulative accretion is $0.13 to $0.18 per share, 2.5% to 3.5% [estimate: counterfactual share count of 108.5m, average repurchase debt of about $2,600m at an incremental 4.5-5.5% pre-tax rate, taxed at 21%]. The 7.2% share reduction converts into roughly 3% of earnings accretion because debt interest consumes most of it. The spread is wider on cash: trailing free cash flow of $2.6bn on 100.6m shares is $25.85 per share, a 7.2% yield on the $358.77 average price paid, against an after-tax marginal borrowing cost of about 3.2% to 4.3% [estimate: Q2 2026 net interest expense of $111.4m annualized on average gross debt near $11.0bn is a 4.05% blended pre-tax rate, taxed at 21%].

The quarterly deck prints the gross arithmetic without the interest: adjusted net earnings grew 2.7%, from $528m to $542m, while diluted shares declined 7.2%, from 108.4m to 100.6m, so roughly seven of the ten points of Q2 2026 adjusted diluted EPS growth came from the denominator. The summary slide reports the +10% without that split [deck: Q2 2026, 2026-07-23, slides 6, 17 and 22].

Per-share outcomes. Confined to FY2023-FY2025, the window on a single continuing-operations basis:

Through 2025 size growth reached the per-share line almost intact because the share count barely moved, and that held across the decade: 102.5m (2016) to 108.2m (2025), 5.6% of cumulative dilution over nine years. The 2026 change is the reverse: acquisitions of $28m of cash, and the per-share improvement coming from the denominator.

The stated framework against the revealed record. Roper's internal measure is cash return on investment, defined by Jellison in 2016 as net earnings plus non-cash charges over gross investment — "the physical plant and equipment plus accumulated depreciation plus net working capital." The denominator excludes goodwill and acquired intangibles, which is where $31,105m of the balance sheet and almost all of the $27bn of deployed capital are recorded, so the measure describes the operating efficiency of the businesses acquired and not the return on the price paid for them. It remains the live language — it appears in nine calls from 2020 through Q2 2026 and the 2023 Investor Day called it "fundamental to our valuation methodology" — and none of those references attaches a percentage to it. The last quantified figure, "over 200% this year," dates from Q2 2017, when the portfolio still included the industrial businesses.

Against the 2023 Investor Day algorithm, the free cash flow leg compounded 12.4% across FY2023-FY2025 against a mid-teens target, and FY2025 free cash flow included roughly $150m of one-time Section 174 benefit. The organic leg delivered 8%, 6% and 5% against a 7-7.5% through-cycle target. The "45%+ operating leverage" leg is scoreable from the quarterly decks, which footnote the definition as incremental adjusted EBITDA on incremental adjusted revenue [deck: Q4 2025, 2026-01-27, slide 25].

Consolidated incremental adjusted EBITDA margin FY2023 FY2024 FY2025 Q1 2026 Q2 2026
Realized 42.3% 37.3% 36.0% 26.9% 24.2%

The 45%+ algorithm has not been met in any year since it was published in March 2023. Incremental adjusted EBITDA margin was 42.3% in FY2023, 37.3% in FY2024 and 36.0% in FY2025, then 26.9% and 24.2% in the first two quarters of 2026, against a six-year FY2019-FY2025 measure of 41.0%.▪ Part of the shortfall is the acquisition engine itself: the Q2 2026 deck attributes 60 of the 130 basis points of consolidated adjusted EBITDA margin decline to businesses owned less than four full quarters and 70 to core [deck: Q2 2026, 2026-07-23, slide 21]. The 45%+ slide states the target without that qualification. The 40.2% in §1.1 measures something narrower: Application Software alone, over FY2023-25, on segment EBITDA struck before corporate expense. Both sit below the published algorithm.

The next decision is already constrained. Management said on the Q2 2026 call that "with leverage currently around 3.4x, near-term capital deployment will favor deleveraging over opportunistic buybacks," and expects $1.1-1.2bn after tax from the Indicor instrumentation sale plus further liquidity from the flow-control businesses, which it excluded from its stated capacity. The stated capacity figure itself declined across the year: "north of $6 billion" (Q4 2025), "north of $5 billion" (Q1 2026), "more than $5 billion" (Q2 2026), each on a forward twelve-month basis. Dividends took 14.6% of FY2025 free cash flow; the quarterly rate went to $0.91 from $0.825 in November 2025, a 10% increase and the thirty-third consecutive annual one.

Candor. The vocabulary has been stable for a decade — cash return on investment, decentralization, niche leadership, a low-range-of-outcomes filter — and management names external causes precisely. Across 43 archived earnings calls, "in hindsight" and "not good enough" never appear, "we should have" appears once and "fell short" once; of the eight calls containing "mistake," six use it idiomatically and the two substantive uses are both about AI development. What has changed is the headline metric. The phrase "cash flow per share" does not appear in the forty calls from Q4 2015 through Q3 2025, then appears six times in Q4 2025, four in Q1 2026 and five in Q2 2026, and "most important financial metric" appears only in the 2026 calls. The per-share framing arrives with the buyback, in the same quarter, and the per-share incentive metric arrives with the 2026 grant cycle.

The plan also changed after the fact. Announcing the first repurchase authorization in Q3 2025 the CFO said: "While M&A will continue to be the majority of our capital deployment allocation, our share repurchase program will allow us to opportunistically complement our M&A program." Through the following eight months Roper repurchased $3.2bn against about $50m of bolt-on acquisitions. Management attributes the reversal to the share price and attributes no part of it to acquisition returns falling short of underwriting.

11. M&A, divestitures and deal track record

Roper is a disciplined serial acquirer on the evidence that is checkable, and the discipline shows in the timing of deployment more than in the price of individual deals.

The pauses. Roper spent $154m across four acquisitions in 2017, the year after paying $2.8bn for Deltek; $226m across seven acquisitions in 2021, at the top of the software valuation cycle; and $25.0m on one acquisition in the six months to June 2026 against $2,727m on its own shares. Three near-stops in ten years, each following a large deal and each into a rising price environment. The sell side. Every disclosed divestiture since 2015 closed above carrying value, several far above: Gatan at approximately $925m against an $801m pretax gain, TransCore at approximately $2,680m against a $2,074m gain, the 51% Indicor stake at approximately $2,604m against a $2,046m gain. TransCore cost $600m in October 2004, so the 2022 exit returned about 4.5x the entry price seventeen years later while Roper kept DAT and Loadlink, the freight networks acquired in the same 2004 transaction. The impairment record. Across $21,341m of goodwill, Roper has taken two intangible write-downs in a decade, both at Sunquest in Q4 2021, and no goodwill write-off.

The impairment record is produced by a qualitative screen: in 2025 Roper tested all 25 reporting units qualitatively and performed no quantitative assessment on any, with individual reporting-unit goodwill from $17.5m to $3,372m. And the price paid has risen. Entry multiples on forward EBITDA moved from 14.0x for Deltek in 2016 to 22.0x and 22.2x for CentralReach and Subsplash in 2025, so the entry yield on acquired EBITDA declined from 7.1% to 4.5%, against a 4.8% blended coupon on the $2bn of notes Roper issued in Q3 2024. On revenue the price has been flat at about 9x for five years, so the EBITDA multiple expansion is the margin of what Roper buys (§11.3). The two 2025 platform deals were dilutive to adjusted diluted EPS in their first year by $0.15 and $0.05 on management's own guidance arithmetic. The 2025 vintage is the most growth-dependent Roper has underwritten.

The multiple path is not a straight line — Syntellis, Replicon and Transact were bought at 14-15x — but the two 2025 platform deals are the highest multiples Roper has disclosed paying. At a 4.5% entry yield a fully debt-funded deal does not cover its own interest in year one before growth or the tax shield, and management's guidance recorded the result: $0.15 of CentralReach dilution and $0.05 of Subsplash dilution to 2025 adjusted diluted EPS.

The EBITDA multiple overstates the price inflation, because what Roper pays per dollar of revenue has barely moved. The three deals with a full announcement disclosure price out at 9.1x forward revenue for Vertafore in 2020, 9.1x for Frontline in 2022 and 9.4x for CentralReach in 2025 [deck: Vertafore acquisition call, 2020-08-13, slide 3; deck: Frontline acquisition call, 2022-08-30, slide 3; deck: CentralReach acquisition presentation, 2025-03-24, slide 2]. Across five years the forward revenue multiple held at 9.1x, 9.1x and 9.4x while the forward EBITDA multiple rose from 18.4x to 19.3x to 22.0x, because the acquired EBITDA margin declined from 49.2% to 47.3% to 42.9% and the growth bought rose from mid-single-digit to 20%-plus. The rising EBITDA multiple is the margin of what Roper buys, and not a higher price per dollar of revenue.▪ The Vertafore figure is quoted gross with no tax benefit disclosed, so the three net bases are not strictly identical.

Against the closest structural comparison the price per dollar of revenue is the whole gap. Roper paid $6.98 of acquisition cash for each $1 of in-year acquired revenue in FY2025, against Constellation Software's $1.37, and $4.00 against $0.99 on cumulative FY2023-FY2025 revenue added. Constellation bought 11 points of revenue growth for $1,513m while Roper bought 6.7 points for $3,290m.▪ Both figures overstate the true entry multiple by the same mechanism, because deals close mid-year and contribute partial-year revenue; the FY2023-FY2025 cut removes most of the timing effect and the ratio stays above four to one. The two companies are not buying the same asset: Constellation buys smaller, more fragmented businesses growing 4% organically, Roper buys larger platforms growing 5.4% [web, csisoftware.com, accessed 2026-09-11]. A 1.4-point difference in organic growth is the visible part of a four-to-five-fold difference in price.

The offset management underwrites is growth. CentralReach was bought on a 20%-plus revenue and EBITDA growth expectation and Subsplash on high-teens revenue growth converting to high-20% EBITDA growth over three to five years. At 20% EBITDA compounding a 4.5% entry yield reaches 9.3% in year four, roughly Deltek's year-two yield. The strategy is coherent; the payback is later and more dependent on the growth rate holding.

Tax structure is a material part of the price. Roper quotes a net purchase price after a net-present-value tax benefit on nine disclosed deals — about $350m on Frontline, $200m on CentralReach, $135m on Syntellis, $120m of federal tax attributes on Vertafore, $110m on Procare, $100m on Transact, $80m on Replicon, $20m on Aderant, $25m on Sunquest — running 4-11% of the gross price and amortised over 13-15 years, so the net multiple management quotes is roughly one to two turns below the gross multiple.

Purchase-price allocation is consistently intangible-heavy. On the three largest recent deals, goodwill plus identifiable intangibles account for almost the whole price: CentralReach $1,049m plus $48m of trade names plus $842m of other intangibles on $1,850m; Procare $1,208m plus $39m plus $762m on $1,860m; Transact $947m plus $41m plus $705m on $1,607m. Customer relationships get 17-20 year lives on platform deals and technology 5-8 years. Amortization of acquired intangibles was $858m in FY2025 and is guided to $833m in 2026, the largest reconciling item between GAAP and adjusted earnings, and the reason deals show accretion on adjusted diluted EPS well before they do on GAAP.

11.4 Post-deal performance, where it is disclosed

Roper does not report revenue by business, so outcome evidence is management commentary on named businesses plus the segment lines. The one quantified multi-business series Roper has published is the 2023 Investor Day's cash-flow compound growth since acquisition: DAT +16% (acquired 2004 inside TransCore), Northern Digital +16% (2011, about $204m), Strata +28% total and +23% organic (2015, about $140m, plus the 2020 EPSi bolt-on at about $365m) and Foundry +21% (2019, about $543m) — slides 104 to 107.

Ahead of the deal model. CentralReach: "continues to execute ahead of our deal model. Recurring software revenue grew well north of 20% with margins expanding" (Q1 2026).

In line. Subsplash "delivering financial results in line with our deal model expectations" (Q3 2025). Transact, as Illumia, "revenue ahead of expectations as it wins share and cross-sells into the combined CBORD and Transact customer base" (Q2 2026), with $20m of cost synergies identified by Q4 2024. Syntellis: 85% of cost synergies implemented within 45 days, and on the Q3 2023 call management raised deal-model EBITDA $5m against announcement to about $90m on $185m of FY2024 revenue, against a $1.25bn net purchase price. That is the one quantified and beaten cost-synergy target in the record; Roper sets no public cost-synergy target on its other platform deals.

Behind the deal model. Procare, closed February 2024 at $1,750m net and an 18.4x forward EBITDA multiple on a mid-teens top-line expectation. By Q3 2025 the accretion was "not as much as we had thought when we did the deal," and management named Procare as one of three items reconciling the difference between the initial 2025 guide and the outcome. The CEO described the governance failure directly: "in Procare, we observe that variance for a longer time before we decided to take action to correct it. Now we immediately jump to a corrective action, a countermeasure." The chief executive, chief financial, chief revenue and chief technology officers were replaced.

Cyclical drawdown then recovery. Foundry, bought April 2019 at about $544m and roughly 7x the revenue Roper expected in its first year of ownership, was "down double digits" through 2024 with the recovery "taken a few quarters longer than we anticipated." ARR returned to year-over-year growth by FY2025.

The decade-long hold. Deltek, bought December 2016 as a mid-to-high single-digit revenue grower, came in at the lower end of mid-single digits in FY2025 against the mid-single-digit-plus rate of the prior decade (§6.1), hit by DOGE and the government shutdown. The 2026 guide assumes no Deltek improvement.

11.5 Indicor — the round-trip that is still open

Roper sold 51% of Indicor to CD&R on 22 November 2022 for approximately $2,604m, of which $1,775m was a cash distribution funded by new Indicor third-party debt and $829m was for the equity stake. Roper retained 49%, initially valued at $535.0m "based on the implied equity value associated with the sale price of the 51% equity interest." Indicor had $916.1m of revenue and $233.5m of income from operations in FY2022.

Roper is required to pay CD&R quarterly, either about $29m a year in cash or in kind through the transfer of about 1.7% of its Indicor ownership a year, with the obligation ending when Indicor reaches $425.0m of EBITDA in any three twelve-month periods or on an Indicor IPO; Roper "intends to continue making these quarterly payments in-kind." CD&R holds a liquidation preference equal to its approximately $829m initial investment plus any in-kind adjustment. Roper's stake has gone 49% (November 2022) to 45.5% (12/31/2024) to 43.8% (12/31/2025) to 43.4% (6/30/2026).

The Level 3 fair value of the retained stake was $676m entering 2024, $772m entering 2025, $796m at 12/31/2025, and $1,792m at 6/30/2026 after a $996m first-half increase. The step came on 5 May 2026, when Indicor agreed to sell its instrumentation businesses to AMETEK at an enterprise value of approximately $5.0bn.

Selling 51% for $829m of equity value implies about $1,626m for the whole of Indicor's equity in November 2022. Marking 43.4% at $1,792m implies about $4,129m at 30 June 2026, roughly 2.5x, on a stake diluted by 5.6 points of ownership in the interval — worth roughly $230m at the June 2026 implied equity value [estimate: 5.6% of $4,129m]. Total realisation to date is $2,604m of cash plus a $1,792m mark plus $55.1m of dividends, about $4.45bn, or roughly 19x FY2022 Indicor income from operations against roughly 11x on the November 2022 cash alone. The June 2022 deck sized the sixteen businesses at about $1.06bn of 2022 estimated revenue and about $0.32bn of 2022 estimated EBITDA, so the $2,604m of upfront cash for a majority position is 8.1x that EBITDA [deck: CD&R status update, 2022-06-01, slides 3-4 and 14]. Three things bound that comparison: Indicor levered itself with about $1,775m of new debt at closing to fund Roper's distribution; Indicor sold its CCC business to Honeywell for approximately $670m on 30 June 2023; and the June 2026 figure is a management Level 3 estimate, not a transaction price. The AMETEK enterprise value of $5.0bn for the instrumentation portfolio alone is a signed third-party price and is the harder number.

Every balance-sheet figure here is at 30 June 2026, 5.5 months after the FY2025 10-K. The FY2025 year-end figures understate current leverage by half a turn and overstate liquidity by roughly two-thirds.

Weighted-average cost of debt. Principal-weighted coupon across the twelve fixed tranches is 3.65%, an annual cash coupon of $310m. The realized all-in rate is near the top of that range: net interest expense of $210.7m for the six months to 30 June 2026 on average gross debt of roughly $10,364m annualizes to 4.07%, after interest income on cash and including $6.3m of deferred-financing-cost amortization.

The notes rank equally with Roper's other unsecured senior obligations and are, in the FY2025 10-K's words, "not guaranteed by any of Roper's subsidiaries and are effectively subordinated to all existing and future indebtedness and other liabilities of Roper's subsidiaries." Liabilities standing ahead of them in that sense total roughly $5,150m at 30 June 2026: deferred revenue $1,708m, deferred taxes $1,897m, accounts payable $174m, accrued compensation $232m, income taxes payable $49m, other accrued $589m and other $500m. The credit agreement gives Roper the right to make wholly-owned domestic subsidiaries guarantors of the revolver, a standing feature present in both the 2026 agreement and the 2022 one it replaced, and it has not been exercised.

12.2 The maturity wall and the cost of refinancing

The maturity table in the FY2025 10-K is already superseded: it shows $1,550m due in 2027 including the then-drawn $850m revolver maturing July 2027. On 30 March 2026 Roper replaced that facility with a new five-year $3,500m revolver maturing around March 2031, and the drawn balance grew to $2,850m.

Rolling the revolver into a 2031 facility while drawing an extra $2,000m concentrated 34% of gross debt in one calendar year. That is manageable because a committed bank line is refinanced well ahead of maturity, and Roper has term-funded revolver balances in the bond market in five of the last nine Augusts. The practical consequence is that the next large bond issuance is a question of when.

The fair value of the fixed-rate notes was $8,154m at 30 June 2026 against $8,500m of par, 95.9%, down from 97.5% at 31 December 2025. Discounting the actual tranche cash flows to that fair value implies a weighted-average market yield of 5.14% [estimate: semi-annual discounting of each tranche's contractual coupons and principal, solved for a single flat yield that reproduces the disclosed Level 2 fair value], 148 basis points above the 3.65% weighted coupon. Repricing every tranche at a flat 5.00% adds about $115m a year of interest, 5.0% of trailing EBIT, and the cost is concentrated in four tranches issued in 2019-2021:

Roper's new-issue cost is slightly below that assumption: the August 2025 offering priced $500m of 2028s at 4.257%, $500m of 2030s at 4.493% and $1,000m of 2035s at 5.136%, a blended 4.76%, and the August 2024 offering priced at a blended 4.8%.

The floating leg. The revolver is the only floating-rate instrument, at 25% of gross debt against 9% at 31 December 2025. Pricing is a SOFR grid tied to the senior unsecured rating, currently SOFR plus 0.920%, plus an 0.080% facility fee on both used and unused portions. Backing the rate out of the income statement gives roughly 5.3-5.6% cash [estimate: H1 2026 net interest expense less accrued note coupons, over an average revolver balance of about $1,925m, adjusted for deferred-financing amortization and interest income]. A 100 basis point move in SOFR changes interest expense by $28.5m a year at the current drawn balance, 1.2% of trailing EBIT and about $0.22 of after-tax diluted EPS.

There is no currency mismatch. All debt is US-dollar denominated, non-US customers accounted for 13% of FY2025 revenue, only about 9% of revenue is in non-USD functional currencies, and Roper repatriated $140m during H1 2026 stating that substantially all foreign earnings can move without incremental US federal tax cost.

12.3 Covenants, ratings and liquidity

The credit agreement's one financial covenant requires a total debt to total capital ratio of 0.65 or less. At 30 June 2026 that ratio is 37.8%, and Roper could fund another $8,175m of debt-financed repurchase before it binds [estimate: a debt-funded buyback raises debt and reduces equity one-for-one, holding total capital constant at $30,069m]. The ratings bind before the covenant does, and they are quantified. Moody's rates the senior unsecured debt Baa2 and S&P BBB+. On 2025-11-21 Moody's affirmed Baa2 and revised the outlook to positive, citing adjusted debt to EBITDA of 3x as of September 2025, with an upgrade requiring below 3x together with adjusted free cash flow to debt in the high teens, and downgrade risk from "leveraging transactions pushing debt-to-EBITDA above 4x, weakening liquidity, or material margin deterioration" [web, summary of the Moody's action, accessed 2026-09-11].

The revolver was drawn down over three quarters: $710m at 30 September 2025, 20% of the $3,500m commitment, then $850m, then $2,000m, then $2,850m at 30 June 2026, 81% [deck: Q3 2025, 2025-10-23, slide 7; deck: Q1 2026, 2026-04-23, slide 7; 10-Q Q2 2026]. Over the same three quarters the stated annual deployment capacity moved from "$6B+" in January 2026 to "$5B+" in April and July. Standing liquidity of roughly $1,009m has to cover the $700m note maturing 15 December 2026 and roughly $180m of H2 2026 dividends before any acquisition spend. The coverage comes from operations: H1 2026 operating cash flow was $1,062m and trailing free cash flow is $2.6bn on management's measure, so H2 free cash flow alone should be close to $1.5bn, and the Indicor proceeds add to it. The narrow point is that for the first time since 2020 Roper's undrawn revolver is smaller than its nearest debt maturity. Of the $365m of cash, $175m is held at foreign subsidiaries, so domestic cash is roughly $190m.

Leases and retirement obligations are immaterial to the capital structure. Total operating lease liabilities were $234m at 31 December 2025 against right-of-use assets of $220m, with a 6.6-year weighted-average remaining term and a 4.3% weighted-average discount rate — 2.1% of gross debt. Retirement obligations are three Section 401(k) defined-contribution plans costing $51.9m in FY2025. There is no defined-benefit plan and no other post-employment benefit liability, so there is no discount-rate or funded-status exposure anywhere in the capital structure.

Negative net working capital is structural. Net working capital, on Roper's definition of current assets excluding cash less current liabilities excluding debt, was negative $1,199m at 30 June 2026 against negative $1,390m at 31 December 2025, because current deferred revenue was $1,708m. Conventional current-ratio tests produce alarming outputs on this balance sheet and describe nothing real.

12.4 Stock-based compensation and the share count

For eleven years the diluted share count rose in a straight line from stock-based awards and the employee stock purchase plan, with no repurchases at all between 2014 and October 2025.

Revenue and stock-based compensation are both as originally reported for each year, so the pre-2022 ratios are on the industrial-inclusive basis; within each era the ratio has been 1.7% to 2.6% for eleven years with no trend. Net dilution averaged 0.63% a year from 2015 through 2023 and slowed to 0.28-0.37% in 2024-2025, partly because employee stock purchase plan shares began coming out of treasury. Roper has never issued equity for an acquisition of any size.

The May 2026 proxy changed the forward arithmetic. Shareholders approved 14,150,000 new shares under the 2021 Incentive Plan, which Roper states is "approximately 13.8% of our shares of common stock outstanding as of March 23, 2026," and which "will last for approximately 4 to 5 years, based on our historic grant rates, new hiring expectations and the approximate current share price." Three figures do not reconcile with each other unless the grant rate steps up sharply. At the 2023-2025 average burn rate of 0.72m shares a year, 14,150,000 shares is 19.6 years of grants. Roper's own 4-to-5-year estimate implies 2.83m to 3.54m shares a year, 2.9% to 3.6% of the 98.9m outstanding, against a 0.62-0.72% historical burn rate. And the H1 2026 actuals match the company's own estimate: Roper granted 0.544m options and 0.845m restricted shares in the six months to 30 June 2026, 1.389m in total, 1.78x the entire FY2025 grant, annualizing to 2.78m.

The mechanism is the share price. Grant-date value rose 19% year on year in H1 2026, to $348.2m from $291.4m, while the share count granted rose 106%, because restricted stock was granted at $352.88 against $601.02 a year earlier and options had a Black-Scholes fair value of $91.94 against $181.63. Holding the compensation budget in dollars while the share price halves doubles the shares issued. The buyback retired shares at $358.79 in the same period that the compensation plan issued them at $352.88. Stock-based compensation expense moved with it: $108.2m in H1 2026 against $82.7m in H1 2025, up 31% on revenue growth of 9.9%, taking the ratio to 2.57% of revenue. Unrecognized compensation cost on nonvested options alone was $59.1m at 31 December 2025, recognized over 1.97 years, and that predates the H1 2026 step-up.

The employee stock purchase plan was also amended effective 1 July 2026: authorized shares doubled to 2,000,000, the payroll-deduction cap rose from 10% to 15% of compensation, the purchase discount rose from 10% to 15%, and the four quarterly offering periods were cut to two. Participants bought 0.041m shares for $12.7m in H1 2026 under the old terms, so the incremental effect is measured in tens of thousands of shares a quarter.

Combining the two: the buyback has retired 8.986m shares into treasury while the plan authorization created capacity for 14.150m new ones, 1.57x as many. An authorization is capacity and only grants dilute, but both the company's own 4-to-5-year estimate and the H1 2026 actual point to roughly 2.8-3.5m shares a year against 0.72m historically. At 2.8m a year on a 98.9m base, holding the share count flat requires roughly $1.0bn a year of repurchase at $360 a share, against zero repurchase in each of 2023 and 2024.

12.5 Structural balance-sheet risks, ranked by expected effect on earnings

  1. The leverage increase from buybacks is self-imposed and brought no EBITDA. Net debt rose $1,951m in H1 2026 against $2,000m of net revolver borrowing, moving leverage from 2.9x to 3.4x with nothing acquired to grow into. Headroom to the 4.0x Moody's downgrade trigger is $1,945m, less than half of one year's free cash flow plus the Indicor proceeds. Probability of breach is low because Roper controls the pace of repurchase and has already reprioritised to deleveraging.
  2. Refinancing the sub-3% tranches costs $90-115m a year by 2031. Trailing interest expense of $394m becomes roughly $485-510m on a static-rate full-repricing basis against trailing EBIT of $2,316m, so coverage declines from 5.9x to roughly 4.5-4.8x on unchanged EBIT. Predictable and dated.
  3. Liquidity headroom is the thinnest since 2020. About $644m undrawn plus $365m of cash, of which $175m is offshore, against a $700m note maturing 15 December 2026. This becomes a constraint only if a large acquisition closes before December.
  4. Floating-rate exposure tripled in six months, to 25% of gross debt from 9%. A 100 basis point move costs $28.5m a year.
  5. Structural subordination of the notes. No subsidiary guarantees, roughly $5,150m of subsidiary-level non-debt liabilities ahead, and a standing contractual right to give revolver lenders guarantees noteholders do not have. This matters only in a distress path no current metric points to.
  6. Dilution reprices upward as the share price falls, per §12.4. A per-share risk, not a solvency one, and it runs against the buyback.

The covenant, pension and lease exposures are not risks here: 37.8% against a 65% limit, no defined-benefit plan, and $234m of operating leases at 2.1% of gross debt.

12.6 The Indicor mark and the capital structure

Stockholders' equity declined $1,181m in H1 2026 despite $1,677m of net earnings, because $2,739m went into treasury stock and $191m into dividends. Of that $1,677m, $1,003m pretax is the Level 3 mark on the retained Indicor stake. Excluding the after-tax mark, net debt to total net capital would be about 38.0% instead of the reported 36.9% [estimate: pretax gain of $1,003m taxed at the 21% federal statutory rate], and both figures are far inside the covenant. The mark does not move the leverage ratio, because the gain is recorded below the operating line in "Equity investment (gain) loss, net" and never enters EBITDA. Management has stated that all future Indicor impacts will be excluded from non-GAAP results in every future period.

13. Financial history and summary

Three changes cut the reported history into pieces. The divestitures of TransCore and Zetec (December 2021) and of a majority of Indicor (November 2022) each reclassified prior periods into discontinued operations, so the same fiscal year appears at different revenue in successive 10-Ks: FY2020 revenue is $5,527m as first filed, $4,854m after the 2021 recast and $4,022m after the Indicor recast. FY2019 was restated once and stopped there, so the current continuing-operations basis exists only from FY2020. FY2016-FY2018 are on the fully pre-divestiture basis and FY2019 on a third basis of its own, which is why the FY2019 and FY2020 growth cells below read n/m. Operating cash flow is the exception: the total-company line was never recast and is identical across three successive 10-Ks, and every free-cash-flow figure here uses the continuing-operations line to match the continuing-operations revenue denominator. Segments were also recut twice, in FY2019 and FY2022, and the FY2022 10-K restated only 2020 and 2021 into the current three segments.

How the computed rows are built. EBITDA is operating income plus the cash-flow-statement depreciation and amortization line, so it differs from management's adjusted EBITDA, which is shown separately. Free cash flow is continuing-operations operating cash flow less capital expenditures less capitalized software. Net debt is total debt less cash, excluding operating lease liabilities, which would add $234m at FY2025. NOPAT is operating income taxed at the effective rate; invested capital is total debt plus stockholders' equity less cash, so goodwill and intangibles are included; return on invested capital is NOPAT over the average of the current and prior year-end figures, computed for each year from that year's own 10-K as originally filed, so numerator and denominator consolidate the same businesses. On the continuing-operations numerator that the rest of this section uses, FY2019, FY2020 and FY2021 are 8.0%, 5.0% and 5.0%, which understates them by 1.0 to 1.7 points because the recast numerator excludes businesses the year-end balance sheets still consolidate (§3.4).

Three cells have causes outside operations. FY2019's GAAP diluted EPS of $16.82 and 37.4% net margin include $921m of pretax gains on the sales of Gatan and the imaging businesses, with about $200m of the tax paid in 2020. FY2022's $42.55 and 84.6% net margin include the gain on the November 2022 sale of the 51% Indicor stake. And FY2022's operating cash flow of $607m and 10.0% free-cash-flow margin are a $954m cash tax payment on those divestitures and nothing else; adjusted for it, FY2022 cash generation was in line with the surrounding years.

13.3 What drove the record

Gross margin. Reported gross margin rose from 61.5% (FY2016) to 69.2% (FY2025), which looks like a software mix shift lifting profitability. Most of the move is the divested industrial businesses leaving both numerator and denominator. Splitting at the basis break separates the two effects: on the old basis gross margin rose 1.7 points from FY2016 to FY2018; on the current basis it declined 1.1 points from 70.3% (FY2020) to 69.2% (FY2025), while operating margin improved 1.4 points and free-cash-flow margin 3.9 points.

The driver of the gross-margin decline is the reoccurring stream, which compounded at 22.6% a year against 17.9% for recurring revenue:

Revenue stream FY2020 FY2021 FY2022 FY2023 FY2024 FY2025
Recurring 1,965 2,553 2,939 3,511 3,976 4,483
Reoccurring 300 361 370 401 624 833
Non-recurring 597 685 721 733 770 814
Product 1,161 1,235 1,341 1,533 1,669 1,773
Recurring + reoccurring, % of revenue 56.3% 60.2% 61.5% 63.3% 65.4% 67.3%

The FY2025 10-K names the mechanism: Application Software gross margin was held to 68.5% by "a lower gross margin profile associated with the higher payments revenue mix at Transact," and Network Software gross margin declined from 85.0% to 84.1% "predominantly driven by the payments revenue mix at Subsplash." Payments attaches revenue at a low gross margin and nearly no incremental SG&A, so the same dollar compresses gross margin and leaves operating margin roughly intact. Extrapolating gross margin from the reported ten-year trend gets the direction backwards.

Application Software organic growth stepped down from 6.5% (Q2 2025) to 5.9% (Q3 2025) to 5.2% (Q1 2026) to 4.5% (Q2 2026), in the segment that is 56.7% of revenue. The 10-Q attributes FY2025 softness to "a decrease in organic non-recurring revenue driven primarily by our business serving the government contracting market," and the Q2 2026 commentary no longer lists acute healthcare among the leaders. Segment revenue also declined sequentially, from $1,192m in Q1 2026 to $1,181m in Q2.

Network Software operating margin declined 2.9 points year over year in Q2 2026. Gross margin rose 1.1 points in the same quarter, so the compression is entirely below the gross line: SG&A moved from 39.3% to 43.4% of segment revenue on the Subsplash acquisition and Convoy investment.

Technology Enabled Products operating margin declined 2.1 points on "input cost pressures at our water meter technology business and revenue mix within our medical products businesses weighted more towards consumables." Organic growth held at 7.1%, so input cost and mix explain the margin move without any volume shortfall.

Leverage and the share count both broke multi-year patterns in the same two quarters, covered in §10.3 and §12.4. Adjusted diluted EPS grew 10% in Q2 2026 on a share count 7.2% lower than three quarters earlier.

Backlog does not corroborate the organic deceleration: 12-month remaining performance obligations were $3,286m at 30 June 2026, up 11.0% year over year, with Application Software backlog up 11.2%. Backlog growth is running roughly double organic revenue growth, and much of the gap is acquired backlog.

Three of these inflect. Backlog in Technology Enabled Products has been flat to down for two years while the segment grew 7% organically, which management explains as Neptune lead times normalising toward pre-COVID levels after the unwind of COVID-era blanket orders; the 12-month measure also excludes the repeat consumables driving NDI and Verathon, so a flat number is consistent with the mix shift. Consolidated 12-month backlog declined sequentially in each of the last two quarters, from $3,425m to $3,286m, while total remaining performance obligations rose, so contract duration lengthened as the near-term book shrank. And the bookings description moved from high teens to mid-single-digit plus across six quarters, on shifting bases.

One disclosure was discontinued. Roper disclosed the split of recurring revenue between SaaS subscription and on-premise annual maintenance at the March 2023 Investor Day — $2.0bn and $900m of $2.9bn — and the FY2025 disaggregation note folds SaaS, post-contract support and annual term licences into one line, so the maintenance base that Deltek's Q1 2028 Costpoint end-of-support is meant to convert at 2 to 2.5x is no longer visible.

14.1 What management's word has been worth

Roper guides four things, all non-GAAP: full-year adjusted diluted EPS, next-quarter adjusted diluted EPS, full-year total revenue growth and full-year organic revenue growth. There is no margin guidance, no free-cash-flow guidance in dollars, no bookings guidance and no annual recurring revenue. Three standing exclusions define the basis, and two are recent: unannounced acquisitions and divestitures throughout; potential share repurchases, added with the Q3 2025 release immediately after the first buyback authorization; and proceeds from Indicor's pending divestiture, added with the Q2 2026 release.

Every quarterly adjusted diluted EPS guide since Q4 2020 has been beaten above the high end of the range, 23 consecutive quarters, with a mean overshoot of $0.09. The size of the beat has compressed:

Year Average quarterly beat against the guidance midpoint
2021 +4.5%
2022 +4.6%
2023 +2.6%
2024 +1.8%
2025 +1.2%
2026 (H1) +2.9%

The 2026 figure is not a clean operating improvement. At least $0.03 of Q2's overshoot is disclosed buyback accretion against the guide, and the CFO described the Q1 raise as "mainly flown through the first quarter beat and then the buyback activity," with the CEO adding that the Q1 beat "was partially from our model, operating and partially buyback."

The full-year adjusted diluted EPS guide has been beaten every year, by a shrinking margin: +7.2% against the initial midpoint in FY2022, +4.1% in FY2023, +1.7% in FY2024, +0.6% in FY2025. FY2025 landed at exactly the top of the January 2025 range, and the CFO framed it as delivering "the top end of our 2025 guidance range provided in January despite lower organic revenue and in-year dilution from recent acquisitions." The earnings held; the revenue that was supposed to produce them did not.

Revenue guidance is where the record breaks.

Fiscal year Organic: initial to final guide Organic actual Total: initial to final guide Total actual
2023 +5-6% to +7%+ +8% not guided initially, to 14%+ +15%
2024 +5-6% to about 6% +6% +11-12% to 13%+ +14%
2025 +6-7% to about 6% +5% 10%+ to about 13% +12%
2026 +5-6% to about 6% H1 +5.3% about 8% to 8%+ H1 +9.9%

The conference decks print the then-current organic guide, so they date each revision. Roper showed 5-6% in February 2023, 6-7% in May and about 7% in September, and delivered 8%; it showed 5-6% in March 2024 and about 6% in September, and delivered 7% [deck: Barclays, 2023-02-23, slide 7; deck: Jefferies, 2023-05-31, slide 7; deck: Goldman Sachs Communacopia, 2023-09-06, slide 7; deck: Morgan Stanley TMT, 2024-03-05, slide 10; deck: Goldman Sachs Communacopia, 2024-09-10, slide 7]. In 2025 the organic guide was cut at Q3 from 6-7% to about 6% and the year landed at 5%. That is the first year in the series in which the organic number moved down through the year, and 2026 has reverted to the earlier pattern at 5-6% in January and about 6% in July.

FY2023 was raised twice on organic and still beaten. FY2025 was guided up on total revenue three times, cut on organic in October, and still came in a point below both the initial range and the reduced one. An analyst opened the Q4 2025 call with "Neil, this is the second quarter in a row you've missed expectations, and you're guiding to a back half acceleration in '26," and the CEO conceded the point.

14.2 The guide is mostly a share-count guide, and the street's upgrades came from below the operating line

Management confirmed the first directly. Asked on the Q1 2026 call whether "the sort of core EBITDA guide is essentially unchanged and it's really a kind of share count-driven guide," the CFO answered: "That's correct... we've mainly flown through the first quarter beat and then the buyback activity for the balance of the year."

H1 2025 H1 2026 Change
Adjusted net earnings $1,045m $1,081m +3.4%
Weighted diluted shares 108.3m 102.6m (5.3)%
Adjusted DEPS $9.65 $10.54 +9.2%

Roughly six of the nine points of first-half adjusted diluted EPS growth came from the share count.

The street's estimate path shows the same shape from the outside. Over the eleven weeks from 2026-06-23 to 2026-09-11, consensus cut CY2028 revenue by 1.17% and left CY2028 GAAP operating income unchanged, then raised CY2028 adjusted diluted EPS by 2.49%. In CY2027 operating income declined 0.77% and adjusted diluted EPS rose 0.78%, a 1.5-point gap in one quarter. And on a longer view, CY2028 adjusted diluted EPS is 1.5% below where it stood in April 2025 while the share count supporting it is roughly 7-8% smaller, so the street's view of Roper's 2028 earnings power has come down by roughly 6-10% [estimate: consensus EPS multiplied by the diluted share count each vintage would plausibly assume — 106-108.4m for the April-2025 vintage, 99-101m now; the direction does not depend on the bounds].

That source of upgrades is ending: "near-term capital deployment will favor deleveraging over opportunistic buybacks."

14.3 The four live splits

Does organic growth accelerate in 2027? Consensus resolves it at 6.0%, the bottom of management's own "5% to 7%, 6% to 8%" framing and below the high-single-digit level management has targeted for years.

When does AI become revenue? Consensus CY2027 revenue growth contains none of the "hundreds of basis points" management describes. Goldman's analyst asked directly about the 2027 contribution and got no number; the CFO's answer on timing was "this is a $100 billion question, and we're just not there yet."

Does the M&A restart happen, and at what price? Management's evidence is qualitative: sponsor conversations "decidedly more constructive," investment banks' books full, distributions-to-paid-in pressure, credit cliffs. Its own timing slipped inside seven weeks, from "break loose later this year and into 2027" (Q2 call, 2026-07-23) to "probably going to be more of a '27 time line versus later this year" (Citi, 2026-09-10). Consensus resolves this at zero, which is standard sell-side practice and not an oversight, and it means the consensus CY2028 revenue line and the consensus CY2028 margin cannot both survive management executing its stated plan: $5bn of deployment adds $140-160m of annual amortization [estimate: CentralReach recorded $51.8m of amortizable intangibles a year on a $1,850m price, 2.8%, and Subsplash $25.5m on $800m, 3.2%] against the $82m of roll-off the 2026-to-2028 schedule provides.

What is the right multiple? The $355-to-$526 span of named targets is where that disagreement shows, and it is unusual dispersion for a business management describes as a low-range-of-outcomes compounder.

14.4 Five things the street is not modelling

  1. Forward capital deployment, worth 4-6 points of annual compounding on management's own bridge.
  2. The amortization consequence of that deployment, $140-160m a year against $82m of roll-off.
  3. AI compute cost, up roughly 3x annualised since January 2026 and expected higher by year end, with the FY2025 10-K stating the pass-through may fail.
  4. The Deltek Costpoint end-of-support event in Q1 2028, which moves Roper's largest maintenance base from maintenance to subscription at "over 2x," landing squarely in the CY2028 window in which consensus revenue was just cut 1.2%.
  5. The Vertafore pricing-meter change, shipping in early 2027, which changes the revenue unit for one of the two largest software businesses one quarter into the year the street needs to accelerate.

15. Market pricing and valuation history

This section records what earnings did, what the market paid for them, what was expected, and why the price moved. It includes no view on whether any multiple is deserved.

Over the ten years to FY2025 Roper's adjusted diluted EPS nearly tripled while the shares roughly doubled. From 12/31/2015 to 12/31/2025 the price went from $189.79 to $445.13, up 135%, and adjusted diluted EPS from $6.68 to $20.00, up 199% or 11.6% a year, so the trailing adjusted multiple moved from 28.4x to 22.3x. Total return with dividends reinvested was +119% from 12/31/2015 to 2026-09-11, 7.6% a year. Over the shorter window the FY2025 10-K performance graph puts $100 invested on 12/31/2020 at $106.25 for Roper against $196.16 for the S&P 500.

From the 2025-03-05 peak to the run date the price declined 34.6%, from $593.81 to $388.52, while the twelve-month-forward consensus EPS rose 16.6%, from $20.23 to $23.58. The forward multiple went from 29.4x to 16.5x. Estimates did not decline while the price did: Bloomberg's twelve-month-forward consensus EPS rose in 29 of the 32 months from January 2024 to August 2026, and the three down months together took $0.34 off it.

15.3 Earnings against expectations

Roper beat the adjusted EPS consensus in all fifteen quarters from Q4 2022 through Q2 2026, with a median beat of 1.6% and a maximum of 4.0%. Revenue was the softer line: three of the last twelve quarters missed the revenue consensus. A company that beat EPS fifteen times running declined on nine of its last twelve prints.

Roper reports pre-market at 06:55 Eastern, so the reaction session is the announcement day itself, measured close-to-close.

Quarter Reaction What the market reacted to
2024 Q2 (7.4)% Organic growth of 4% against a full-year target of 6%, with Network Software held back by "pressure with our Freight Matching businesses" at DAT and the writers' and actors' strikes at Foundry. Management kept the 12% total and 6% organic full-year outlook and raised only the bottom of the adjusted DEPS range, which required a materially stronger second half
2024 Q4 +5.1% The 2025 adjusted DEPS guide of $19.75-20.00 was about 1% below the $20.08 consensus then standing, so the move was not the EPS guide. The call added FY2024 revenue growth of 14% with 41% core margin leverage, $3.6bn deployed in a year management called "a little quieter than we originally expected," net leverage of 2.6x, and "over $5 billion that we can deploy toward high-quality acquisition opportunities this year," plus a long passage on cheaper foundation models widening the use cases. Capacity and deployment, not earnings
2025 Q3 (5.7)% Adjusted DEPS beat the top of the guide by $0.02, and the organic revenue guide was cut inside the same call: "given the delays at Neptune and the temporary impact of the government shutdown, which is slowing year-end commercial activity at Deltek, we now expect organic revenue to land in the 6% area versus our previous 6% to 7% range"
2025 Q4 (9.6)% The largest one-day decline of the decade outside March 2020. Q4 organic growth of 4% was "below our expectations," and the initial 2026 guide of $21.30-21.55 sat below the $21.69 consensus. Management declined to underwrite a recovery: "we're not starting the year assuming organic growth will inflect in 2026," with no benefit from the One Big Beautiful Bill for government contracting, no Neptune recovery, and "our guidance does not assume a meaningful revenue uplift from our AI development work"
2026 Q2 +5.5% The second full-year raise of 2026: adjusted DEPS to $22.15-22.30, "up $0.30 at the midpoint and up $0.80 from our original guide in January," total revenue growth to north of 8% and organic to the 6% area. The call also reported DAT's freight market improving with "a modest benefit in '26" and Neptune's first half "stronger than we modeled"

The asymmetry is visible in the two January prints. Both guided initial full-year adjusted DEPS about 1% below the December consensus; the 2025 guide was met with +5.1% and the 2026 guide with (9.6)%. What changed between them was the organic growth rate the guide implied and management's willingness to underwrite an inflection.

The 2025-26 decline is the deepest in the daily record since 2014 and the only one still open; at $388.52 the shares are 34.6% below the March 2025 peak and 23.1% above the February 2026 low. No single session explains it: the largest one-day move inside the window was (9.6)% on 2026-01-27, and the two large earnings-day declines together account for about 15 of the 47 points. Forward consensus EPS rose in every one of those months except October 2025, when it slipped $0.05. The multiple went from 28.9x to 14.3x and back to 18.0x. What changed, in sequence: at the July and October 2025 prints, organic growth landed at the bottom of the guided band for company-specific reasons; at the January 2026 print, management would not underwrite an inflection and guided below consensus; and at the April and July 2026 prints, the deceleration stopped, with two raises taking the 2026 guide $0.80 above where it started. The recovery from $315.53 to $388.52 came almost entirely after the Q1 and Q2 2026 prints.

The 2021-22 decline of 27.8% started from the highest December forward multiple of the decade, 32.1x, while forward consensus EPS kept rising through the period; inside that window Roper agreed the CD&R sale of the majority industrial stake. The March 2020 decline was the fastest and the fastest recovered: 1.2 months down, 2.2 months back, with ten of Roper's fifteen largest daily moves since 2015 falling in that one month.

Construction notes that change the numbers. Three lines report in a currency other than the one they trade in: Constellation Software reports in USD and trades in CAD, Topicus reports in EUR and trades in CAD, and Halma reports in GBP and trades in pence. EPS was re-pulled with the fundamental currency forced to the listing currency and the pence price divided by 100, so each multiple divides like for like; without that, Constellation printed 27x instead of 20x and Halma printed 3,230x. Constellation and Topicus FY2028E are blank because two and one contributing estimates is not a consensus. TransDigm and MSCI have no price-to-book because both have negative book equity. The GAAP EPS columns are Bloomberg's normalised figure on every row for comparability, so Roper shows 13.84 against the $14.20 filed; §15 uses the filed figure. Index rows have no market capitalization, enterprise value or leverage.

Where Roper falls on the cross-section as of 2026-09-11: 17x 2026E earnings against a 24x median for the 33 peer rows, 16x 2027E against 21x, and 15x EV/EBITDA against 17x, with a year-to-date price return of (13)% against a (14)% median, a one-year return of (25)% against (18)% and a three-year return of (21)% against +14%. Among the fifteen structural comparables only SS&C (11x) and Itron (15x) are below Roper's 17x on 2026E earnings; Dover and Fortive are nearest above at 18x, Constellation Software is at 20x, Tyler at 26x, AMETEK at 29x and Halma at 32x.

17. Forward model summary

A driver-based operating model, FY2026 to FY2033, running from revenue through free cash flow. Year 0 is FY2025 as reported and ties to the financial history: revenue $7,903m, operating income $2,235m, free cash flow $2,436m, diluted weighted-average shares 108.2m. No valuation, no multiples applied to the projections, no discounting to a per-share value.

17.1 What the model has to get right

Roper's revenue growth has two independent sources and the model treats them separately. Same-store drivers — price, retention, seat and unit counts, payments volume, meter content, single-use conversion — produced 5.4% organic growth in FY2025 and 4.9% in Q2 2026. Capital deployment produced the rest: $27,009m of acquisitions over ten years, 173% of cumulative free cash flow, converted into roughly $1,408m of acquired revenue across FY2023-FY2025 alone.

A third mechanism operates between them and is the largest source of confusion in Roper's own disclosure. Reported organic growth includes acquired businesses once they have been owned a full comparable period, so a deal closed in mid-2025 lifts reported organic growth in the second half of 2026 with no change in demand.▪ The model prints both a same-store rate and the rate Roper would report, and the gap between them is that effect.

FY2026 is anchored, not forecast, because two of four quarters are reported and the third is weeks from the run date. All three scenarios share the same FY2026 revenue build and diverge from FY2027.

FY2026 Model base External reference
Revenue $8,543m, +8.1% Guide "north of 8%"; consensus $8,566m
Organic revenue growth, as reported 6.1% Guide "6% area"
Adjusted EBITDA margin 38.6% Q2 2026 actual 38.6% (39.9% a year earlier)
Operating income $2,416m, 28.3% margin Consensus $2,416m, 28.2%
Interest expense, net $430m H1 2026 actual $210.7m
Adjusted DEPS $22.13 Guide $22.15-$22.30; consensus $22.222
Free cash flow $2,652m, 31.0% of revenue Guide "safely over 30% of revenue"
Net debt / EBITDA 2.59x 3.4x at 6/30/2026, before the Indicor proceeds

The base's $22.13 is two cents below the bottom of the guided range because it assumes no further second-half repurchase and no Q3 or Q4 beat, against 23 consecutive quarters of beating the high end. The FY2026 leverage path: Roper enters the year at 3.4x, generates roughly $1.7bn of second-half free cash flow, pays about $190m of dividends, buys back nothing further, and receives $1.1-1.2bn after tax from the Indicor instrumentation sale, which takes net debt to about $8.5bn against roughly $3.3bn of EBITDA. Management's stated capacity of "$5 billion or more of M&A in the next 12 months" then checks out arithmetically: about $4.1bn of debt capacity to a 3.5x ceiling plus about $2.5bn of FY2027 free cash flow after dividends.

Three results come out of the drivers instead of being set directly. Application Software's GAAP operating margin expands 350 basis points over eight years while its EBITDA margin declines 90, because acquired revenue enters at a 38% EBITDA margin while acquired-intangible amortization declines from 9.8% of consolidated revenue to 7.7%. Network Software's operating margin declines 380 basis points, and it declines faster in the base case than in the bear, because deploying 25% of a much larger acquisition programme into a segment running at a 51% EBITDA margin dilutes it — the same mechanism that took the segment from 57.4% in Q4 2024 to 50.9% in Q2 2026. And the base case reaches management's compounding claim without reaching its organic target: free cash flow per share compounds 14.7% a year from FY2025 to FY2033 and adjusted diluted EPS 13.7%, against "mid-teens," while same-store organic growth never exceeds 6.9% against a stated through-cycle 7.0-7.5% and an "entitled" rate north of 8%.▪ That is management's own account of the compounding, stated at Citi on 2026-09-10: "you have 6%, 7% organic growth... so sort of high single-digit organic EBITDA growth. Then we have our baseline capital deployment, which then bridges you to like mid-teens."

The bear case does not require the moat to break. It requires gross retention to slip two points, the freight recovery not to arrive, payments volume to stay where it is, agentic products to be absorbed into the annual price increase, and the acquisition pipeline to stay frozen at $1.5bn a year. Each of those five is a live question in the current disclosure. The bear case also ends with more shares than the base, 87.7m against 86.8m, because the bear's 90%-of-free-cash-flow repurchase cap collides with 2.8m of annual issuance.

One limitation applies to the whole scenario set: none of these amplitudes has a realized analogue in this portfolio. Deltek, Vertafore, Frontline, Procare, Transact, CentralReach and Subsplash are more than half of revenue, and the only broad demand shock in the window is the 2020 quarter, when Roper still owned the industrial businesses sold to CD&R. The FY2023-FY2025 freight drawdown is the closest realized stress and it is confined to one segment. A 93% gross retention assumption and a 2.9% same-store growth outcome have never been observed in these businesses.
