Three features of that table go beyond the ranking. The M&A row has opposite signs on the two measures. Cutting deployment from $4,200m to $2,500m a year lowers FY2033 operating income by $408m and free cash flow by $579m, and raises adjusted diluted EPS by $4.38, because capital not spent on businesses is spent on shares. That is not a modelling artifact; it is the arithmetic Roper ran in the eight months to July 2026, when it bought $3.2bn of its own stock and $50m of businesses, and it is why adjusted diluted EPS rose 10% in Q2 2026 on adjusted net earnings up 2.7%. Gross retention is the largest same-store driver by a wide margin — two points on a $4,483m recurring base moves FY2033 operating income by about $390m, more than three times the effect of the entire Technology Enabled Products gross margin — and it is also the least observable driver in the disclosure, since Roper publishes no annual recurring revenue, no net revenue retention and no churn at any level. The interest-rate row does not touch operating income and moves free cash flow by $86m, so the sub-3% refinancing is predictable and small against the drivers above it.

17.5 Assumptions and where each is contested

The model has forty drivers. Those that move the output appear below with their basis and the substantive argument against each. Six are weak enough that the output is conditional on them, and five do not survive their own evidence.

Driver Bear Base Bull Basis Where it is contested
Application Software gross retention 93% 95% 96% Management's "mid-90s," repeated every quarter; purchase-accounting customer lives of 18-20 years imply 5.0-5.6% attrition The purchase-accounting check is not independent, since the lives are management's own estimate. The disclosed business-level figures straddle the base (Deltek 97%, Vertafore 92%). The decisive point is the unit of measure: the one business with a second cut, CentralReach, retains mid-to-high 90s on logos and low 90s including clinician seats, and the model prices per seat. A band of 91-95% fits the evidence better
Application Software price escalation 4.0% 4.5% 5.0% Management's "vast majority" of about 5 points of attrition offset by price One of four unidentified terms fitted to a single observed quantity: retention, price, expansion and new logos sum to the disclosed 7% organic recurring growth, and any two can move two points in opposite directions and reproduce it. No realized price increase has been published at any business in ten years of transcripts, and the one contract-level price datum in the record runs at 0.7% a year
Application Software net expansion 4.5% 5.5% 6.0% Residual: 105% net retention less 95% gross less 4.5% price Pure residual. The "105-ish" figure is from October 2024 and was stated "across the blended enterprise," which includes DAT's month-to-month carrier subscriptions. Applying an all-segment figure to one segment could err either way: the per-business figures are all higher (Vertafore 108%, Aderant 113%, CentralReach 115-120%), while the seat populations under Deltek, Vertafore, Strata, Frontline and Transact are shrinking or about 70% penetrated
Application Software new-logo ARR 2.0% 2.0% 2.5% A plug that closes the equation Does not survive its own evidence. The range contains no downside case, and the stated justification argues for a lower bear: the billable populations are shrinking or already penetrated. Roper's own disclosures put the new-logo universe close to exhausted in the largest verticals — Deltek at 98% of the top 100 federal contractors, Vertafore at 100 of the top 100 brokers, Strata plus Syntellis at about 70% of US health systems. A defensible bear is 1.0-1.5 points
Cloud-conversion uplift 0.1 0.4 0.8 pts The 2023 Investor Day's $900m maintenance base converting at 2-2.5x over "every bit of a decade" Both inputs are three and a half years old and unrestated. The conversion started in 2023, so part of it already runs inside the realized organic rates, and adding an increment from FY2028 risks counting the same dollars twice. Deltek's Q1 2028 Costpoint end-of-life is a hard date and supports the timing
Agentic AI attach, FY2030 0 1.5% 3.0% One conference remark: "hundreds of basis points, but it's not a doubling" The only quantification is a spoken range from management that declined to size 2027 and said of 2026 "it will not be for us this year." The bear of zero is a no-upside case, not the downside Roper itself disclosed: the FY2025 10-K says AI capabilities "could quickly become commoditized" and the Q2 2026 10-Q adds that AI offerings "may negatively impact demand for our offerings"
Agentic SKU incremental EBITDA margin 20% 40% 55% Analyst judgment; nothing in the disclosure constrains it The nearest analogue inside Roper's own accounts is integrated payments, its other revenue stream with a variable third-party input cost, at a 32-42% gross margin and a 12-16% operating margin for the Procare-plus-Transact cohort. That analogue is at or below the bear, not near the base. The realized position today is cost without revenue
Application Software payments volume growth 2% 8% 14% The historical reported growth of the stream Does not survive its own evidence. Every organic observation contradicts the base: 4.1% in Q1 2026, 0.7% in Q2 2026, 2.5% for the half, with both acquired books fully in the base. The FY2025 growth of 47.7% was two acquired payments books arriving. The stated cause is implementation throughput at Procare, promised as fixable for four consecutive quarters. Evidence supports a base of 3-4%
Application Software non-recurring growth (6)% (3)% (4)% The structural licence-to-subscription substitution Holds. The reported line grew in FY2024, FY2025 and H1 2026, but that is acquired revenue arriving: the CFO's organic cut was −4% in Q2 2026 against +1.9% reported, and the mechanism is disclosed. The inverted bull is deliberate, because conversion moves revenue into the recurring line at 2-2.5x
Network Software recurring growth, FY2027 3.0% 6.5% 9.0% A freight recovery management will not yet call 6.5% exceeds every organic reading the segment has produced since FY2022 (4.6, 2.5, 4.1, then 5.0% and 3.6% in 2026), and the most recent quarter decelerated into the year the base accelerates. The DAT complex is 18-26% of the segment, so a 6.5% segment rate needs DAT to add three to four points over a remainder growing 4-5%, while MHA declined in Q2 2026
Network Software transactional growth 1% 9% 15% Analyst judgment on the Convoy and Outgo monetisation Does not survive its own evidence. Before Subsplash the transaction-priced stream compounded at roughly 2-3% a year, and MHA's administrative fees, $150-220m of it, declined in Q2 2026. Blending Subsplash giving at $40-50m growing fast with a remainder growing 2% reaches 4-5%. Everything above that depends on Convoy and Outgo pricing part of the $100-200 per-load saving, for which no take rate, attach rate or automated-load count is disclosed
Neptune units (1.0)% +0.5% +2.0% The AWWA replacement cycle applied to an installed base grown forward from 2003 The midpoint is defensible as a replacement-cycle average; the ±1.5-point band contradicts the base rate it cites, since Badger Meter's utility water revenue moved +20.3%, +12.5% and (8.8)% across the same window. Realized evidence runs below the base: Neptune declined in both 2026 quarters and management underwrote "a slight decline" for the year
Neptune content per connection 2.5% 4.5% 6.5% The 42% and 26% ultrasonic price premiums plus AMI and software attach The only realized price evidence is 0.7% a year from the Erie County contract renewal, and the bear at 2.5% is more than three times it. The ultrasonic premiums are a one-time uplift per connection converted, not an annual rate, and Badger Meter puts US AMI conversion at about 40% of connections after two decades. What supports the base is the 22-year record: roughly $200m (2003) to roughly $700m (2025) [estimate] on a flat unit base is 5.8% a year of content and price
Verathon growth, FY2027 5% 9% 13% The 2023 Investor Day's about $350m of 2022 revenue at a low-double-digit profile Every input is four years old and Verathon's revenue has never appeared in a filing. What supports it is a segment-level check that uses no Verathon disclosure: Technology Enabled Products grew 7.1% organically in both 2026 quarters while Neptune declined, so with Neptune at roughly 40% of the segment the remaining 60% has to grow about 11-12%, which brackets the base
NDI and the residual five 3% 6% 9% Boston Scientific's electrophysiology growth as the demand proxy The block is a $615-665m residual and none of its six businesses has disclosed revenue. The demand link is inferential in two unmeasured steps, since the sensor attach rate per catheter is undisclosed and the model treats it as one-for-one with procedures. The level survives on the same segment arithmetic that supports Verathon; the band is asserted
Technology Enabled Products gross margin, FY2027 55.6% 57.8% 59.0% Recovery of the bronze cost through regular-way pricing The decomposition does not reach the base. Gross margin moved 170 basis points from H1 2025 to H1 2026, of which the copper cost is 43-51 basis points, so full commodity recovery reaches about 57.4% and the base needs about 40 more from reversing part of a consumables mix management calls permanent. The last margin guide for this segment, "sort of flattish" for FY2026, was missed by 230 basis points in H1
Annual M&A deployment from FY2028 $1,500m $4,200m $5,800m Management's "$5 billion or more over the next 12 to 18 months" Against the flow of cash the base is conservative: cumulative FY2026-33 deployment of $33,596m against roughly $32,799m of cumulative free cash flow is 102%, where the prior decade ran 173%. Against the shape of the record it is not. Annual deployment ran $3,722m, $154m, $1,276m, $2,387m, $6,018m, $217m, $4,280m, $2,053m, $3,613m, $3,290m — Roper has never exceeded $4,000m in two consecutive years, and each of its three largest years was followed by a near-stop. The base has seven consecutive years between $4,000m and $5,621m with no pause
Entry EV/revenue paid 7.5x 6.5x 5.5x The realized 6.36x across FY2023-25 The realized figure mixes bolt-ons with platforms, and the platform multiple has risen: Deltek 5.2x (2016), Vertafore 9.0x (2020), Frontline 9.1x (2022), CentralReach 9.4x (2025). The four most recent average 6.9x on revenue and 19.2x on forward EBITDA, so pairing 6.5x with the 38% acquired margin implies 17.1x EBITDA, about two turns below what Roper has paid lately. The bear has been exceeded outright in four of eleven disclosed deals
Acquired asset EBITDA margin 35% 38% 40% The four disclosed deal decks Those four average 35.75%: CentralReach 42.9%, Procare 36.5%, Transact 32.3%, Subsplash 31.3%. The base is 2.25 points above the mean of its own evidence and above three of the four observations. Across all ten disclosed deals the mean is about 40%, with the first six averaging 42.8% and the last four 35.8%, so the trend is down and 35.5-36% matches the recent vintage
Acquired asset growth after close 6% 10% 14% CentralReach 20%+, Subsplash high teens, Procare mid-teens at underwriting Outcomes are mixed. The harder counter is at segment level: Application Software organic growth decelerated in every year from FY2022 to FY2025 and again in both 2026 quarters, across the period of heaviest deployment. If acquired cohorts grew at double the organic rate for two years and then joined the base, reported organic growth should have risen as each cohort crossed the twelve-month line; it declined instead
New-deal acquired-intangible amortization 3.2% 3.0% 2.8% CentralReach at 2.8% and Subsplash at 3.2% of purchase price The level is right on a whole-life average and the flat convention is not. Roper assigns 17-20 year lives to customer relationships and 5-8 to technology, so the charge is front-loaded: CentralReach's $842m of amortizable intangibles produce roughly 3.5-3.6% of price in years one to six against the 2.8% whole-life average used. Every vintage inside the projection window is in its first six years, so the flat rate understates amortization by roughly 60-80bp of price a year and flows straight into the Application Software margin expansion above
Legacy acquired-intangible amortization $833m $833m $833m The disclosed Note 5 schedule for FY2026-28 FY2026-28 are disclosed and cannot be attacked. The decay those three years imply is 5.0-5.1% and the model decays at 6% a year from FY2028, which raises GAAP operating income in every projected year. Holding bear equal to bull conceals that the post-2028 path is not disclosed and that the 5-8 year technology tranches from the 2020-2025 deals expire in a lumpy pattern
Target net leverage ceiling 2.8x 3.0x 3.3x Management's stated 3.0-3.5x band The base is the bottom of the stated band and 0.4x below where Roper operates, with the bull still short of the stated top. Moody's affirmed Baa2 at 3.0x with a 4.0x downgrade trigger, leaving about $1,945m of headroom at the June 2026 position. The ceiling matters because the model borrows to it every year: 0.25x on FY2033 EBITDA is about $1,819m of one-time capacity
Indicor proceeds $1,200m $1,700m $2,000m The two disclosed figures plus a later CFO remark The two disclosed figures conflict by $100m on each basis, and the bear takes the higher of the two after-tax numbers, so it is not the low case. The base adds about $500m for flow control, which management explicitly excluded from its capacity framework, on one CFO remark seven weeks later that conflicts with the filing by $500-600m. No scenario contains a failure to close, and the AMETEK transaction is subject to regulatory approval
Share repurchase ceiling 90% 45% 30% Analyst judgment, as a percentage of free cash flow The realized distribution is bimodal and contains none of the three values: nothing across nine consecutive 10-Ks, then $2,727m in H1 2026 against $1,005m of half-year free cash flow, 271%, funded by revolver. A percentage-of-free-cash-flow cap is a modelling device, and combined with the fixed repurchase price it becomes one of the two largest drivers of the per-share output
Gross share issuance 2.8m 1.5m 0.9m The historical 0.66m a year Does not survive its own evidence. Two regimes are observed and the base matches neither. Historical gross issuance was 0.66m a year; the forward regime is roughly four times that, with 1.389m granted in H1 2026 and the proxy's own statement that the new pool will last "approximately 4 to 5 years" implying 2.83-3.54m a year. Allowing for grants that do not all convert, the forward rate is about 2.4-2.8m, which is where the bear sits, and the bull of 0.9m is above the decade-long realized rate
Dividend per share growth 8% 10% 10% Six consecutive years inside 9.7-10.6% Holds. Declared dividends per share grew 9.7%, 10.2%, 10.4%, 10.3% and 9.8% across FY2021-25, and the November 2025 increase was 10.3%. The payout ratio has been held roughly stable at 13-15% of free cash flow. The bear of 8% has no precedent in the ten-year window
Application Software incremental EBITDA margin 38% 44% 49% Back-solved from the realized 40.2% blended rate A back-solve, not a measurement, and an unstable one: at an 80% acquired share and a 35% acquired margin the same arithmetic gives 61%, at 70% and 40% it gives 35%, and the ±5-point band does not span that. The latest quarter gives 42.5% directly, consistent with management's core Application Software margin declining 20 basis points that quarter. The stated "45%+ operating leverage" has never appeared in the reported numbers: segment EBITDA margin declined from 43.4% (FY2023) to 42.5% (FY2025)
Network Software incremental EBITDA margin 44% 50% 58% Core margin flat on 4-5% organic growth The base is well supported. The bull is the failure: it depends on the FY2020-25 whole-period incremental of 59%, which came from cutting cost against a shrinking customer base — SG&A dollars declined from $593m to $588m in FY2024 while revenue grew $36m. That mechanism cannot repeat while the segment grows
Corporate expense 3.90% 3.70% 3.52% The FY2025 ratio of 3.67% The base is already below the current run-rate of 3.78% in H1 2026. The binding defect is the interaction with the separate stock-based compensation driver, because corporate expense contains enterprise stock-based compensation: the bear pair leaves 1.10% for ex-compensation corporate general and administrative expense, which freezes it in nominal dollars for eight years, so the scenario ordering inverts on the line that actually contains discretionary cost
Capex plus capitalized software 1.50% 1.35% 1.25% The guided 1.0-1.5% and realized 1.32% Holds. Mix drift toward Application Software, which capitalizes 1.77% of its revenue against 0.6% elsewhere, moves the consolidated figure by about 6 basis points, well inside the band. Foundation-model inference cost is operating expense, so the AI build does not land here
Stock-based compensation 2.80% 2.30% 2.00% The eleven-year 1.7-2.6% band Does not survive its own evidence. The base is below the current reading of 2.10% (FY2025) and 2.57% (H1 2026), and below the direction of every disclosed input: grant volume roughly doubled in H1 2026, expense lags grants across the vesting period, and the enlarged plan pool has barely begun granting. Evidence supports at least 2.6%, with the current bear the more defensible centre
Book effective tax rate 22% 21% 20% Management's FY2026 guide and the post-2022 record of 21.5%, 21.2%, 20.6% Holds. The two outlier years in the ten-year series are explained and non-recurring, and cross-border rate risk is small at 13% non-US revenue
Cash tax rate 19.5% 18.0% 17.0% Analyst judgment on the tax-amortizable intangible step-up No cash-taxes-paid series exists, so the 300bp gap has no realized check. Sizing the shield supports the direction: nine disclosed net-present-value tax benefits total roughly $1,140m amortized over 13-15 years, on the order of $100-115m a year, five to six points of cash tax rate. The failure is the tail — FY2025 included roughly $150m of one-time Section 174 benefit "with the remainder expected to be used over three to five years," and the model holds 18% flat through FY2033
Blended interest rate by FY2032 5.40% 5.00% 4.60% The 5.14% implied market yield and the 4.76% August 2025 new issue Every sub-3% tranche matures by February 2031, so by FY2032 the legacy coupon advantage is gone and the model raises roughly $11bn of new net debt at marginal rates. The observable marginal costs today are 5.14% implied and a revolver at roughly 5.3-5.8% that is 25% of gross debt, so 5.1-5.3% is the defensible base
FY2026 adjusted EBITDA margin 38.3% 38.6% 38.9% The Q2 2026 print The base equals a single quarter's print, and a ±30bp band is about $26m on $8,543m of revenue — narrower than variance already printed inside FY2026, since Technology Enabled Products operating margin moved 90 basis points between Q1 and Q2
FY2026 interest expense, net $436m $430m $424m H1 2026 actual of $210.7m The base implies an H2 about flat with the Q2 run-rate, which is inconsistent with the model's own assumption that the Indicor proceeds pay down the revolver. A three-month slip on $1.2bn at 5.5% is about $16.5m, roughly 2.75x the entire band
Share repurchase price $388.52 $388.52 $388.52 Held flat as a roll-forward convention This is a directional assumption, not a convention. Shares are retired at a constant price in every year and every scenario, so as the projected cash flow per share rises the model retires stock at a compressing multiple of it: $388.52 is 14.8x FY2026 base free cash flow per share and 5.8x the FY2033 figure, and in the bull it reaches 3.4x FY2033 adjusted diluted EPS. That is why base free cash flow per share compounds 14.7% against 11.8% revenue growth, and why the sensitivity table shows adjusted diluted EPS rising when M&A deployment is cut. The level is defensible for FY2026-27 against a realized programme average of $358.79 and a run-date close of $388.52; holding it for eight years is not

The acquisition line is the whole CY2028 revenue gap: consensus CY2027 total growth equals its organic assumption, so it embeds zero acquired revenue, while the base deploys $4,000m in FY2027 and $4,200m in FY2028 — below the $5bn a year management guides to and below the $8,956m deployed across FY2023-25. The margin path runs the other way: consensus expands GAAP operating margin 169 basis points from CY2026 to CY2028, of which the disclosed amortization roll-off on a frozen deal book supplies about 85, while the base expands it 80 because restarting M&A adds roughly $126m a year of new amortization against $82m of roll-off. Consensus is more optimistic on margin and more pessimistic on revenue, and its two assumptions are mutually exclusive.

17.7 What the model gets wrong

Incremental operating margin runs above the historical best in six of eight years. Roper's realized incremental operating margin was 27.4% (FY2023), 29.2% (FY2024) and 27.6% (FY2025), with a ten-year best of 29.2%; the base case gives 28.2% in FY2026 and then 35.7%, 30.2%, 29.9%, 30.3%, 30.9%, 29.6% and 30.5%. Two identifiable mechanisms produce the overshoot — organic revenue supplies a larger share of the revenue increase than in the FY2023-25 cohort, roughly half against a quarter, and acquired-intangible amortization declines as a share of revenue — and the FY2027 reading of 35.7% is the worst of them, coming from a Technology Enabled Products gross-margin recovery management guides but has not delivered. FY2027 is the least reliable year in the projection.

Segment sizing inside Technology Enabled Products is estimated, not disclosed: Neptune at about $700m comes from a verbal "I think, something like 40% of the segment" that has never appeared in a filing, Verathon at about $480m is a 2022 figure compounded forward, and Northern Digital's revenue is not disclosed. The segment's three growth drivers therefore have estimated weights.

The model is annual and Roper's cash flow is heavily second-half weighted, so any comparison to a quarterly figure needs that adjustment. And nothing is modelled for the flow-control businesses still inside Indicor beyond $500m of FY2027 proceeds in the base.

18. Risks

Ranked by the product of revenue or equity at stake and the likelihood the mechanism produces a reported effect within eight quarters. Financial base: FY2025 revenue $7,903m; software recurring $4,483m (56.7%); software reoccurring $833m (10.5%); software non-recurring $814m (10.3%); product $1,773m (22.4%).

R1 — AI substitution inside the seat-priced software base. Highest severity: $4,483m of recurring revenue is priced against it.

Roper itself states all three channels. Demand: agentic software reduces the licensed-user count at customers whose headcount Roper prices against, and the Q2 2026 10-Q says AI offerings "may negatively impact demand for our offerings." Cost: Roper builds on OpenAI, Anthropic, Google and Microsoft models, and the 10-K states that its exposure to their pricing increases as AI becomes more central and that the increase may not be passable to customers. Differentiation: "AI capabilities could quickly become commoditized." Two points of gross-retention deterioration on the recurring base is about $90m of revenue, roughly 1.1 points of consolidated growth, before any net-retention offset.▪ On the cost side, software core EBITDA margin declined 10 basis points in Q2 2026 with the AI accelerator team in the base, and the CFO put headcount at "maybe the halfway point of where we think that investment is going to be... but probably much higher on spend because we've started at the more senior level." The offsetting revenue is prospective and the cost is current.

Leading indicators: organic recurring revenue growth across the software segments, 7% in both 2026 quarters and guided to "inflect higher" in H2 — the first quarter it does not is the signal. Software-segment core EBITDA margin. Application Software organic non-recurring revenue, down 4% in Q2 2026. Any move from per-seat to consumption pricing in the disclosed reoccurring line.

R2 — Balance-sheet capacity after the buyback. High, and already in the reported numbers.

$3,224m of repurchases between November 2025 and June 2026, funded largely by $2,000m of net revolver borrowing, took net debt to $10,955m and leverage to 3.4x. Revolver availability declined from about $2,644m to about $644m against a $700m note maturing 15 December 2026, and net interest expense rose to $111.4m in Q2 2026 from $79.1m a year earlier. The credit-agreement covenant is not the live constraint — the ratio is 37.8% against a 0.65 limit, so an equity write-down of roughly $12.6bn would be needed to breach it. The constraint is drawable liquidity and the timing of the Indicor proceeds.

Mitigant, from outside management: Moody's affirmed Baa2 with a positive outlook in November 2025 and published a 4.0x downgrade trigger, leaving about $1,945m of headroom at the June 2026 position, and trailing free cash flow to gross debt of 22.9% already meets the agency's stated upgrade test.

Leading indicators: the revolver balance in each 10-Q; whether the AMETEK purchase of Indicor Instrumentation closes in H2 2026 as expected, since it is subject to regulatory approval; any rating action.

R3 — Deltek and federal government contracting. High; the most-asked topic on the last nine calls.

Deltek sells to federal contractors, and enterprise expansions there are sold as perpetual licences, so a budget pause hits revenue in the year instead of over a subscription term: "it's more acute too because the GovCon Enterprise segment is mostly — if they're doing expansions or add-ons, it's mostly through perpetual licenses, so that will impact in year" (Q1 2025 call). The FY2025 10-K attributed the Application Software organic shortfall to this. Deltek is 60% federal-contractor-facing and 40% other professional services, and its revenue inside Roper is about $0.83bn to $1.07bn [estimate: about $535m of 2017 expected revenue at acquisition compounded at 5-8% for nine years], placing the federal-contractor portion at roughly 7-8% of consolidated revenue. Underneath the budget cycle is a slower structural fact: the billable firm count declined 6.9% in FY2025 and roughly 40% over the decade.

Mitigant: 40% of Deltek serves non-federal professional services. Management says it removed a point or two of Deltek organic growth from the 2025 plan.

Leading indicators: Application Software organic non-recurring revenue by quarter; enterprise software bookings on a trailing basis; appropriations passage and shutdown duration; Deltek's ground-to-cloud conversion rate, which lowers reported non-recurring revenue even when the business is winning.

R4 — Acquisitions have stopped. High, and currently active.

Growth above the 5-6% organic rate depends on redeploying free cash flow into acquisitions. Spend was $2,053m (2023), $3,613m (2024) and $3,290m (2025), and about $50m in the first half of 2026. Acquisitions contributed 3 points of the 9% total revenue growth in Q2 2026 and about 7 points of the 12.3% in FY2025, so a full year without them removes roughly 3-7 points of total revenue growth against the 2023-2025 pattern. Management targets "$5 billion or more towards acquisitions over the next 12 to 18 months" and has said deployment will favour deleveraging first, and its own timing slipped inside seven weeks from "later this year and into 2027" to "probably going to be more of a '27 time line."

Leading indicators: quarterly acquisition spend; bolt-on cadence; the gap between private and public software multiples, which management names as the binding condition.

R5 — Goodwill tested qualitatively across 25 reporting units. Medium-high on magnitude, lower on near-term probability.

Goodwill is tested at 25 reporting units against three reportable segments, with individual balances from $17.5m to $3,372m, and the FY2025 test was qualitative for every unit with no quantitative assessment performed. The filing also states that "recently acquired reporting units generally represent a higher inherent risk of impairment," and Roper deployed $8,956m across 2023-2025. At 30 June 2026 goodwill was $21,331m and other intangibles $9,347m against $35,170m of total assets and $18,700m of equity; by segment at 12/31/2025 the goodwill-to-revenue ratios are 3.6x (Application Software), 2.8x (Network Software) and 0.6x (Technology Enabled Products). Writing the largest single unit to zero would be $3,372m, about 18% of equity.

Leading indicators: the first year any unit moves to a quantitative test; a named business missing its acquisition model, as Procare already has without an impairment following.

R6 — Network Software's cyclical demand in the company's highest-margin segment. Medium-high, and the source of the last three years of misses.

The segment's businesses price against volumes Roper does not control: freight loads at DAT, construction starts at ConstructConnect, visual-effects production at Foundry, group-purchasing volume at MHA. Organic growth was 4.1% in FY2025 and 3.6% in Q2 2026, below both other segments, and segment operating margin declined to 41.0% from 43.9%. This is also the segment whose cyclicality disclosure was deleted in FY2022.

New in Q2 2026: the Montgomery broker-liability ruling described in §5.2 raises insurance and diligence costs for brokers, who are DAT's paying customers on one side of the network. Legal commentary describes it as removing brokers' preemption defence and reshaping their liability exposure; Roper's CEO described it as favourable because it emphasises carrier vetting. No financial effect has been disclosed either way.

Leading indicators: DAT carrier subscriptions, which bill monthly; spot-versus-contract freight rates; construction starts; post-production employment.

R7 — Technology Enabled Products margin. Medium; already in the reported numbers for three quarters.

Bronze ingot inflation at Neptune plus a mix shift toward lower-gross-margin consumables at Northern Digital and Verathon. Segment operating margin was 33.3% in Q2 2026 against 35.4%, gross margin 56.9% against 58.6%. On FY2025 segment revenue, a 210 basis point operating-margin loss is about $38m a year.

Peer comparison: Badger Meter's utility water sales declined 8.1% in the same quarter and 8.8% in the half on uneven AMI project pacing, and Itron's revenue declined 7.2%, so the whole North American water-metering market contracted.

Leading indicators: copper prices; Neptune order cadence and backlog; the ultrasonic-versus-mechanical meter mix; the consumables share of NDI and Verathon revenue.

R8 — Cybersecurity, third-party concentration and realized incidents. Medium, with a heavy tail.

Roper hosts customer systems on four named providers and states that "concentration with a limited number of providers increases exposure to outages and pricing changes." The Q2 2026 10-Q added the software supply chain — source-code repositories, build pipelines, code-signing, developer tools "(including AI coding tools)" — as an attack surface, with the propagation path spelled out, and added AI-powered attack methods including deepfakes, prompt injection and data poisoning. Two events are on record: Vertafore was subject to litigation over data exposure, which was dismissed, and unauthorized or inadvertent employee use of AI tools has occurred and is expected to continue. The data held spans P&C insurance agencies, hospitals, clinical and diagnostic laboratories, K-12 districts, higher-education campuses and ABA therapy clinics, the last four under FERPA or HIPAA. No exposure is sized in any filing.

Leading indicators: an 8-K under Item 1.05; the insurance sentence, which moved in FY2025 from a cost concern to adding that defect and vulnerability claims "may not be fully covered by insurance"; customer security-mandate cost commentary, now a named expense driver.

R9 — Concentrated exposure to public budgets, aggregated. Medium, and currently unquantified by anyone.

The per-vertical exposures are traced in §1 and never summed. Deltek's customers bill the federal government; Frontline's districts are funded by state aid and local property tax; Illumia's institutions depend on postsecondary enrolment and the federal-aid step-down; Neptune's utilities fund replacement from rate cases; CentralReach's clinics bill insurers and Medicaid; the hospital, laboratory and post-acute businesses serve customers billing Medicare and Medicaid. On the segment weights in §1 and §4, plausibly on the order of a third of consolidated revenue moves with tax-funded or rate-regulated budgets. That is a different risk shape from the diversification-across-uncorrelated-niches argument, because a single appropriations cycle can move four verticals in two segments at once.

R10 — AI regulation lands on two business lines by name. Medium.

The FY2025 10-K added a standalone factor naming the EU AI Act's risk classification and stating that "several states, including Colorado and California, have enacted or are considering AI-specific regulations addressing transparency, bias, and accountability, particularly in the housing and employment fields," with the consequence that Roper may have to "cease offering or using certain AI-enabled features or services in particular jurisdictions." The two named fields map onto Frontline (K-12 hiring and human resources) and the insurance-distribution businesses, where underwriting and placement decisions are the regulated act. Neither business discloses revenue.

R11 — Customer headcount is the pricing base. Medium, slow-moving, unmeasurable from disclosure.

Roper's software is priced per user at customers who are themselves professional-headcount businesses. If AI compresses those headcounts, the billable base contracts at 100% logo retention.▪ The one disclosed analogue is CentralReach, where gross retention is mid-to-high 90s at the logo level and "more of a sort of a low 90s gross retention" when therapists entering and leaving the market are counted. The practitioner is the level the seat is charged at. No seat, user or subscriber count is published for any Roper business.

Leading indicators: professional and business services payrolls; law-firm headcount; the spread between recurring revenue growth and the annual price increase.

R12 — Aderant and the billable hour. Medium; Aderant is the segment's fastest-growing business.

Aderant's product is time capture, billing and collections for large law firms, so its transaction base is hourly billing. Firm-level AI adoption rose from 26% in 2024 to 42% in 2026 and more than half of legal professionals expect AI efficiency to reduce the prevalence of the billable hour [web]. Aderant grew mid-teens in FY2025, about ten points above the segment, so it supplies a disproportionate share of Application Software's organic growth and the concentration runs both ways. Roper's position is that Aderant serves "the business of law" and that ProPricer and VPD address fixed-fee pricing, with "relatively low uptake across the industry" so far.

The correlated bad quarter

These risks are not independent. The scenario that produces the worst reported quarter combines five of them, and four are already partially in the numbers: government-contracting budget uncertainty extends and Application Software organic non-recurring revenue declines again; freight and construction volumes stall and Network Software organic growth stays near 3.6% while the Subsplash payments mix keeps diluting margin; bronze costs stay elevated and Neptune orders remain delayed, holding Technology Enabled Products margin near 33%; AI investment continues at the "much higher on spend" rate while AI revenue stays immaterial, turning software core margin negative; and the private-to-public multiple gap does not close, so no acquisitions land and leverage at 3.4x prevents the buyback substituting.

The common driver across the first, second and fifth is the cost of capital and the caution it produces in customer and sponsor budgeting. The common driver across the fourth is the pace of customer adoption, which management named as the one thing it cannot forecast: "the big X factor... is what's the rate of adoption at the customer level... until we get clearer signal on that, we have to be unfortunately vague on the magnitude of impact in the near term." The one large offset independent of all five is the Indicor instrumentation proceeds, about $1.1-1.2bn after tax, which depends on regulatory approval of a transaction between third parties.

19. Source disclosure

Filings and transcripts. Ten annual reports on Form 10-K, FY2016 through FY2025; quarterly reports on Form 10-Q for 2024-Q3 through 2026-Q2; 24 quarterly earnings releases furnished on Form 8-K, Q3 2020 through Q2 2026; proxy statements on Form DEF 14A for 2018 through 2026; the August 2025 notes-offering free writing prospectus; 43 earnings-call transcripts, Q4 2015 through Q2 2026; and 38 presentation transcripts, 2016 through 2026, including the March 2023 Analyst and Investor Day, the June 2022 CD&R special call, the December 2016 Deltek acquisition call and the September 2026 Goldman Sachs Communacopia and Citi Global TMT appearances. Fifteen investor-presentation decks, including the 125-page 2023 Investor Day and the Vertafore, Frontline and CentralReach acquisition presentations.

Peer filings. Annual and quarterly filings for Tyler Technologies, Veeva Systems, SS&C Technologies, Bentley Systems, Autodesk, Intuit, Verisk, MSCI, Moody's, S&P Global, FactSet, CoStar, Danaher, AMETEK, Fortive, Dover, IDEX, Teledyne, Badger Meter, Itron, Xylem, Mueller Water, Teleflex and Stryker, with the annual and quarterly series pulled from the SEC XBRL companyfacts API on 2026-09-11. Ambu A/S files in Denmark, so its interim reports were taken from the company's own published announcements. S&P Global Ratings issuer files on Dodge Construction Network (2022-12-15 and 2024-12-06) and Pushpay Holdings (2024-07-30) supplied the competitor financial detail in two Network Software lines.

Market data. Bloomberg terminal, pulled live on 2026-09-11: 3,192 daily observations of price, total-return index and market capitalization from 2014-01-02; 152 month-ends of forward consensus EPS, forward P/E, sales and EBITDA; 115 quarters of announcement dates with GAAP EPS, adjusted EPS and the consensus estimate; annual reported fundamentals; current BEst estimates by fiscal year through FY2029 with dispersion; and the 36-row comparable-company table.

Data built for this work. A ten-year annual financial history (1,123 line-item rows, FY2016-FY2025) and a twelve-quarter history (628 rows, FY2023Q3-FY2026Q2), both reconciled between the XBRL tags and the filing tables; the valuation history and drawdown series; the four price and multiple charts; the 36-row comparable-company table; a forty-driver operating model with three scenarios and its projection output; and a sixteen-company serial-acquirer panel used for the outside reference classes in §14, covering annual fundamentals FY2003-FY2025, acquisition and buyback cash flows FY2007-FY2025 for the thirteen SEC filers, and 1,253 quarterly reported-versus-consensus EPS observations from 1998 to 2026.

Web sources. 38 domains have a clickable citation, across 74 inline web-tagged claims. The heaviest use is regulatory and primary-source material (gao.gov, ecwa.org, iopscience.iop.org, dlapiper.com, whitecase.com), company and investor-relations pages (foundry.com, verathon.com, truckstop.com, dat.com, ambu.com, allegion.com, ir.flywire.com, newsroom.paypal-corp.com, www1.appliedsystems.com, surgicalroboticstechnology.com), trade press (fleetequipmentmag.com, beckershospitalreview.com, marketbrief.edweek.org, reinsurancene.ws, iireporter.com, inc.com, agencychecklists.com, awn.com, startupticker.ch, fed-spend.com) and market-research aggregators (mordorintelligence.com, idataresearch.com, futuremarketinsights.com, openpr.com, globenewswire.com). Aggregator market-sizing and share figures are flagged low-confidence wherever used, and third-party share reports on agency management systems and laboratory information systems were found internally inconsistent and are excluded. No web claim here is flagged as unverified: every web source cited for a material claim was reachable and its passage checked. Appendix B gives the passage for each.

Estimates. Seventy-three figures have an [estimate] tag, in six families: business-line revenue reconstruction from a disclosed anchor rolled forward or solved out of a disclosed growth identity (about 20); per-unit price or volume derived from a revenue band divided by a disclosed count or a published price (about 12); arithmetic on disclosed figures such as counterfactual share counts, interest, tax and covenant headroom (about 15); back-solves from reported cost of sales or gross margin (about 6); pro-rata allocations of items Roper does not split by segment (about 5); and market sizing from company-stated market counts (about 3), plus one bill-of-materials build for the Neptune meter. Every bound travels with its number.

Gaps and failures.

  • No sell-side research on Roper exists in the local digest: zero of 376 indexed reports mention the company. No broker model, thesis or price-target page was read, so the external expectations in §14 depend on Bloomberg BEst aggregates plus web rating aggregators, and the consensus framing pressure-tested in §8 is reconstructed from the covering analysts' own questions on three dated transcripts.
  • Analyst-level estimate dispersion for revenue, margin and EPS is not available from any local source. Bloomberg publishes consensus means, and the FY2028 high, low and standard deviation are not published. The dispersion reported in §14 is measured on price targets, which is a weaker proxy, and is labelled as such.
  • No segment-level consensus estimates exist anywhere, so the per-segment forward rows in §14 are management guidance.
  • Bloomberg publishes no consensus operating-margin or EBITDA-margin series for Roper, and no consensus for operating cash flow, repurchases, dividends, returns, net debt or leverage, which is why those rows in §13.1 stop at FY2025.
  • The year-over-year textual redline product does not cover Roper, so the risk-factor delta ledger in §18 and the AI-supplier language counts in §2 and §5 were built by direct comparison of the ten archived annual reports. The Item 1 and MD&A year-over-year deltas were not built.
  • The guidance-extraction pipeline for Roper failed on an unrelated command-line tool version error, so the guidance record in §14 was rebuilt by hand from the 24 archived earnings releases and 43 transcripts.
  • The XBRL companyfacts interface excludes dimensional facts, so every segment row was read from the 10-K and 10-Q segment notes and MD&A tables.
  • Segment data on the current three-segment basis does not exist before FY2020, and no through-cycle segment margin history covering 2008-09 or 2015-16 can be built.
  • Daloopa was built for Roper during the work but derives from the same EDGAR filings as the XBRL pull, so it is not independent corroboration and was not used to overturn any figure. Historical statement data therefore comes from two independent readings of the same filings, the XBRL tags and the filing tables, which agreed wherever both included the line.
  • No intraday price data was pulled, so the earnings-day reactions in §15 are close-to-close and a move cannot be split between the 06:55 release and the 08:00 call.

20. What we still don't know, and what would resolve it

Fourteen gaps are material enough to change a conclusion above if they were filled. The first is flagged at the top of §3 and the twelfth again in §17.3.

  1. What the corporate centre earns on the price it pays. Roper has never published a realized cash-on-cash return, an internal rate of return, a year-five EV/EBITDA or a numeric hurdle for any completed acquisition, and the 125-page Investor Day deck contains none. The 2020-2022 vintage is now at or past its year-five mark, so one such figure would settle whether the underwriting in §3.4 works. The cash-return threshold that decides which deals clear the financial screen has the same problem: its last numeric statement, "over 200%," dates from Q2 2017 on the industrial portfolio and uses a denominator that excludes the goodwill and intangibles where the capital now sits.
  2. A published return on capital excluding goodwill. Halma prints both halves of the same return every year: Adjusted ROTIC of 16.2% on a goodwill-inclusive base and Adjusted ROCE of 85.1% on a base that excludes goodwill and acquired intangibles, against a published 10.2% cost of capital [web, halma.com, accessed 2026-09-11]. The 69-point gap is the purchase price, stated annually. Roper reports the ex-goodwill side under a different name, cash return on investment, and has not quantified it since 2017, while the goodwill-inclusive counterpart has to be computed from the statements. Halma's two figures are not comparable to Roper's 6.4% without adjustment, because ROTIC is struck after tax and after finance costs on a base that excludes GBP 769m of net debt. The disclosure format is what would resolve this, not the level.
  3. Post-acquisition performance on the businesses that hold the money. The only quantified series Roper has published covers four businesses that cost under $1.9bn, about 7% of the decade's deployed capital, and excludes all ten of its largest acquisitions (§3.4). Roper reports revenue, growth and margin for no individual operating company, so what happened at Vertafore, Frontline, Deltek, Procare or Neptune is recoverable only from management commentary. Core EBITDA margin, the one same-store measure, is disclosed as a year-over-year basis-point change and never as a level, so the 35-40% band the 2026 bonus plan pays against cannot be located against where the owned base operates.
  4. The organic growth rate of the base Roper has owned for five years or more. Acquisitions contributed 6.7 to 8.1 points of total growth in FY2023-25 while acquisition spend was $27.5m in H1 2026, so the reported deceleration from 9.1% to 4.9% mixes cohort composition with same-store demand. FY2027 will be the first year in which reported organic growth is close to a pure same-store number. Would resolve it: a mature-cohort organic rate, or the per-business revenue that would allow one to be built.
  5. What Roper will pay for the next $5bn. Entry EV/EBITDA multiples are disclosed by no company in the sixteen-company panel, so the 13-18x management now expects has no computable reference distribution. The substitute in §14 is dollars deployed per dollar of acquired revenue, which is sensitive to where in the year a deal closes. Roper's own realized entry multiples are the only anchor, and the two most recent are the highest it has disclosed.
  6. Whether the guidance-beat record has a peer analogue. Peer guidance-versus-actual records exist in no local source for any company in the panel, so Roper's 23-quarter run of beating the high end of its own quarterly guide is benchmarked against a consensus-beat panel, which is the looser test. Roper's consensus-beat run is 40 quarters and its guidance-high-end run is 23; any hazard rate taken from the panel applies to the first.
  7. What a company that does all four of these things at once goes on to do. Roper has paused acquisitions, started a large buyback, raised its long-term organic target and decelerated organically, all inside twelve months. Each leg has a base rate in §14. The joint event has one loose analogue, Danaher since FY2024, which two years on has not reverted: acquisitions at zero, buybacks continuing at $3,088m, revenue growth of −0.1% then +2.9%, and GAAP operating margin down 270 basis points. One observation cannot support a probability.
  8. Whether the reoccurring payments stream is booked gross or net. Roper's revenue note describes it only as "transactional and volume-based fees facilitated through our software... recognized at a point in time under a usage-based model," which does not settle the principal-versus-agent question. If it is booked gross, both the revenue growth rate of the fastest-growing line and the gross-margin decline it explains are partly presentation, and the comparison against software peers who net their payments is not like-for-like.
  9. Business-line revenue, share and retention. Roper discloses revenue for none of its 29 businesses. DAT, Vertafore, Deltek, Neptune, Verathon and Northern Digital are each large enough to move a segment, and each is sized here within a band of ±25% or wider. Northern Digital drives the growth and the margin mix of Technology Enabled Products on management's own account and its revenue is not disclosed anywhere. MHA's realized administrative-fee rate is the largest unquantified take rate in the company. Business-level retention was published once, at the 2023 Investor Day, and never updated.
  10. Annual recurring revenue, net revenue retention and churn, at any level. Gross retention is the largest same-store driver in the model's own sensitivity table, and the only source for it is a repeated verbal phrase with no definition, no series and no segment split. No seat, user, subscriber or practitioner count is published for any business, so the AI seat-compression mechanism in §18 cannot be measured from outside.
  11. What Indicor is worth and what it earns. The last Indicor operating figures are FY2022: $916m of revenue and $234m of income from operations. Four years separate those from a $1,792m Level 3 mark. No public disclosure covers the roughly $1,775m of debt raised at closing, the 2023 sale of CCC to Honeywell for about $670m, or the flow-control businesses whose value management excluded from its capacity framework. AMETEK's own disclosure on the instrumentation purchase would put a multiple behind the $5.0bn enterprise value and check Roper's proceeds estimate independently.
  12. How these businesses behave in a recession. Deltek, Vertafore, Frontline, Procare, Illumia, CentralReach and Subsplash are more than half of revenue, and none has been observed through a broad demand shock under Roper's ownership: the one in the window is the 2020 quarter, when Roper still held the industrial businesses sold to CD&R. The FY2023-25 freight drawdown is the closest realized stress and it is confined to one segment. The scenario amplitudes in §17 and the severity ranking in §18 are therefore constructed, and no realized amplitude stands behind them.
  13. The record before FY2016. Roper's comparable financial history does not reach past FY2016, so the shareholder proponent's sixteen-year 8.3% average return on invested capital and the Board's refusal to restate it both stand on two overlapping years (§3.4). FY2018 computes to 9.3% on the as-filed basis and FY2017 to about 7.7% once its tax rate is normalised; the other fourteen years cannot be checked.
  14. What the portfolio shares. A shareholder proposal to spin the two software segments and retain Technology Enabled Products reached the 2026 ballot and drew 0.6% support. What the three segments actually share — customers, sales channel, the central AI team, the acquisition funnel, the balance sheet — is not described anywhere, and Technology Enabled Products took 4m of the last ,960m of acquisition capital while its strategic status appears in no filing.

Appendix C — External data sources

Eight external datasets are available for a company of Roper's type. None has been pulled. Each entry names what it is, what it measures and which part of the analysis it would strengthen. Mosaic sources assemble a partial picture from public mentions and are not comprehensive.

Google Trends search interest — relative search interest for a brand or product over time, and against named competitors on a common query basis. For Roper the useful queries are the business names: Deltek Costpoint, Vertafore AMS360, Aderant Expert, DAT One, Nuke, GlideScope, Neptune water meters, plus the competitor terms Unanet, Applied Epic, Truckstop, Brightwheel and Ambu aScope. It would give a demand and share-of-attention series where no unit count exists, which is §6's growth attribution and §4's share-direction question. Status: not pulled.

App and web engagement (mosaic) — daily and monthly active users, time spent, downloads and churn, assembled from public mentions. Relevant to the three businesses with a consumer-facing surface: Procare's parent app, Subsplash's church apps (management states 2.3bn app launches in 2025) and DAT One's carrier app. It would put an engagement series under the payments and network businesses whose unit counts are undisclosed, which is §1's driver tree and §3's switching-cost test. Partial mosaic, not comprehensive. Status: not pulled.

Web technology and CDN adoption share (W3Techs, BuiltWith, HTTP Archive) — the share of public or top-N websites running a vendor's product, tracked over time. Applicable to ConstructConnect's and Subsplash's web properties and to the detectable footprint of agency and church website platforms. It would give an independent adoption trend against Applied Systems and Pushpay, which is §4's share-direction question. Status: not pulled.

Developer-ecosystem adoption (package downloads, GitHub, developer surveys) — the momentum of a vendor's software development kit, command-line tooling or platform among developers. Roper's businesses publish few public packages, so coverage would be thin, but Foundry's Nuke plug-in ecosystem and NDI's tracking software development kit both have public developer surfaces. It would test §2's claim that the technology layer is not where Roper's advantage is. Status: not pulled.

Search-interest trends for the company and its products — the same instrument as the first entry applied at the parent level and across the named peer set (Constellation Software, Tyler, Veeva, SS&C, Bentley, AMETEK, Danaher). It would give a relative-attention series to set beside §6's peer growth cohort. Status: not pulled.

Hiring and headcount signals (job postings, LinkedIn, layoff notices) — open-role counts by function, the total job-posting trend, and headcount actions. This is the most directly useful source in the list for Roper: it would put a number on the AI accelerator team's ramp, which management describes only as "about 30 folks" from two in October 2025 with spend "up about 3x since January" against an undisclosed base; it would show engineering headcount by operating company against the claim of 3x to 5x agentic development productivity; and it would track sales headcount at Procare, the business management says it is fixing. It bears on §2, §8, §17's corporate-expense and stock-based-compensation drivers, and §18's cost-side AI risk. Status: not pulled.

Service reliability and outage incidents (status pages, Downdetector) — the frequency and severity of outages and their root causes over time. Roper's software businesses run mission-critical systems of record for law firms, government contractors, hospitals and school districts, and the Q2 2026 10-Q newly disclosed software-supply-chain and Shadow-AI exposure. A status-page and incident history would give the only external evidence on operational reliability, which is §3's switching-cost argument from the customer's side and §18's cybersecurity risk. Status: not pulled.

Internet traffic and app usage telemetry (Similarweb and comparable) — third-party estimates of web and app traffic and product usage. Applicable to DAT against Truckstop, ConstructConnect against Dodge Construction Network, and Subsplash against Pushpay, all three of which are two-firm markets in which neither side publishes usage. It would put a measured series under the load-posting and project-database scale claims in §4.2, which currently depend on each company's own boilerplate on incompatible bases. Partial mosaic, not comprehensive. Status: not pulled.

Evidence
